title: এসআরএফটিআই-তে হিন্দু জাগরণ মঞ্চের হামলা, শিক্ষার্থীদের শান্তিপূর্ণ প্রতিরোধ, প্রতিষ্ঠানে শুরু ছাত্র ধর্মঘট
content:
সত্যজিৎ রায় ফিল্ম অ্যান্ড টেলিভিশন ইন্সটিটিউট-এ হামলা চালাল হিন্দু জাগরণ মঞ্চ। তারা এসেই গেট ভাঙার চেষ্টা শুরু করে এবং এক নাগাড়ে পাথর, ইঁট, বোতল ইত্যাদি ছুঁড়তে শুরু করে। টানা প্রায় দু’ঘন্টা তারা একটানা এই ঘটনা ঘটিয়ে চলে।


 


সুদর্শনা চক্রবর্তীর

 প্রতিবেদন


 


সত্যজিৎ রায় ফিল্ম অ্যান্ড টেলিভিশন ইন্সটিটিউট-এ হামলা চালাল হিন্দু জাগরণ মঞ্চ। ৪ অক্টোবর, রবিবার তারা বিকেল চারটের কাছাকাছি সময়ে মিছিল করে এস আর এফ টি আই-এর  মূল গেট-এর সামনে পৌঁছায় ও সঙ্গে সঙ্গেই হিংসাত্মক কার্যকলাপ শুরু করে। টানা দু’ঘন্টা তারা গেট-এর সামনে যথেচ্ছ হিংসা সংঘটিত করে।


 


এস আর এফ টি আই-এর ছাত্র ইউনিয়ন-এর সভাপতি ব্লসম হাজারিকা এদিনের আক্রমণ বিষয়ে জানান, তাঁরা আগেই যেহেতু এই মিছিল ও জমায়েতের খবর পেয়েছিলেন ও পোস্টার ইত্যাদিও দেখেছিলেন, তাই পুলিস প্রশাসনকে চিঠি দিয়ে আগে থেকেই জানিয়ে রেখেছিলেন, তাঁদের নিরাপত্তা সুনিশ্চিত করার জন্য। প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃপক্ষ তাঁদের শান্তি বজায় রাখতে বলেছিলেন এবং ক্যাম্পাসে থাকা সব শিক্ষার্থীরাই সেই পরামর্শ মেনেই ছিলেন।


 


“আমরা সবাই গেটের ভেতরে অনেকটা দূরে দাঁড়িয়ে ছিলাম। গান গাইছিলাম। তারমধ্যেই স্লোগান শুনতে পাই যে ওরা আসচে। আমরা তখন জোট বেঁধে দাঁড়িয়ে ছিলাম গেটের থেকে অনেকটা ভেতরে। ওরা এসেই গেট ভাঙার চেষ্টা শুরু করে এবং এক নাগাড়ে পাথর, ইঁট, বোতল ইত্যাদি ছুঁড়তে শুরু করে। টানা প্রায় দু’ঘন্টা তারা একটানা এই ঘটনা ঘটিয়ে চলে। আমরা কোনো রকম উসকানিতে পা দিইনি। গেট থেকে অনেক দূরে দাঁড়িয়ে আমরা গান গেয়েছি।”

— discombobula_ted (@Rotten_shire99)

October 4, 2026


 


আক্রমণকারীদের মুখে ছিল “জয় শ্রী রাম”, ” দেশ কে গদ্দারো কো/গোলি মারো শালো কো” আর পাকিস্তান বিরোধী স্লোগান। বিপরীতে পড়ূয়ারা জয় ভীম, ইনকিলাব জিন্দাবাদ স্লোগান দিয়েছেন শান্তিপূর্ণভাবে। এক সময়ে যখন তাঁরা ‘জনগণমন’ গাইতে শুরু করেন, এমনকি তখনোও লাগাতার পাথর ছোঁড়া চালিয়ে যায় আক্রমণকারীরা। গেট-এ ঝোলানো মহাত্মা গান্ধী ও বাবাসাহেব ভীমরাও আম্বেদকর-এর ছবি ছিঁড়ে ফেলে তারা।


 


“দু’জন ছাত্র মাথায় চোট পায়, তাঁদের হাসলাতালে নিয়ে যেতে হয়েছে। তারজন্যও অনেক ক্ষণ অপেক্ষা করতে হয়েছে। ৬.৩০-র আগে তা সম্ভব হয়নি। আরো অনেকেই দুষ্কৃতিদের ছোঁড়া পাথর, বোতলে আঘাত পেয়েছেন। আহত হয়েছেন উপস্থিত থাকা অধ্যাপকদের মধ্যে এক-দু’জনাও,” জানালেন ব্লসম।


 


প্রথমে ৫০-৬০ জন মিছিলকারী থাকলেও, পরে সেই সংখ্যা বেড়ে আনুমানিক ২০০ জন মতো হয়। গাড়ি নিয়ে এসে তার উপরে উঠে স্লোগান দেওয়া ও হামলা চালাতে থাকে তারা। গেটের সামনের দিকে ১৫-২০ জন পুলিসকে দেখতে পেয়েছিলেন ভেতরে থাকা পড়ুয়ারা। আগে থেকে চিঠি দেওয়া সত্ত্বেও কোনো রকম বাড়তি নিরাপত্তার ব্যবস্থা ছিল না। মূল গেট-এর সামনে জমায়েত ও হামলা আটকাতে কোনো ব্যারিকেড-ও করা হয়নি। দুষ্কৃতিদের একজন গেট টপকে ভেতরে ঢুকেও পড়েছিলেন, যদিও তিনি তারপর একইভাবে বেরিয়েও যান।


 


সন্ধ্যা ৬’টার পর, প্রায় ৬.৩০টার কাছাকাছি পুলিস কিছুটা সক্রিয় হয়ে আক্রমণকারীদের সরাতে শুরু করে ও তারা ধীরে ধীরে চলে যায়। এরপর পড়ুয়ারা উপাচার্যকে ঘেরাও করেন ও আলোচনার পর একটি দাবিপত্র দিয়ে ঘেরাও তুলে নেন।


 


যে দাবিগুলি তাঁরা রেখেছেন:-


 


১) ৪ অক্টোবর ২০২৬ যে ঘটনা ঘটেছে উপাচার্য ও রেজিস্ট্রারকে তার দায়স্বীকার করতে হবে


২) এস আর এফ টি আই-এর শিক্ষার্থীদের সঙ্গে যে হিংসাত্মক ঘটনা ঘটেছে তারজন্য ক্ষমা চাইতে হবে


৩) এই প্রতিষ্ঠানকে অতি দ্রুত সেই সংগঠনের নামে এফ আই আর করতে হবে, যারা এদিনের মিছিল ও পড়ুয়াদের উপর আক্রমণ সংঘটিত করেছে


৪) পুলিসের নির্দিষ্ট কর্তৃপক্ষকে দ্রুত চার্জশিট দায়ের করতে বলতে হবে


৫) অখিল ভারত জাগরণ পঞ্চায়েত ও হিন্দু জাগরণ মঞ্চের আক্রমণের নিন্দা জানিয়ে সাংবাদিক সম্মেলন করতে হবে


৬) উপাচার্য, রেজিস্ট্রার ও অ্যাডমিনিস্ট্রেটিভ অফিসার-এর ইস্তফা।


 


দাবিপূরণ না হওয়া পর্যন্ত তাঁরা প্রতিষ্ঠানের শিক্ষাচর্চা বন্ধ ও ধর্মঘট শুরু করলেন বলে উপাচার্যকে জানিয়েছেন।

author: Emily Lassam
title: French high school students on the march
content:
“I like this kinda thing because it’s revolutionary”, a 16-year-old high school student told me as we stood out the front of her school in Nice at 7am on the last Wednesday in September. As we talked, students started arriving from across the city to join the blockade of the school, the Lycée Parc Imperial, the largest in the area.

Hundreds of students trickled in, and suddenly it was hard to tell where the sea of high schoolers started and ended. Some carried things to help build the barricades to stop anyone from entering the school.

I asked the 16-year-old if she knew all the students or whether they were from other schools. She pointed out a group of high schoolers who must have travelled from another school and said: “I don’t know them, but we are all comrades”.

This wasn’t the first blockade she had been part of at this school, but she said it was different to previous blockades. This time, it isn’t just one school but more than 1,000 being blockaded.

Videos and photos of French students holding Palestinian and Algerian flags, calling for revolution, chanting against the far-right National Rally and fighting against intense repression are sweeping social media.

This comes at a moment when a growing wave of student protests and revolts is sweeping across the world. Last year, there were the Gen Z revolts that were led by students and swept across Nepal, Indonesia, Madagascar and a whole series of countries in the Global South.

In July, hundreds of thousands of students in India joined huge protests and forced the education minister to resign. At the end of August, tens of thousands of students in Germany struck from school to protest the introduction of forced military conscription. Across Chile in early October, thousands of students and teachers took to the streets to protest possible education cuts. And in Australia, high schoolers have been at the forefront of the fight against Pauline Hanson, organising two successful school walkouts in opposition to her.  

French students are protesting the terrible conditions in their schools, for both students and teachers. Schools are forced to deal with inadequate funding, large class sizes, decrepit facilities and low staff pay and morale. To make matters worse, further cuts are planned in the upcoming national budget. And it’s not just schools facing cuts.

President Emmanuel Macron has announced the budget will include £54 billion in cuts and a fourth wage freeze for the public sector. On 29 September, thousands of public sector workers went on strike in anticipation of these cuts, with many strikers visiting high schools to show their solidarity with students. Teachers are also planning to strike on 6 October.

Students at Parc Imperial said their school was far from the worst, but even here the conditions are terrible. Class sizes often exceed 35 students, and the classrooms meant to accommodate them are too small and have limited, if any, heating and cooling. Temperatures can reach 40 degrees inside in summer and are freezing in winter. During the day, they said, students often do nothing for long periods because there aren’t relief teachers to cover absent teachers, often because the conditions are so bad. Students are also angry about the competitive Parcoursup system that pits them against each other to get into university.

While students and teachers struggle to manage in these conditions, the head of Parc Imperial lives on campus in luxury with his own gym and “wine cave”. Bad as this is, the main enemy, the high schoolers said, is the government. Macron puts billions into the military and police but refuses to adequately fund schools.

The cops’ crackdown on the high schoolers has been severe. The 16-year-old Imperial Parc student showed me the gauze, disinfectant and cream she had brought in her bag in case any students were injured. She hadn’t expected to use it, but ended up caring for a number of people whom the cops had tear-gassed and injured. She said she had been “naive to think the police would do nothing because we are minors. I am 16, most people are 17, 15, 14 we are very very young”. Across the country, police have injured hundreds and arrested thousands of high schoolers.

One of the first schools to start the blockade movement was Paul Éluard in Saint Denis (north of Paris). Saint Denis is a poor and migrant area that has been particularly neglected by the Macron government. Students report that the food there is inedible, rats and …

author: Jim McIlroy
title: Snap protest demands Labor pressure US to stop its war on Cuba, Venezuela
content:
The Australia-Cuba Friendship Society (ACFS) and the Australia-Venezuela Solidarity Network (AVSN) called a snap rally on October 3 to demand the United States stop threatening and blockading Cuba, Venezuela and Latin America.

It was part of an international day, called by the US United National Anti-War Coalition, to defend the sovereignty of Latin America, particularly Cuba and Venezuela.

US peace organisation CODEPINK said on September 30 that it had information that the US Army Reserve was preparing to invade Cuba, in three to four months’ time. The US Southern Command is allegedly massing military police, engineers, medical units, battlefield surgical capacity and major logistics forces.

The rally demanded that the federal Labor federal government call on the US government to stop its invasion plans of Cuba and lift the 60-year blockade, and end the 10-year blockade on Venezuela.

It also called for Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and Cilia Flores’s release from the notorious US Federal Prison in Brooklyn, where they have imprisoned for eight months on trumped-up charges of drug trafficking.

Coral Wynter, from AVSN and Socialist Alliance (SA), told the rally: “All of Latin America is now under threat from a resurgence of the 19th century Monroe doctrine, with fascist-leaning, US-dominated puppet governments agreeing to US military bases and foreign interference.

“The US commits silent genocides on the people of Latin America with its illegal sanctions. We cannot let this happen. We cannot remain silent in the face of imperialist aggression. History is written by people who rise up and fight for justice,” Wynter said.

Other speakers included Patrick Newbold from ACFS and Red Spark, and myself from AVSN and SA.

Australia Venezuela Solidarity Network (AVSN)

Australia Cuba Friendship Society

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Cormac Mills Ritchard
title: Demolishing the idea of public housing
content:
The United Nations’ special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, usually deals with slum demolitions in third-world countries. Last month, he took aim at the Victorian Labor government, claiming its demolition of Melbourne’s 44 public housing towers and the “forced evictions and mass displacement of approximately 10,000 residents” could be a violation of their

human rights

. This follows a Victorian parliamentary inquiry in December, which called for an

immediate pause

 to the demolitions, and a class action against the demolitions filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal (IMCL), which has been granted special leave to

appeal

 to the High Court on 7 October.

Despite growing challenges, Premier Ben Carroll is ploughing ahead with the demolition of Melbourne’s public housing towers. Of course, Labor doesn’t characterise what it’s doing as “eviction” and “demolition”, but “renewal” and “redevelopment”, which it claims will increase the number of residents on the estates from 10,000 to 30,000, and replace towers that have “reached the end of their useful life”. There is no truth to this.

If Labor’s multi-billion-dollar project is aimed at addressing the waiting list for social housing, it’s missing a couple of zeros. Only 11,000 of the new residents will be in social housing, an increase of just 1,000. As of June this year, there were 58,021 people on the Victorian Housing Register’s

growing waiting list

, of which 33,253 have been assessed as “priority”—mostly those who are currently homeless or experiencing family violence. The redevelopments will mean that just 1,000 more people will have places in social housing ... by 2051.

The redevelopment won’t help others affected by the housing crisis, either. The other 19,000 residents of the new mixed-tenure developments will live in a combination of build-to-rent, a model that the

 Age

 has found to be between 20 and 70 percent

more expensive

 than the market rate, and “affordable housing”, which is not that affordable and does not provide long-term security, as exposed by a recent

Four Corners


investigation

. 

The North Richmond public housing precinct is a telling example. In September, the state government briefed the City of Yarra on its plans for the tower at 139 Highett Street. The

Age

 reported last month that the tower, which currently has 220 public housing units, will be replaced with a development that has

only 150 social housing units

 and 650 build-to-rent units.

Simon is a former resident who grew up in the North Richmond precinct after his parents emigrated from Vietnam. After the latest announcement about the precinct, he attended a community meeting of public housing tenants who demand the towers be refurbished rather than demolished. He told

Red Flag

 that his parents, a labourer and kindergarten worker, were both poorly paid. Living in the public housing tower allowed them to escape the anarchy of the private rental market. “We knew what the rent was next week and didn’t have to worry about eviction or not being able to afford food. I could attend school and university without many issues. That security meant you could plan your life”, he said.

“Social housing” is an umbrella term that covers both public housing, run by the government, and community housing, run by not-for-profits. When Labor talks about social housing, it usually means community housing—so its claim to be replacing 10,000 public housing places with 11,000 social ones actually represents a huge cut in public housing.

Public housing rent is capped at 25 percent of a household’s income or the market rate, whichever is lower, while community housing providers can charge up to 30 percent. However, community housing organisations (CHOs) are entitled to 100 percent of any tenant’s Commonwealth Rent Assistance and can charge extra fees on top. In its

submission to the inquiry

, IMCL notes that some of its clients pay up to 50 percent of their income to a CHO through “rent, utilities, lift fees, concierge and management fees”. Community housing residents also have fewer rights than public housing residents; West Heidelberg Community Legal found that “long-term community housing tenants were 3 to 5 times more likely to face eviction than public housing tenants”.

Worse still, unlike the government, CHOs don’t have to allocate places based on need, which means that the more the social housing waiting list is serviced by community rather than public housing …

author: Sarah Glynn
title: French lessons on authoritarianism and solidarity: The lycée student blockades
content:
For French lycée (high school) students, this week has been an important step in their education. You can study books about the role of the state and of the forces of law and order, of political deception and media bias, and of organisation and solidarity; but that is not the same as practical experience.

This week they learnt the meaning of authoritarianism, and that the official values of the French Republic — liberté, égalité, fraternité (liberty, equality, fraternity) — have to be fought for again and again. They have also provided a lesson in solidarity for us all.

As in other countries that have undergone years of neoliberal austerity, French schools suffer from chronic underfunding. This affects everything from teacher shortages to building maintenance, and is especially bad in poorer areas. The students have had enough of this undermining of their futures and are on strike.

They are protesting the lack of crucial teachers and other staff, large class sizes, overloaded timetables, badly maintained buildings, and the discriminatory system for allocating university places.

Their main form of action has been blockades of their lycées, supplemented by spontaneous marches and supported by general assemblies.

President Emmanuel Macron’s government is responding to discontent the way it always does — with violent suppression. Instead of listening to the students and acting on their concerns, they have sent in the police — riot cops armed with tear gas against teenagers demanding a better education.

Protests first erupted on September 21 at the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, in the south-eastern suburbs of Paris, which was short of several teachers. By the end of the week, actions had spread to around 60 lycées throughout the Île de France (the Parisien basin).

The action was taken up in lycées in other parts of France, on September 28 and the following day, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne (students’ union) called for blockades everywhere. Lycée students marched with striking public sector workers. Police arrested 440 students.

Blockades and other actions continued on September 30, and students from more privileged schools came out in support of the students and the principle of equality.

The Lycée students were joined by students at a number of universities, on October 1. The Union Étudiante (University students’ union) claimed they closed 640 lycées and around 30 university campuses. Their statement read: “These blockades are an expression of young people’s anger at the contempt they face. Over nearly 10 years of anti-social and discriminatory policies, Emmanuel Macron and his successive governments have eroded our living and learning conditions.”

About 2000 people were arrested on October 1. Actions continued the following day.

Representatives of the Lycée students finally met with the Minister of Education after 10 days of protests, but reported that they had not received a “concrete announcement”. More actions are planned for October 5 and preparations are underway for major protests on October 6, supported by the trade unions.

The streets were turned into a battleground as police fired off rounds of teargas and dragged thousands of teenagers into custody, using the sortof violence that we are sadly becoming accustomed to.

A 14-year-old suffered a broken jaw and missing teeth after being hit with a teargas cylinder at point blank range. Another teenager lost an eye. A newly-emerged video shows a police officer holding a youth in water, as if to drown him.

The government could not have chosen a better way to ensure that the protests spread. The Union Étudiante said: “They think they’re putting an end to the movement, but all they’re doing is fuelling it.”

Protesters in France, including lycée students, readily take to the streets, but this time the response has exceeded expectations — in both size and determination – boosted by the aggressive behaviour of a police force that is clearly enjoying its license to terrorise.

Teachers have been supportive of the students’ demands, and also of the students themselves and their right to protest and not suffer police attacks. Trade unionists and elected representatives have tried to give the students an element of protection. And popular support is evident in the reactions of passers-by and of people watching the protests from neighbouring flats and cafés.

However, not everyone is happy to support the protests, and much of the media — which is largely owned …

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: Germany’s far right surges
content:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in several state elections across Germany in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, the party won a frightening 44 percent of the vote and fell just three seats short of forming government. Two weeks later, it won 38 percent in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, doubling its vote share from the previous election. Even in liberal, multicultural Berlin, the AfD vote went from 9 percent to 16 percent.

The results have sent political shockwaves across not just across Germany but the whole of Europe. It is no wonder why. The AfD is on the extreme wing of the broader far-right surge worldwide. Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic opposition to Chancellor Angela Merkel’s bailouts of the Greek government, the party has moved radically to the right over the last decade.

Today, the AfD calls for mass deportations and a strict blood-based concept of German citizenship, while opposing the right to political asylum. It also campaigns for separate schools for the children of migrants. The party also argues that focusing on the crimes of the Nazi period encourages national humiliation and therefore opposes Holocaust memorials. In 2023, AfD leaders attended a secret meeting in Potsdam with wealthy donors and prominent neo-Nazis to develop a plan to expel from the country millions of migrants and refugees and hundreds of thousands of German citizens of non-German background.

The AfD is riddled with veteran neo-Nazis. While the party initially placed barriers on fascists joining, these have been loosened as the AfD has moved further right. Björn Höcke, leader of the AfD in the eastern state of Thuringia, has been a key figure driving this shift. Prior to his public rise with the AfD, Höcke wrote articles under the pseudonym “Landolf Ladig” for neo-Nazi publications, praising Hitler and the Nazi regime. 

At campaign speeches, Höcke has repeatedly used the slogan “everything for Germany”, which was the official motto of the Nazi paramilitary wing (the

Sturmabteilung

, known as the Brownshirts or Storm Troopers). In an infamous 2017 speech in Dresden, Höcke sparked outrage by calling the Holocaust Memorial in Berlin a “memorial of shame”. The AfD branches in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern are closely associated with Höcke’s faction in the party.

A 2024 investigative report by Bavarian Radio found that AfD parliamentarians employ more than 100 individuals with ties to far-right extremist organisations. Numerous former activists and staff from the National Democratic Party—an openly neo-Nazi party since renamed The Homeland—are employed as strategy writers, social media managers and advisors. The AfD’s youth wing is effectively controlled by Nazis.

The AfD is so extreme that other European far-right leaders like France’s Marine Le Pen, Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Britain’s Nigel Farage have broken ties with the party, expelling it from their European Parliament coalition. However, the Trump administration and Elon Musk in the US and the Putin regime in Russia are all friendly with the AfD.

While the AfD has been gaining ground for some years, the latest results are a significant step forward and confirm that, despite the ebb in support for some figures like Trump, the fascist right has firmly entrenched itself as a permanent feature of contemporary capitalist politics across the globe.

That the AfD is so extreme only reinforces the seriousness of the situation. It also raises the question of why people in Germany, after the experiences of the Nazi period, would support such a filthy, bigoted party.

The primary driver behind the AfD’s rise has been the collapsing social base of the traditional parties in the German government. In a story repeated across the world, decades of support for neoliberal economics and centrist politics by the centre-right and centre-left have alienated millions of people from the establishment parties. The shift to the right in mainstream German politics in recent years has created plenty of kindling for the AfD fire to burn.

After all, it was not the AfD that invented the demonisation of Muslims and Arabs in Germany. Both the centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) have stoked racism for years, promoting harsher border control regulations and punishing refugees and migrants in the process. A key turning point came when Angela Merkel surprisingly allowed more than 1 million Syrian refugees into Germany in 2015. In …

author: Igor Ojeda
title: Brazil’s elections and environmental policy: A choice between continuity and dismantling
content:
Never before in the history of this country has the climate crisis been as relevant to a presidential election as it, very likely, will be in the 2026 vote. Once again deeply polarised, this year’s electoral contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party and Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party is taking place against a decisive climatic and geopolitical backdrop.

Less than a year ago, in November 2025, Brazil hosted the United Nations’ annual climate summit, COP, that restored the country’s status as a key player in the global climate debate. This was a particularly important development given that Brazil currently ranks among the top five contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, primarily due to agriculture, cattle ranching and deforestation.

Four years after the last Brazilian presidential election, in which Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin, the effects of the climate crisis have intensified. As scientists and environmental, social and civil society organisations have been warning for years, the planet is increasingly suffering the severe consequences of this reality, with a rise in the frequency and intensity of extreme natural events, in addition to the increase in average global temperatures. In Brazil, the historic drought in the Amazon in 2023 and the unprecedented floods in Rio Grande do Sul in 2024 were just a few examples.

The arrival of the El Niño weather phenomenon, forecast to last until early 2027 and once again cause severe droughts and above-average rainfall, alongside rising food prices, contributes to the growing importance of the climate debate in the electoral landscape.

In the geopolitical arena, the Brazilian presidential election will serve as yet another stage for the struggle for global hegemony between the United States and China — a contest currently focused largely on the race to control reserves of so-called critical minerals and rare earth elements. Beyond their strategic value for a clean energy transition, these resources are essential inputs for the defence industry.

“The election will reflect this struggle for hegemony,” says geographer Bruno Malheiro, a professor at the Federal University of Pará (UFPA).

“One side, Flávio Bolsonaro’s, will be clearly structured around a policy of alliance and total alignment with the United States over critical minerals and rare earth elements,” Malheiro says. “On the other side, President Lula’s, we see a more open, multifaceted diplomatic policy, yet one clearly tethered to China in terms of economic strategy.”

An analysis of both candidates’ platforms, as well as their speeches, stances and track records, including Lula’s third term and Jair Bolsonaro’s administrations alongside Flávio’s tenure in the Senate, reveals two different paths. While the incumbent president signals a continuation of policies, with equally significant advances and limitations, his rival envisions a return to his father’s administration, grounded in the dismantling of environmental policies and a disregard for the climate agenda.

Political scientist Maureen Santos is a climate justice activist and international relations professor. In terms of the Paris Agreement negotiations, she believes that the fight against deforestation and illegal mining, and other issues, President Lula’s platform for the 2026 elections “doesn’t change much” compared to the proposals from the previous election or his current administration’s policies.

“However, it seems to me there is an attempt to forge a stronger connection with other areas of the government,” she notes.

To her, however, the platform does introduce some new elements. In particular, Lula places greater emphasis on policies concerning critical minerals and rare earth elements. Yet, Santos criticises the lack of measures ensuring greater state control over the exploitation of these resources.

“Rhetoric about sovereignty obviously matters, but how can Brazil exercise sovereignty, for instance, given the new environmental licensing law, which relaxes licensing requirements, or the absence of a state-owned company for this sector?” she warns. “It is very difficult to envision sovereignty if the country continues to merely sell commodities.”

According to Santos, although Lula’s platform mentions technology transfer, processing and value addition, there are doubts about whether this will actually materialise, given the negotiations the government has been conducting on this …

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: Student Union independence under threat at Sydney University
content:
The University of Sydney has announced its intention to intervene in the student union and potentially undermine democratic elections.

The announcement follows a controversy, concocted by the right-wing Murdoch media, about an election ticket contesting this year’s Students’ Representative Council election. The ticket, called Globalise the Intifada, drew hysterical condemnation from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, federal Education Minister Jason Clare and a spokesperson for NSW Premier Chris Minns. Albanese told Sydney’s

Daily Telegraph

 the slogan “is an absolute outrage that has no place in Australia”. 

Vice-chancellor Mark Scott and chancellor David Thodey joined the chorus of condemnation.

In a statement released on 29 September

, they said: “We deplore the manipulation of the recent election campaign to spread hurtful and distressing language across campus”. 

The university also said it will commission an independent review of the SRC’s “current affiliation and funding arrangements ... to ensure compliance with legal, regulatory, and psychosocial safety requirements”. The review will also focus on student and staff codes of conduct and on campus security. 

Behind closed doors, Scott and Thodey floated even more drastic measures. A source present at last week’s University Senate meeting

told

Honi Soit

, the student newspaper, that Scott raised the possibility of the university taking control of student elections and conducting them online. A university spokesperson refused to answer

Honi Soit

’s questions about the discussions. 

The university’s investigation rests on the spurious claim that phrases in support of Palestine, such as “globalise the intifada” and “from the XXXX to the sea”, threaten the safety of Jewish people. 

In Arabic, “intifada” simply means “shaking off” or “uprising”. It commonly refers to the First and Second Intifadas, mass movements of Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank against Israeli apartheid and settler-colonialism. The phrase denotes the steadfast resistance of the Palestinians to decades of ethnic cleansing and apartheid. 

Governments, corporate media and university managers spend huge amounts of time and energy painting these phrases as calls to violence. Meanwhile, they turn a blind eye to the very real violence that Israel is committing in Gaza and the West Bank. New satellite imagery of the city of Rafah in Gaza illustrates the scale of Israel’s assault. Before 2023, the city looked like any other: houses, public squares, parks. Today, the city is a wasteland, all the buildings reduced to rubble. 

Our government and our universities are complicit in this violence. Many universities maintain research partnerships with weapons companies that sell arms to Israel and conduct exchange programs with Israeli universities. Yet we are expected to believe that student activists campaigning against racism and genocide are the violent actors!

These attacks on student political organising don’t come from nowhere. This confected crisis is taking place in the context of the sham royal commission into antisemitism. Vice-chancellors grovelled before the commissioner as they were grilled about why they allowed Palestine solidarity protests on their campuses. The conflation of anti-Zionism with antisemitism has been a constant of the entire affair. 

Universities are under significant pressure from both the government and pro-Israel organisations to clamp down on free speech and solidarity activism on campus. This aligns with their own self-interest in squashing mounting criticism of their complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and their desire to attract funding from arms companies and the broader corporate sector, which by and large supports Western imperialism and Israel. 

Widespread hostility to university ties to Israel among students and staff has been on display recently at Sydney University. The controversy around the ticket has distracted from the fact that the election also included a referendum on the administration’s complicity in Israel’s genocide. More than 4,000 students voted, and an overwhelming 92 percent of students voted in favour of breaking the university’s ties with arms companies and Israeli institutions.

Anyone who supports Palestine, who supports student unionism or who supports freedom of speech must speak out against Sydney University’s recent decision.

author: Paul Gregoire
title: NSW extends youth bail crackdown, despite reduction in youth crime
content:
The Chris Minns Labor government wants to extend its 2024 youth bail crackdown in regional New South Wales, saying on September 15 it will remove the sunset clause to a law targeting 14- to 17-year-olds who have been charged with a serious motor theft or break and enter crimes and are on conditional release.

NSW Labor announced its “crack down” on young people in 2024 as Victoria, the Northern Territory and Queensland were rolling out similar laws.

The Justice Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous) Bill (No 2) 2026, introduced on September 15, includes an amendment to section 22C of the Bail Act 2013 (NSW) which removes the October 1 sunset clause. It will be extended until April 4, 2028.

The Aboriginal Legal Service NSW/ACT (ALS) criticised the move as discriminatory as it targets First Nations youth and “will only entrench them in a cycle of crime and disadvantage”.

After less than year in operation, the ALS confirmed that more than 80% of alleged youth offenders had been refused bail with 90% of them being Aboriginal.

However, a federal parliament inquiry, Australia’s Youth Justice and Incarceration System, challenged the notion that there even is a youth crime crisis. “Evidence revealed that as the detention of children often leads to higher rates of re-offending, a punitive approach to youth justice undermines rather than contributes to community safety,” it said as part of its recommendations.

Labor said that it had always wanted to extend the law until 2028. It said that it “requires a judge to have a high degree of confidence the accused will not offend while on bail”, prior to granting it.

Section 22C also stipulates that “to avoid doubt, the requirement under this section to establish that bail should be refused” is up to the prosecution.

A statutory review of the law, tabled the same day, recommended extending the section 22C law despite youth crime rates having stabilised in regional NSW. The report also noted that the commission of the specific crimes has dropped as well.

The review recommended extending the law to accompany “a voluntary diversion pilot in Tamworth”. The pilot is set to be rolled out on Gomeroi Country in early 2027, with $8.4 million budgeted over 2026–27.

This will comprise of a “wraparound support to children between the ages of eight and 13 with complex needs who are engaged in, or at risk of engaging in concerning or high-risk behaviour”.

A second pilot program is due to be announced shortly.

When the section 22C law was unveiled in early 2024, it was accompanied by a $26.2 million youth justice “early intervention and prevention program” for Moree, also on Gomeroi Country.

NSW Police has been testing drone surveillance policing in the same town and recently announced it was extending the six-month trial for another two years. Tamworth might be the next town to be subjected to police harassment from the sky.

The final report on Australia’s Youth Justice and Incarceration System was released on September 18. The committee heard that while mainstream media outlets have pushed the youth crime “crisis” narrative, there has been a 5% decrease in crime over the previous year. This is in line with a general decrease in youth crime across Australia over the past 15 years.

The committee recommended that the Attorney General (AG) work with state and territory governments to establish national youth justice minimum standards.

It recommended that authorities collaborate with the AG on how the youth prison system should be reformed.

The committee suggested a minimum age of criminal responsibility of 14 years old, that detention or imprisonment of a child be a measure of last resort, and that the use of spit hoods, solitary confinement and the detention of youths in adult prisons are prohibited.

Further recommendations are: Access to health, education and other supports; systems that promote continued connection with community; culture while in detention and that youth justice officers receive adequate training.

The report recommends the OPCAT system, a UN-based preventive prison inspection regime that uphold human rights.

Australia moved to implement the OPCAT in the wake of 2016 Don Dale child prison abuse revelations. However, it then ran OPCAT inspectors out of the country.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has repeatedly rejected independent Senator Lidia Thorpe’s suggestion that Labor establish minimum prison standards for children. He insists the federal government has …

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: On the campaign trail with Victorian Socialists
content:
“We need Jasmine in parliament!”, called out Abdul. He runs Konjo, an Ethiopian cafe in Footscray. He’d just let us use the cafe as a backdrop for a promotional video we were making for the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign. I’m running as the party’s candidate for the Western Metropolitan upper house region, and the cafe is adorned with a huge picture of Jasmine Duff, our candidate for Footscray. It is one of hundreds of campaign signs on front fences and on stakes in people’s front yards across the electorate. 

Since the last federal election, it feels like support for Victorian Socialists has grown. Back then, Jasmine was the candidate for the federal seat of Fraser—encompassing Footscray and suburbs to the west and south, including Yarraville, Sunshine and St Albans. At the booth I staffed, and have done for the last few election cycles, she received more than 20 percent of the vote. In Seddon, the booth at the scout hall recorded 18 percent for Jasmine. 

Near that scout hall, I recently met a woman who had always voted Green. She told me she had volunteered with Sea Shepherd in her youth and cared deeply about the environment, as well as sexism in our society. We talked about how society is getting worse. We talked about the fear of heading into an El Niño at the same time as the government has just fast-tracked the development of the NextDC hyperscale data centre up the road, which stores millions of litres of fuel and can act as a heat pump, warming the surrounding area by several degrees. I ended the conversation with an iced tea to quell the coughing fit I’d gotten from the surrounding plane trees. She was excited to talk to me, and ready to vote socialist for the first time. 

Conversations like this are happening not just in Footscray but across Melbourne’s west. In Braybrook, I knocked on Helena’s door. Her front yard was an oasis compared to the dry and hot suburban street. I spied orchids, ferns and other luscious plants. When I said that politics was rigged for the rich, Helena replied: “It always has been. The rich get richer and the poor get poorer”. Helena is a Maltese woman in her 70s. She arrived in Australia in the 1970s, and spoke about the trials of being a working-class migrant. She asked how she could help us. Later that week Van, the VS candidate for Laverton, went back and put a campaign sign on her front fence. 

In Sunshine West, I met a young Bangladeshi student, Julfiqar. He can’t vote because he isn’t a citizen. This is a common interaction and always feels unjust. People live and work here but are denied a basic democratic right. We chatted anyway, because he has a keen interest in politics and wanted to know what we stand for. He’s a student at Swinburne University and has interacted with the socialist club there. We talked about the campaign my comrades were involved in there to stop the university from interfering in who would be the imam for Friday prayers. The university had intervened because the imam spoke about Palestine—a step too far, apparently. Julfiqar was also passionate about the student protests in Bangladesh in 2024 that ended the sixteen-year rule of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. At the end of the conversation, despite not being able to vote for us, Julfiqar wanted to help. He agreed to put up Van’s sign on his front fence. 

In Altona, part of the Williamstown electorate, I spoke to a woman who works at Victoria University. She expressed horror at the rise of Pauline Hanson and One Nation. When I explained that our candidate, Oskar Martin, also worked at VU in the Aboriginal Archives with Gary Foley, her face lit up. It isn’t often that you get an opportunity to vote for a young Aboriginal man who wouldn’t be afraid to stand up to Hanson, and he’s also your workmate. We talked about racism, but also the way that people are just struggling to get by. The cost of everything has gone up, as have billionaires’ profits. The only thing that seems to be going backwards is our wages. 

A sense of struggling just to get by is the common denominator in most of our campaigners’ conversations. Even those who feel a bit more secure or better off are worried about those around them. 

In Seddon, I spoke to a couple, Jasmine and Tom, who said they had been discussing the Victorian Socialists’ campaign with their friends the night before. We’re impossible to ignore, as we have hundreds of signs up in the area. Among many topics, one we kept coming back to was the …

author: Freya Hedley
title: One Nation doesn’t offer young or trans people a future
content:
The public’s distrust of the two parties, and the system in general, has become more pronounced over the last five years. Neither Labor or the Coalition have done anything to allay people’s fears, instead adopting some of One Nation’s (ON) policies.

Working class people’s lives have gotten harder, because wages have stagnated and the prices of basic goods and housing have continue to rise. People’s shopping baskets are lighter, but costing more.

Most young people have only experienced low wages and the loss of services.

People are scared, but also pissed off. This mood was palpable during COVID-19, but it never really went away after the pandemic restrictions lifted.

We are scared for our futures in a chaotic world, where governments wage continuous wars, and the climate emergency is getting worse.

The institutions people once believed in have betrayed them.

When people are in a state of constant anxiety, they look for the easiest answer.

That’s a factor in why ON won the by-election of the historically safe Labor seat of Secret Harbour in Western Australia.

But while ON likes to portray itself as a “protest” party — against the two major parties — its policies are just as pro-capitalist. Billionaire Gina Rinehart’s donation of a $2 million plane to Pauline Hanson and the Murdoch media’s adoration of ON makes that pretty clear.

Voting ON would be like shooting ourselves in the foot. This is because Hanson is opposed to wage rises above the rate of inflation; ON opposed the Fair Work Commission’s June decision to raise the minimum wage by 5.97%. The party will never support workers and less so unemployed workers or anyone on welfare.

Hanson subscribes to former Coalition Prime Minister Scott Morrison’s view that Australians deserve “a fair go for those who have a go”. It suggests that fairness only applies to the “deserving”.

ON has welcomed the NDIS cuts, even though they will destroy the lives of thousands. It believes that “people taking advantage of the [NDIS] system” and said “bogus therapies” must be discontinued.

ON wants Australia to withdraw from the United Nations Paris Agreement on cutting carbon pollution. It not only denies the climate science, it accuses the media of reinforcing the “illusion” of climate change by reporting on forest fires, droughts and floods.

I am a proud transgender woman and running for Socialist Alliance in the Victorian elections. Hanson’s supporters probably see me as an easy target for harassment and violence. I have already had to delete around 70 vitriolic comments from my candidate Facebook page, mostly ablest and some transphobic.

It is terrifying to know that ON, which has the backing of powerful establishment forces, is deeply against one’s fundamental right to exist.

One Nation Senator Tyron Whitten claimed that parents who support their trans kids are participating in “child abuse”. Parminder Singh, a ON candidate in Western Australia’s election last year, said that gay people are mentally ill. He apologised and Barnaby Joyce has ridiculously tried to claim that ON is one of the “gayist” political parties. But clearly, ON does not support fundamental human rights.

When you’re talking with people about who to vote for, make sure to mention that a ON is is the establishment’s “protest” party. With more power, it will make everyone’s life harder.

People are rightly fed up and there are political alternatives to the mainstream parties.

Socialist Alliance in Victoria has been at the forefront of grassroots campaigns to end Australia’s support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, opposing the destruction of public housing, and standing up against racism.

We are helping organise the protest against Hanson on October 4 in Djilang.

Our election platform says the state must prioritise working people’s needs and direct the country’s shared wealth, created by workers, back to us first.

To quote American musician Jeff Rosenstock from my all-time favourite album Worry: “They want you to be a ghost, when they rob you of your hope, but we’ve got power when they’re not expecting anything.”

People power is the reason Coles decided not to renew its contract with AI corporation Palantir and people power is how we’ll create a more inclusive and just system for us and the planet. Join us!

[Freya Hedley is standing for Socialist Alliance in South Barwon in the Victorian elections. Get in touch to help the campaign out on geelong@socialist-alliance.org or Instagram.]

title: Fransa’da daha iyi eğitim için 413 okulda eylem
content:

Ülkenin önde gelen lise sendikalarından USL Genel Sekreteri Marius Mesnil, katıldığı bir televizyon yayınında, hükümetin liselilerin taleplerine ilişkin adımlarını yeterli bulmadıklarını yineledi. Mesnil, lise kuşatma eylemlerinin kararlılıkla sürdürülmesi çağrısı yaptı.

Öğrenciler öğretmen ve personel eksikliği, kalabalık sınıflar, aşırı yoğun ders programları, bakımsız okul binaları ve bazı dersliklerde masa gibi temel ihtiyaçların dahi bulunmamasını protesto ediyor.

Öğretmen açığının kapatılması, daha fazla personel, daha az kalabalık sınıflar, yenilenmiş okul binaları ve daha iyi öğrenme koşulları için somut adımlar atılması isteniyor.

author: Fozzie
title: Chapter 16: Absolute and Relative Surplus Value
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to chapter 16 of Marx's Capital volume one.

In this, the first of the three chapters that take us from analyses in terms of value, to those of the monetary form of the value of labor-power, Marx reminds us of the distinction between absolute and relative surplus-value, of how they are produced and of the relationship between the two. Absolute surplus-value emerges early when capitalists only command or subsume the labor of others formally, that is to say, without taking over and transforming tools and how they are used. Under those circumstances, their only available strategy for increasing the extraction of surplus-value involves getting people to work longer. Because workers control their tools and the rhythm of their work, capitalists have little leverage to extract more surplus-value via the intensification of labor. Relative surplus-value emerges as capitalists do obtain that leverage, by gaining control over tools and organizing them in factories that facilitate oversight and control. Protected by new property laws, they reshape both tools and their use to raise productivity and increase surplus-value—both by reducing the labor time necessary to produce each unit and by increasing the intensity of labor.

Given the increasing centrality of productivity, he also reminds us of how the conditions and meaning of productive labor depends upon the context. At the level of the individual, a productive worker is simply one who produces some product directly, using mind, hands and tools to transform raw materials. That was the generic concept he set out in the first section of Chapter 7. But as human society developed most labor became social, such that individuals came to collaborate in the production of ever more things and in so doing formed a collective worker with a division of labor—that he analyzed in some detail in Chapter 14. With the rise of various kinds of class society, including capitalism, antagonistic relationships develop as some are able to impose surplus work on others and appropriate the resulting surplus product. Within capitalism that surplus product takes the form of surplus-value, so that from the point of view of the appropriating capitalists the only productive workers, i.e., the only workers whose labor makes it possible to impose more work, are those who produce surplus-value, i.e., surplus labor whose products can be used to impose more work in the future. As a result, there is a clear distinction between the vernacular, everyday sense of being productive, i.e., being able to produce something, and the only kind of productivity that matters to capitalists. This is consistent with the emphasis we saw in Chapter 1 between use-value and exchange-value/value. Use-values and the ease with which we can obtain them preoccupy those of us who work; the exchange-value of the surplus production preoccupies those who put us to work.

In illustrating the capitalist case, Marx draws a parallel between those industries that produce things and those that produce services.

Given that such “productivity” involves exploitation, he adds that, “To be a productive worker is therefore not a piece of luck, but a misfortune.” (1)

Marx then goes on to remind us of the connections that he demonstrated in Chapter 15 between absolute and relative surplus-value. Namely, how the methods used to produce relative surplus-value, i.e., introducing new machines and new technology, also made possible the prolongation of the working day and the intensification of work, both of which added surplus-alue by extracting more work from those subject to the new methods. What he does not remind us of here, is how the shift to relative surplus-value strategies was the result of the success of workers’ struggles to shorten the working day and by so doing undermine absolute surplus-value. (2) Nor does he reiterate his previous analysis of how new machines are designed and new technologies are chosen with the objective of undermining those struggles through the reorganization of the labor process. (3)

These reminders are followed by a brief analysis of the impact of natural conditions on the availability of surplus labor, both potential and actual. Where nature has provided plenty to meet limited needs and wants, as has sometimes been the case in the tropics, little work has been required and this resulted in a lot of spare, disposable time.(4) Marx’s remarks here have received substantial support from later …

author: gavroche
title: XX Congreso CGT: Miguel Fadrique revalida la Secretaría General, pero Nuria Negro obtiene el apoyo de más sindicatos
content:
De

Sindicalismo.org


El XX Congreso Confederal de CGT termina con una organización prácticamente dividida en dos. Miguel Fadrique consigue 689 votos frente a los 639 de Nuria Negro, pero la candidatura alternativa recibe el respaldo de 90 sindicatos frente a los 84 del secretario general reelegido. El resultado llega después del fuerte rechazo que recibió la gestión del Secretariado Permanente saliente durante el propio Congreso.


Victoria por apenas 50 votos


Miguel Fadrique Sanz continuará al frente de CGT después de imponerse en una de las votaciones más ajustadas del XX Congreso Confederal. Fadrique obtuvo

689 votos

, mientras que Nuria Isabel Negro Blanco alcanzó

639

. Solo 50 votos separaron a las dos candidaturas. Sobre un total de 1.328 votos repartidos entre ambas opciones, Fadrique consiguió aproximadamente el 51,9 % y Negro el 48,1 %. Una diferencia de apenas 3,8 puntos que deja lejos cualquier imagen de una mayoría incontestable.


Pero el resultado contiene otro dato especialmente significativo. Los 689 votos de Fadrique procedieron de

84 sindicatos

, mientras que los 639 de Negro correspondieron a

90 sindicatos

. El secretario general gana, por tanto, en número de votos, mientras que su alternativa consigue el respaldo de

seis sindicatos más

. La explicación está en el sistema de representación congresual, en el que los sindicatos no disponen necesariamente del mismo número de votos y su peso depende de la representación que les corresponde.


Fadrique gana en votos; Negro, en número de sindicatos


La diferencia permite dos lecturas que no son contradictorias. Miguel Fadrique gana legítimamente la votación y renueva la Secretaría General, pero Nuria Negro consigue extender su candidatura entre un número mayor de sindicatos.

689 frente a 639 votos y 84 frente a 90 sindicatos

 muestran dos bloques con un peso muy parecido dentro de la organización.


El dato resulta todavía más relevante porque la votación no se produce en un Congreso tranquilo. CGT llegó a Parla con fuertes debates internos acumulados durante los últimos años y las diferencias quedaron expuestas desde las primeras sesiones. La candidatura de Negro representaba precisamente una alternativa a la continuidad del Secretariado encabezado por Fadrique.


La reelección llega después del rechazo a su gestión


El resultado debe leerse también junto a lo ocurrido el día anterior. Como informó Sindicalismo.org, la gestión del Secretariado Permanente saliente encabezado por Miguel Fadrique recibió un

fuerte rechazo durante el XX Congreso

. Una parte importante de las delegaciones cuestionó la gestión realizada durante los últimos cuatro años, dejando una situación poco habitual: el secretario general consigue posteriormente renovar su mandato, pero lo hace después de que su etapa anterior haya recibido una contestación considerable dentro del propio Congreso.


Son, en cualquier caso, dos votaciones diferentes. Una valoraba la gestión desarrollada por el Secretariado Permanente durante el mandato que terminaba y otra decidía quién debía dirigir la organización durante los próximos cuatro años. Confundir ambas sería incorrecto, pero políticamente resulta imposible analizarlas como si no tuvieran relación. La combinación de ambos resultados muestra una organización donde existe un cuestionamiento importante de la dirección saliente y, al mismo tiempo, una mayoría suficiente para que Fadrique continúe.


Un Congreso marcado por las acreditaciones y las críticas internas


Las tensiones tampoco se limitaron a las votaciones. Durante el Congreso diferentes delegaciones denunciaron problemas relacionados con las

acreditaciones, el acceso al plenario y los turnos de palabra

. Según fuentes de los sindicatos afectados, algunas delegaciones inicialmente excluidas consiguieron finalmente entrar, aunque continuaron las críticas sobre el procedimiento seguido y las posibilidades de intervención de determinados sindicatos.


Estas denuncias proceden de los sectores afectados y críticos con la organización del Congreso y deben diferenciarse de los resultados oficiales de las votaciones. Sin embargo, forman parte del contexto en el que se produjo la elección del nuevo Secretariado y ayudan a explicar el elevado nivel de enfrentamiento vivido durante las sesiones.


Una CGT prácticamente dividida en dos


La fotografía que deja la elección resulta difícil de interpretar como un respaldo masivo a una única orientación.

author: Abe Walker
title: The Battle for the Soul of the UAW: Union Democracy and the Seductions of Power
content:
After years of struggling in relative obscurity, democratic socialists were jubilant to have elected one of their own to high-profile office. With bold rhetoric and meme-friendly soundbites, their candidate captured the hearts and minds of a working-class base eager for an alternative to the establishment’s caustic brand of demagoguery. Ignoring calls for moderation, the campaign took on a defiant, openly confrontational tone. Its outcome shocked the old guard, upended the status quo, and served as a warning to entrenched interests everywhere.

The year was 2023, and Shawn Fain had just won the presidency of the United Auto Workers union. Fain quickly became the public face of a resurgent workers movement that seemed poised to usher in a new wave of labor militancy. But there would be little time for celebration once the weight of the task ahead set in. Indeed – like a certain big city mayor – Fain would quickly discover that his election fight was only a preview of the battles to come.

Fain is now standing for reelection, with ballots set to be tallied next month. Three years ago, few could imagine that Fain would face a viable challenger as he eyed a second term. Yet today, his star has long since dimmed, and his fate now hangs in balance. The upcoming vote will serve as a referendum on his tenure, and while he remains the clear favorite, there is considerably less enthusiasm behind his current bid.

Fain’s dramatic rise and fall can only be understood in the context of the reform movement that propelled him to power. Fain traces his lineage to a long history of rank-and-file agitators who challenged the 74-year reign of the incumbent Administration Caucus from below. In the 1960s, the Revolutionary Union Movement organized Black militants to combat the union’s complicity in de facto factory segregation. In the 1980s, the New Directions caucus fought against the introduction of lean production and concessionary bargaining. These efforts scored some victories in local elections, but the possibility of taking power on a grand stage remained elusive. The established powers proved remarkably resilient, using their vast patronage network to absorb dissidents and marginalize challengers. Dissent was managed, co-opted, or crushed.

Meanwhile, union leaders embraced “jointness” and labor-management cooperation, seeking to align workers’ interests with corporate competitiveness. A series of concessions in the 2000s culminated in two-tier contracts that subjected new hires to substandard wages and reduced benefits, creating artificial hierarchies that fractured shop-floor solidarity. Givebacks at Detroit automakers were compounded by organizing challenges in the South, where the union failed to make inroads at the German and Japanese plants that were overtaking the sector. As membership plummeted, union officials oversaw a managed decline, presiding over plant closures and outsourcing. Insulated from rank-and-file agitation and accountable to no one, it was a short step from sweetheart deals and graft to outright corruption. The breaking point arrived in the late 2010s with the exposure of a scandal involving the misuse of union funds for personal expenses, and officials accepting bribes from the very auto executives they were supposed to bargain against. Two former presidents were sent to prison, and a federal monitor was appointed to oversee the union’s operations under a consent decree. But this legitimacy crisis came with a silver lining, shattering the old guard’s aura of invincibility and creating an opening for change.

Amidst the wreckage, a coalition of frustrated auto workers founded Unite All Workers for Democracy (UAWD). Drawing tactical inspiration and support from broader labor-left networks, including Labor Notes and the Democratic Socialists of America, UAWD presented democracy as an antidote to corruption. Through painstaking grassroots organizing (and an assist from the federal Monitor), UAWD successfully forced a referendum on direct elections in 2021, which passed with 63% of the vote.

After breaking the old guard’s monopoly on power, candidates had to tailor their messaging to appeal directly to the militant rank-and-file base. Shawn Fain ran on the strength of his populist, class-conscious rhetoric. He framed the election as an existential battle between the working class and the billionaire owners, while promising an end to concessionary bargaining and cozy labor-management partnerships.

author: Thomas Klikauer
title: German Car Workers Rally Against Job Cuts
content:
In September, 175,000 workers at 280 locations in Germany’s automotive and supplier industry engaged in a day of protest against the planned job cuts in the car industry. It shows that Germany’s workforce is prepared to fight for its jobs and its future. However, at several large Volkswagen (VW) locations, the true collective power of workers remained largely hidden behind factory gates.

At Volkswagen’s prime location in Wolfsburg, thousands gathered inside the factory gates. At an adjacent “public” rally only around 300 workers came. At Volkswagen’s Kassel-Baunatal location, about 850 workers took part in an “inside the factory” event, according to IGM’s Vertrauensleute, or union stewards. Representing workers in Germany’s still mighty car industry, the IGM union had planned for mostly union representatives [Vertrauensleute] to participate.

On the positive side, this might have been because IGM was unsure whether workers would follow its call to protest. On the downside, it might have been because the union wanted to confine the protest to its “controllable” union body rather than risk a true – and perhaps uncontrollable – protest by disgruntled workers against VW’s management. IGM wants to negotiate with that management and, as in the case of VW, has a relationship with it that is commonly seen as that of an assistant to management.

Worse, at another Volkswagen location, Braunschweig, union representatives – furnished with a union-developed “discussion guide” – were sent into VW’s production, even though the participation of all three shifts had been agreed beforehand.

On the whole, the “Union Day” of action has shown two things: first, the union can mobilize workers against management’s planned job cuts; and second, at the same time, local union representatives can limit or contain workers’ protest. German workers tend to follow their union. They are still more like Heinrich Mann’s rather tame Loyal Subject than anarcho-syndicalists – people who combine anarchism with revolutionary trade unionism.

Beyond that, one of the key questions isn’t just how many people took part: 175,000, or more, or fewer? It must also be asked who decided what form the “Union Day of Action” should take. Which proposals from workers about how best to challenge management were addressed, and which were eliminated by the union apparatus? Why did it appear, at several VW sites, as if management had received protection from the ever so compliant section of the union apparatus?

The reason for the “Union Day of Action” at Volkswagen was the planned removal of more than 60,000 jobs in Germany by the Volkswagen corporation. According to the most recent collective agreement between IGM and VW (from December 2024), VW’s works council – the legally elected body of workers’ representatives – and IGM accepted what is called “the socially acceptable removal” of more than 35,000 jobs at VW’s German locations by 2030. The term “socially acceptable removal” is not only the language of managerialism; it also means that workers who leave through retirement, by finding a new job, etc. are not replaced.

To make matters even more confusing, Germany’s labor relations operate with union representatives [Vertrauensleute], who have no legal support other than the strength of a local union organization, and, parallel to that, a legally elected and protected works council.

The former tends to be more progressive, while the latter tends to operate within the confines of Germany’s labor law – it operates as an offsider to management. Worse, union representatives who show compliance with Germany’s labor laws – no wildcat strikes, etc. – are selected and promoted by the union body and are often rewarded with election to the works council, which means, at VW for example, an almost lifelong job.

By splitting Germany’s workers into three institutions – an external union apparatus, a factory-based official body (the works council), and a factory-based union body – the “divide and conquer” strategy comes to life.

Volkswagen‘s management explicitly linked the collective agreement to a long-term reduction in production capacity and a reduction in annual labor costs of €1.5 billion ($1.7bn). Accordingly, redundancies are excluded until the end of 2030.

The agreed job cuts were to be achieved primarily via the so-called “demographic curve” – the retirement of workers. In 2026, Volkswagen’s top management calculated a need for further “adjustments” (meaning job cuts) …

author: Unknown
title: The social meaning of peace: Kurdish seasonal agricultural workers
content:
The problem of seasonal agricultural labor cannot be understood separately from the region’s economic structure. Kurdish cities have fertile plains, abundant water resources, and a young population. Yet instead of developing this potential locally, the region has become part of a system that forces people to leave their homes in search of work.


Every year, pickup trucks and minibuses leave the plains of Mardin (Mêrdîn), Batman (Êlîh),  Diyarbakır (Amed), Urfa (Riha), Siirt (Sêrt), Şırnak (Şirnex), Van (Wan), and Muş (Mûş). Carrying hundreds, sometimes thousands, of families, they embark on long journeys, from the citrus groves of Çukurova to the hazelnut fields of the Black Sea, from the potato fields of Konya to the cotton fields and vineyards of the Aegean. These families spend much of the year far from home.


Seasonal labor is not simply a matter of “fate” or “natural poverty.” It is part of a system produced by the war in Kurdistan. Villages emptied and burned by soldiers during the 1990s, restrictions on pastures and highland grazing areas, and agricultural lands placed under embargo cut thousands of families off from their land and livestock. Even according to official figures, thousands of settlements were forcibly evacuated. Farmers dispossessed of their land were pushed into working-class neighborhoods in the cities and transformed into a reserve of cheap labor for the country’s agricultural regions. The deliberate exclusion of the region from investment, industry, and productive development further entrenched this pattern.


A people whose culture and language are denied, who have been dispossessed of their land, and whose labor is bought at the lowest possible price are forced to travel to cities across western Turkey in search of work. Seasonal labor is where state repression and class exploitation intersect. For that reason, it cannot be treated simply as a “labor law issue.”


Anatomy of a season


The journey is often organized through an informal intermediary known as an

elçibaşı

 or

dayıbaşı

. Before workers even leave home, the intermediary negotiates their daily wage, takes a commission, and often delays payment. Those who object may find themselves unable to secure work the following year. The pattern repeats itself at every stage of the season:


Departure and transportation:

 Recruitment is organized through

elçibaşı

 or

dayıbaşı

 intermediaries, often through informal agreements with little or no transparency. Workers are left to travel in overcrowded and unsafe vehicles.


Housing conditions:

 Families live in tents or under plastic sheeting beside the fields, often without adequate access to clean water, toilets, electricity, or other basic infrastructure.


Working conditions:

 They work long hours for low wages that are often paid late, without social insurance or meaningful job security.


Social relations and safety:

 In the regions where they work, they face discrimination and exclusion, may be targeted for speaking Kurdish, and remain vulnerable to racist attacks.


The legal framework does little to address these conditions. Turkey’s Labor Law No. 4857 excludes agricultural enterprises employing fewer than 50 workers from its scope. Although regulations and government circulars exist concerning mobile seasonal agricultural workers, the absence of effective enforcement and oversight means that they often remain little more than paper protection. Every year brings new reports of workers dying in road accidents. Each time, the deaths are described as “fate,” while responsibility goes unaddressed.


Women and children, the invisible labor force


Women and children bear some of the heaviest burdens of seasonal agricultural labor. Women leave for the fields early in the morning. When they return to the tents in the evening, their second shift begins: cooking, cleaning, childcare, and other domestic work. They are also frequently paid less than men for the same work. From the perspective of the women’s freedom movement, seasonal agricultural labor is a stark example of the gendered exploitation of labor, where patriarchal structures intersect with capitalist exploitation.


Children, meanwhile, are often forced to leave school and work in the fields to contribute to their families’ income. Over time, many become permanently disconnected from education. author: Mada Masr
title: Dozens join syndicate demonstration to call for Matsda2sh journalists’ release
content:
Dozens of journalists participated on Saturday in a symbolic sit-in inside the Journalists Syndicate to call for the release of the Matsda2sh journalists, whose whereabouts remain unknown after security forces launched an arrest campaign targeting six of the independent fact-checking platform’s staff on Monday.


While the sit-in was scheduled to end at 5 pm, several members of the syndicate’s general assembly announced that they would remain inside the syndicate, keeping the sit-in open-ended until the Matsda2sh journalists are released.


The syndicate’s board also announced that an emergency meeting would be convened on Monday with a single clause on the agenda: how to respond to the arrest of the six journalists.


Syndicate head Khaled al-Balshy told attendees that the Supreme State Security Prosecution informed the syndicate’s lawyer that the detained journalists have not yet been investigated by the prosecution.


This was confirmed to

Mada Masr

 on Saturday by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ head, Hossam Bahgat, who said that the prosecution head had denied a

report

 published by the privately owned Al-Masry Al-Youm claiming that the prosecution had issued a decision to detain the journalists for 15 days.


In its

statement

, Matsda2sh called upon journalists to take action in the wake of the campaign against them, describing the arrest campaign as a “grave event in the history of Egyptian journalism.” The platform also indicated an ongoing smear campaign against them leveling what it called “flimsy, baseless accusations” against their professional reputations and personal lives.


Accusations against Matsda2sh have circulated in the media since

Friday

, largely reproducing the allegations first made by the Interior Ministry that the journalists are affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood.


It took the Interior Ministry over 48 hours since it initiated the campaign to announce its arrests of the Matsda2sh journalists — Abdallah Qadry, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud, Mohamed Adel and Omar Helal.


Lawyers representing the six proceeded directly to the Supreme State Security Prosecution headquarters upon the ministry’s announcement and submitted notifications to the prosecution to ensure they could attend interrogation sessions with the journalists.


The journalists had not been formally brought before the prosecution as of time of publishing.

Dozens join syndicate demonstration to call for Matsda2sh journalists’ release

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Far Right Makes Gains in Brazil as Flávio Bolsonaro Tops Lula in First Round of Presidential Race
content:
Brazil’s presidential election is headed to a runoff between leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after neither candidate cleared 50% in Sunday’s vote, in which the right made gains in Congress and in governor races across the country. Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote compared to Lula’s 45%. The second round of voting is on October 25. If elected, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to grant amnesty to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest and serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup in 2022 to overturn Lula’s last victory. He has also vowed to strengthen ties to the Trump administration, which is accused of trying to influence the result in Bolsonaro’s favor.


“The momentum has been with the right since 2018,” says Brazilian philosopher Rodrigo Nunes, who explains that public disillusionment with politics is part of that shift. “Lots of people see the far right as promising them, 'Well, if this is all there is, if all we can expect from the future is ever more dog-eat-dog conditions, an ever more competitive struggle of all against all, at least what the far right says is the state will get off our backs.'”


Nunes is author of

Neither Vertical nor Horizontal: A Theory of Political Organization

 and the new book

Anatomy of Disintegration: What Brazil Reveals About the Global Far Right

. He recently wrote about the stakes of the Brazilian election for

North South Notes

.
