title: Hakemler soruşturmasında karar: MHK Başkanı Ferhat Gündoğdu dahil 5 kişi tutuklandı
content:
“Hakemler dosyası” soruşturması kapsamında gözaltına alınan 7 kişiden, MHK Başkanı Ferhat Gündoğdu’nun da aralarında bulunduğu 5 kişi tutuklandı. İki kişi ise yurt dışı çıkış yasağı uygulanarak adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakıldı.

İstanbul’da “Hakemler dosyası” olarak bilinen soruşturma kapsamında gözaltına alınan 7 kişi, emniyetteki işlemlerinin ardından dün adliyeye sevk edildi. Savcılık işlemlerinin ardından tutuklama talebiyle sulh ceza hakimliğine sevk edilen MHK Başkanı Ferhat Gündoğdu, Ferdi Karadoruk, Yunus Yıldırım, Alican Sağlar ve Emre Kosif’in tutuklanmasına karar verildi.

Ahmet Şahin ve Sebahattin Şahin ise yurt dışına çıkış yasağı uygulanarak adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakıldı. Soruşturma kapsamında tutuklanan isimler;

Ferhat Gündoğdu (Merkez Hakem Kurulu - MHK Başkanı)

Ferdi Karadoruk (TFF Faal Futbol Hakemleri ve Gözlemcileri Derneği Başkanı)

Yunus Yıldırım (TFF MHK Eski Üyesi)

Alican Sağlar (TFF Hakemleri ve Gözlemcileri Derneği İstanbul Şubesi Teşkilat Sorumlusu)

Emre Kosif (TFF Hakemleri ve Gözlemcileri Derneği İstanbul İl Hakem Kurulu Başkanı)

Adli kontrol kararı verilen isimler;

Ahmet Şahin (TFF MHK Eski Başkan Vekili)

Sebahattin Şahin (MHK Üyesi ve TFF Eğitim ve 4. Bölge Sorumlusu)

İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı Yasa Dışı Bahis ve Spor Suçları Bürosunun koordinasyonunda, İstanbul Emniyet Müdürlüğü Mali Suçlarla Mücadele Şubesi ekiplerince yürütülen “Hakemler dosyası” soruşturmasında bazı şüpheliler hakkında “eziyet” ve “resmi belgede sahtecilik” suçlamalarına ilişkin iddialar bulunduğu belirtilmişti.

Soruşturma kapsamında yapılan açık kaynak araştırmaları ile MASAK ve HTS incelemeleri, müşteki ve tanık ifadeleri ve bilirkişi tespitlerinin ardından MHK Başkanı Ferhat Gündoğdu ile MHK üyesi bazı hakem ve gözlemcilerin suçla bağlantısı olabileceği değerlendirilmişti.

Bunun üzerine İstanbul, Ankara, Elazığ ve Manisa’da belirlenen adreslere operasyon düzenlenmişti. Operasyonlarda Ferhat Gündoğdu, TFF Faal Hakemler Derneği Başkanı Ferdi Karadoruk, eski TFF Merkez Hakem Kurulu Başkan Vekili Ahmet Şahin, eski TFF Merkez Hakem Kurulu Üyesi Yunus Yıldırım, TFF Eğitim ve 4’üncü Bölge Sorumlusu Sebahattin Şahin, TFF Hakemleri ve Gözlemcileri Derneği İstanbul Şubesi Teşkilat Sorumlusu Alican Sağlar ile TFF Hakemleri ve Gözlemcileri Derneği İstanbul İl Hakem Kurulu Başkanı Emre Kosif gözaltına alınmıştı.

Soruşturma kapsamında Süper Lig hakemi Yasin Kol ile Süper Lig yardımcı hakemi Göktuğ Hazar Erel’in de İstanbul Emniyet Müdürlüğü Mali Suçlarla Mücadele Şubesi ekipleri tarafından gözaltına alındığı bildirilmişti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: groundxero
title: Barricades, Internet Shutdown, Mass Detentions: Delhi Police Violent Crack Down on Protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and SIR
content:
Thousands of protesters gathered around Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 2 October, defying the denial of police permission and a sweeping security clampdown imposed to prevent the protests from taking place. Barricades sealed the designated protest site from all four directions, mobile internet was suspended across central Delhi, several Metro stations were shut, and riot-control forces were deployed in large numbers. What followed was a day of mass detentions, many involving the use of force against women, students, journalists and other protesters. The violent crackdown came amid a renewed call for mobilisation for a ‘Jail Bharo Andolan’ and ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with organisers calling the 2 October action only the beginning of a wider protest movement.


 


New Delhi, 2 October 2026


by

Mouli Sharma


 


“Thousand is a lowballed estimate,” said a lawyer’s group called

Lawyers for Detainees

, one of several such collectives formed after the historic protests that shook the national capital a mere three months ago after uproar against repeated failures and irregularities in the conduct of public examinations under the tenure of former Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Now, recent history is attempting to recreate itself as a similar uproar against the government’s Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and the recent revelations of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s alleged role in the same has led to widespread national outrage.


 


“85 people have been detained in this station alone,” said Adv. Surya Prakash, who was present at the Badarpur police station. “We have reports that at least 20 buses filled with detainees left the protest site during the day. Many detainees were released informally at random locations far away from the centre of the city, while still more were taken to stations like this one. The actual number of detentions is much higher than whatever numbers will be produced here at the stations,” he said.


 


The figure, though, may include repeat detentions, the most prominent case being of AISA president Neha Bora herself, who was detained at least three times from the same location outside the Royal Plaza Hotel, near the East entrance of the protest site near the Kerala Bhawan canteen, first alongside psephologist and activist Yogendra Yadav, a second time with several student protesters of other parties, and a third time again with fellow AISA leader Anjali of the Delhi University. Former Delhi CM Atishi, independent journalist Harsh Yadav, and at least 700 more students were detained through the day.


 


“700 is the count we have so far from police stations taken across the city,” said Adv. Vertika Mani, also a part of the lawyers’ collective. “But that obviously cannot account for the many detainees who were released at unofficial locations.”


 


The CJP’s ultimatum to the government of witnessing a ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ should Gyanesh Kumar fail to resign within 48 hours (given on 25 September, the deadline for which had long since passed) kicked off with a bang on Friday, as an identical call for the police-defying protest in Shivaji Park, Mumbai was given by countless student, labour, farmer and other political organisations at the eponymous Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, led by prominent activists including Neha Bora, Yogendra Yadav, Nandita Narain, and Prashant Bhushan. Hundreds of civilians took to the streets on the morning of 2 October, on the occasion of Gandhi Jayanti, only to be met with armed state forces deployed in massive numbers and a once-designated protest site cut off from their access through curfews (Section 163 of the BNS was declared in the region, without any justification beyond prevention of a ‘crowd forming’) and police barricades blockading entrances to the site from all four directions, dispersing protesters across a wide 2km radius.


 


What followed was a circus of media, police, and protester, as for four hours following the 11 am time given for the assembly, bus after bus was filled with peaceful protesters ‘detained’ under the simple justification of following ‘orders from above’. At least one protester, a young man named Roveen from the All India Students’ Association (AISA) (of whom Neha Bora is national president), was grievously assaulted by the police and had to be taken to a …

author: Katharine Trendacosta
title: Site-Blocking Will Not Defend IP, No Matter the Bill’s Name
content:
There has been a raft of site-blocking bills in the latest Congress, and the latest is called the “Deterring Extraterritorial Foreign Exploitation of Networks Damaging Intellectual Property” aka the “

DEFEND IP Act

.” The problem is that instead of “defending IP,” this bill will incentivize censorship, overblocking, and bad faith attempts to block access to a website. DEFEND IP Act, and all of these site-blocking proposals, threaten the open web.

 


We keep seeing attempts to pass site-blocking legislation–from SOPA/PIPA in 2012 to

Block BEARD

,

FADPA

, and

ACPA

 this year. Every one of them has at its core the rotten idea that enforcing copyrights requires building a censorship machine for websites into the architecture of the internet. This is, of course, a disaster for a free and open web. There is no way to create a mechanism for blocking access to an entire website that does not invite both deliberate abuse and lots of collateral harm to free and lawful speech.


DEFEND IP deputizes every service provider into a copyright cop, so long as a rightsholder has accused a website of copyright infringement. Let’s be clear: this isn’t about removing access to an infringing work–that already exists via the DMCA. This isn’t about getting damages from the website or the uploader. It is about making an entire website inaccessible for everyone trying to visit it.


DEFEND IP lets any rightsholder go to a court and get an order requiring service providers to block access to an entire website after alleging copyright infringement. What DEFEND IP does not have is any deterrent for someone seeking to block a website in bad faith. There are no punishments for getting a website blocked for protected speech. There are no meaningful remedies for those whose speech is vanished from the internet due to an entire website being disappeared. It creates a one-stop shop for getting an entire website–again, not an instance of infringement but an entire site hosting all sorts of user content–removed. But for those whose business, speech, or access to information is affected, there is no easy way to get the site restored.


DEFEND IP scales up the extraordinary legal structures that already exist for copyright enforcement. In doing so, it likewise scales up the problems those regimes pose to protected speech.

 


We see this with DMCA takedowns all the time. We see it with bad faith

takedowns

 used to silence criticism or commentary. We see it with the voluntary use of copyright filters by sites like YouTube, where seconds of sound matching seconds of sound in another video can prevent an entire work from reaching its audience. In these existing systems, there are at least some mechanisms of challenge available to the targeted creator. DEFEND IP has none. Instead, site owners, users, or readers will have to find a lawyer and go to court and hope to challenge the order, a slow, expensive, and daunting process


Those existing systems are already frustrating for the targeted creators and users, but under DEFEND IP a whole class of people doing protected speech will find themselves deplatformed because of the actions of others


This bill is not a defense of creativity or creators. It is a way to reshape the internet by building a vast new infrastructure of censorship. Congress should put aside DEFEND IP and the failed idea of site-blocking laws, for good.

author: Sofia Little
title: Get the Flock Out
content:
On September 23rd, the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held a hearing titled “Always Watching: Flock’s Nationwide AI Surveillance Network,” examining the privacy risks, data sharing, and misuse of private automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks.

The hearing was chaired by Sen. Hawley (R-MO) and featured five witnesses, including Lindsey Isaacs, a wrongfully accused driver, Alasdair Whitney from Legislative Counsel Institute for Justice, Sheriff Ross Teeple, Benn Jordan, a self-proclaimed “hacker”, and policy counsel analyst Chad Marlow from the ACLU, where they have coined a campaign called “Get the Flock Out.”

The hearing highlighted pertinent concerns about how ALPR technology can be used and shared. Public concern about Flock cameras has also grown in recent months. A September 2026 Navigator Research survey found that 62% of registered voters were concerned about Flock camera use, including 66% of Democrats, 55% of Republicans, and 70% of Independents.

Flock Safety was founded in 2017 by CEO Garrett Langley, operating as a small startup meant to provide ALPR cameras to homeowners associations and neighborhoods looking to reduce petty theft and local property crimes. Now, it has grown into something alarmingly dystopian: an AI powered network of over 120,000 cameras across 49 states that photograph, scan, tag, and log every driver that passes, whether or not they are suspected of any crime.

License plate reader technologies have existed since the 1970s, in the form of speed, toll, and red-light cameras. These are only triggered by a specific action, such as running a red-light or driving through a toll booth, and only track license plate numbers. The entry of venture capitalist funding and advanced AI technology into the mass surveillance industry has transformed these automatic traffic enforcement cameras into a complex web of invasive surveillance tools.

During the hearing, ACLU’s Mr. Chad Marlow argued that companies operating ALPR systems are profiting from the collection and sharing of information about people’s movements. The ACLU has called for greater limits on how ALPR data can be collected, accessed, and shared.

Privacy concerns extend to how ALPR data can affect people seeking reproductive health care. During the hearing, Sen. Booker (D-NJ) raised concerns that states could use ALPR technology to track people traveling to obtain reproductive care. The concern comes amid documented cases of law enforcement using vehicle surveillance systems to investigate people seeking or suspected of seeking abortion care.

Unfortunately, this ‘hypothetical’ scenario has become the reality for women across the country.

Witnesses Alaster Whitney and Sheriff Ross Teeple both testified about the overreach of Flock’s ALPRs, with Whitney highlighting jurisdiction concerns which police officers have already been accused of taking advantage of.

In Texas, a sheriff’s deputy used 83,000 Flock ALPRs to track a woman who allegedly performed a self-administered abortion, at the behest of her abusive partner. In Massachusetts, a police officer used Flock networks to stalk a former romantic partner who said she had changed her identity to escape from his abuse. In Kentucky, a police officer was accused of searching his child’s mother 1,000 times through Flock’s network, though she has a protective order. The Institute for Justice has catalogued more than 200 incidents of these ALPR abuses, including romantic stalking, wrongful stops and detentions, non-law enforcement use and other types of misconduct.

These encroachments do not just stop here, as Sen. Padilla (D-CA) spotlights the use of loopholes within Flock, which ICE officers take advantage of to track immigrant communities. While Flock has guaranteed no direct access to the Border Patrol subagency, Witness Marlow points out all it takes is one sympathetic person connected to ICE for the agency to obtain access to billions of pictures of citizens, including facial properties.

Concerns about ALPR surveillance have crossed traditional political lines. During the hearing, Sen. Hawley noted that supporters of the Second Amendment have “long feared national databases of any kind.” This has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum highlighting the bipartisan opposition.

While Flock operates as a leading company which produces ALPRs, they are not the sole producers. Companies like Axon and Motorola have slowly begun increasing …

author: EDRi
title: The KIDS Act will make the internet less safe
content:
On 16 September, the European Commission presented the KIDS ACT, its plan for making online experiences safer for young people. Far from being a move to lead the EU towards better digital environments, this move is a missed opportunity to address the root cause of why online platforms are harmful to children – and everyone else. This blog analyse the proposal’s shortcomings.

During her annual address to the European Parliament, the President of the European Commission announced her intention to protect young people from platforms and services that deprive children of their childhood and of their focus. The next day, the Commission published the KIDS ACT (an acronym for ‘Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy’). This announcement arrives after a period of much debate around protecting young people online, and even announcements of social media bans from countries across Europe. As a response to this discussion, on April 22, youth organisations across Europe came together to demand real change, instead of exclusions and bans, from EU lawmakers.

The Commission had the opportunity to change the rules of the dangerous game that makes people unsafe online. Instead, it’s mostly restricting who gets to play. Not only is the KIDS ACT a terrible proposal, it’s also a missed opportunity for the European Commission to lead the EU towards a safer digital environment for children and everyone else. The proposal instead determines who is allowed to use services built upon harmful design choices, and clumsily tries to make some of these choices safe for a narrow age bracket, rather than addressing why they can be harmful in the first place. In doing so, it leaves largely untouched the business models that put us all at risk, and sets complex standards for safety which will cement Big Tech dominance. Let’s unpack the proposal.

The KIDS ACT mostly delays young people’s exposure to online harms. On the one hand, it would ban social media accounts for those under 15*. On the other hand, it would require companies to apply certain protections to minors’ accounts against pervasive exploitative tracking, intrusive default settings, and AI companions designed to create emotional dependencies, among other risky features.

What is striking is that these protections apply only to people aged 15*-18. It’s as if these services, practices and functionalities will magically cease to be harmful on someone’s 18th birthday. We all remain vulnerable to manipulative design and unfair personalisation even as adults: not even the most digitally literate person can examine every single default setting, decode every recommendation system, or resist every strategically timed prompt designed to get us to keep clicking. Fairness must be built into the environment itself, not left to the skills of the people using it. Many of the measures proposed in the KIDS ACT address harms that are not specific to childhood and were therefore meant to be tackled through the forthcoming Digital Fairness Act (DFA), which the Commission said will address addictive design for all consumers. The risk is that by treating these practices primarily as child-safety problems, the Commission is lowering the ambition of the rules still to come. Under the appearance of acting on online harms, the KIDS ACT may rob us of stronger protections for ALL of us, including children.

The underlying logic of the KIDS ACT is that, while some risks can be mitigated for people aged 15-18, those under 15* years old should be banned from social media altogether. This blanket age-based exclusion treats children’s online presence as the problem, rather than following young people’s own call to examine the conditions under which digital services expose them to harm. Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, young people — including those under 15 — have the fundamental right, online and offline, to participate in society, access information, communicate with others, play, and develop their identities. Age-gates undermine these rights.

They would also fundamentally change the open nature of the internet: services would have to treat users as children by default unless they prove their age. The Commission’s approach would create a two-tier internet in which children but also adults who cannot or do not wish to pass an age check are excluded from spaces that have become important for education, socialisation, access to information and participation in public life. Open Source Is Not the Same Thing as Liberation

Open Source Is a Tool, Not a Commandment

There is a peculiar form of ideological dogmatism that has emerged within parts of the FOSS movement. Even in anarchist circles, some people seem to believe that opposition to intellectual property must take precedence over virtually every other ethical consideration. After all, if copyright, patents, and other forms of intellectual property are inherently illegitimate, then any attempt to place limits on how the things we create are used or distributed must necessarily be reactionary, right? Even when those limits are intended to protect workers, creators, and wider communities from exploitation by capital?

Anarchists do not seek to abolish one particular category of property while leaving other relations of domination untouched. Nor do we advocate stripping workers of control over the fruits of their labor in the name of an ideological dogma that ultimately has little to do with fostering anarchism.

The rise of so-called “generative AI” has made this contradiction impossible to ignore. My recent essay on this technology was criticized by some open-source diehards because, in their view, no one has the right to restrict the flow of information — even when that flow gushes directly from the minds and labor of workers and creatives into the bulging bank accounts of Silicon Valley billionaires.

To be clear: I am not opposed to free and open-source software. The forum I run (Raddle.me) was built on software (Postmill) that my cofounder released into the commons from the outset under a FOSS license. Even when fascists forked her code to spread hate and harassment, and when a scummy developer violated the license and tried to pass her work off as his own for profit, we did not respond by retreating behind a closed-source license. As anti-authoritarians and anti-capitalists, we certainly could have justified doing so when her work was being used to harm marginalized communities and enrich capitalists, but the license was kept open.

The same principle applies to my own writing. I release all of my essays freely, and I give zine-makers permission to reprint them without restriction. I believe in sharing knowledge and making creative work accessible. People have the option to donate to support my work if they want to. What I oppose is capital taking that generosity, enclosing it within a for-profit ecosystem, and turning it into another mechanism for extracting wealth from the people who created it.

This is not an argument that copyright is inherently liberatory. It is an argument that the abolition of intellectual property is not, by itself, liberation.

I feel compelled to take a stand against the increasingly rigid open-source absolutism that has taken hold in parts of the milieu: against the ruling class taking our collective knowledge, privatizing it, and selling it back to us. I do not consider this a pro-IP argument, but I’m sure plenty of people will disagree. It is an argument against AI slop …

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Live in the Real World
content:
Our dependence on our phones isn’t an accident. We depend on them logistically for our navigation, payment, and communication. But our phones and the apps they contain are also designed to build emotional dependence — there are entire teams of top-of-their-field psychologists, engineers, sociologists, and designers getting paid hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to make apps even just a little bit more addictive. The emotional and logistical dependence on our phones intertwine in a mutual feedback loop, making it difficult to reduce either.

Every interaction we have with our phones deepens opportunities for state surveillance. Our online activity creates a database of our interests, purchase history, friend networks, location, and activism that the FBI of yesteryear could only have dreamed of. But the biggest problem, as with any addiction, is how something that is fun and useful in small doses can start to take more and more of our time and attention, preventing us from doing other things that we value. So what is there to do?

For most of us, the apps that most deeply build psychological dependence on our phones are social media apps and games. These often take, in some ways, the place of cigarettes in our society today — we do them on a quick break, or when we need to ‘unwind’. But like nicotine, they mostly sate the need that they themselves create. After unwinding in this way, do you feel deeply rested and reset?

If there is an app that you feel wastes your time, or you dislike how much you use, just delete it! You can always re-download it. Note down in your organizer the date and time you deleted the app, and why. If you redownload the app, note that down too. It’s helpful to understand our own patterns of use, to help us understand where we use “tools” or “toys” out of necessity or fun, versus out of psychological dependence.

Think about other activities you can do when you would have used your phone. If you delete an app, it’s easy for some other app to quickly replace it. Be realistic about what might feel fulfilling and restful while deprogramming, in those times and in that headspace. Watching landscapes slide past, noticing the people around you, thinking about your present, past or future, having a conversation with a friend or stranger, reading: each of these might feel more wholesome or restful than your phone. Your Slingshot organizer may be able help you… Don’t you think the edges of the date pages could use additional intricate doodles? Or perhaps you can journal a bit, filling in past date entries with what you remember doing, seeing, eating, or thinking on that day? Use the blank pages in the back to write poetry or outline a manifesto or draw art. Let your boredom be a canvas, a portal to discovery, not something to avoid.

These activities won’t feel as stimulating or give you the same dopamine rush as the apps you’re used to. It’s normal to feel a sense of confusion or loss in this process. Perhaps at some deep level the bright, shifting light of the screen feels like a flickering fire: a thousand generations of finding safety and community in campfires draws us inexorably to this bright cold flame. Try changing your phone’s settings to have the display be in black and white, or switch to a dimmer, less attractive color palette.

We can also feel emotional dependence on the instant knowledge and communication phones provide. What if we can’t respond right away to a friend or loved one? It’s so easy to ask a question to AI like Siri or Google and get an affirming answer! Like puppies or young children, we become anxious without the constant presence of that communication or knowledge. Try consciously pushing your limits more often — if you don’t know something, discuss it rather than looking up ‘the answer’ right away. Delete search bars and AI assistants from your phone and download the Wikipedia app, so if you do need to look something up, you will break that instant gratification loop, finding your own answer and giving yourself context along the way. And try setting aside a specific time of the day to answer your messages. Let friends or loved ones know you might not respond quickly outside of that time.

Logistical dependence is hard in a different way. Practical uses for our phones are often the most problematic sites of government and corporate surveillance, and reinforce emotional dependence by repeatedly forcing us back to our screens.

Try leaving your phone on airplane mode …

author: Dion Nissenbaum
title: SCOTUS Greenlights Use of Federal Citizenship Tool to Vet Voters
content:
The ruling was a rare victory for Trump in his effort to impose more federal control over the country’s electoral system.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Supreme Court cleared the way Friday for election officials to resume using a federal immigration status verification system to check voter rolls for potential noncitizens — a significant victory for President Donald Trump’s administration, but one that’s likely to have little impact on the November midterm elections.

The unsigned opinion hit pause on a lower court’s ruling from June while the case works its way through the appeals process. The lower court had found that the Department of Homeland Security had violated voter privacy by expanding the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system, better known as SAVE, so that states could run their voter rolls through it to check for any noncitizens.

Friday’s ruling is not expected to lead to any widespread removal of voters before the November election because federal law prohibits election officials from systematically unregistering voters within 90 days of an election.

However, as a result of the ruling, the Trump administration will be able to restart use of the SAVE system to scrutinize state voter rolls after the election, and election officials will be able to use the SAVE system to check the citizenship of individual voters in the meantime as well.

The Department of Homeland Security has maintained the SAVE system for decades to check immigrants’ eligibility for public benefits. But in 2025, the Trump administration revamped the tool to allow election officials to check voter rolls in bulk against federal citizenship and immigration records and to search using Social Security numbers, making it far easier to screen registered voters for potential noncitizens.

The case against the expanded SAVE was brought by a coalition of groups, including the League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center, that argued that the Trump administration violated Americans’ privacy by expanding how the system is used.

“Today’s decision is profoundly disappointing, as it puts Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections,” Abigail Kunkler, an attorney for the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said in a statement on behalf of the plaintiffs.

She said the case “is not over” and noted the lower court had ruled that the expanded SAVE violates multiple laws. “We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans’ voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands.”

Trump administration officials celebrated the court victory.

“Yes, you read that right. We had to file an emergency petition in the Supreme Court just so we could use government data to help states stop noncitizens from illegally voting,” James Percival, the Department of Homeland Security’s general counsel, said on X in reaction to the decision.

The Department of Homeland Security has said that election officials in 25 states, mostly Republicans, have run their voter rolls through the SAVE system. Some of those officials praised SAVE as a valuable tool for weeding out ineligible voters, but others have found it to be unreliable.

A ProPublica investigation from earlier this year found that the Trump administration’s rush to turn the system into a voter verification tool made it prone to false positives. In at least five different states, the system has flagged people as noncitizens who were actually citizens.

In Texas, Votebeat reported that the system flagged hundreds of people who had registered to vote through the state Department of Public Safety, which requires proof of citizenship from any prospective registrants. State and local election officials have confirmed that several of those people are indeed eligible to vote.

In a dissent to Friday’s opinion, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson cited the problems in Texas as a main reason she opposed the Trump administration’s use of the SAVE system to check voter rolls. Jackson noted that one plaintiff in the case had her voter registration revoked without her knowledge and that two others had to provide proof of citizenship to remain on voter rolls.

“The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences …

author: Monica Atieno, Angela Chukunzira and Athandiwe Saba
title: Inside Kenya’s Hidden Deals with Big Tech
content:
When an outsourcing company working for Meta found itself being sued in Kenya, it took its problem to the President.


The dispute had begun in May 2022, when former Facebook content moderator Daniel Motaung sued Sama and Meta over working conditions. Another 43 moderators brought a case in March 2023. The workers had been employed by Sama to moderate Facebook content, work that required them to repeatedly view disturbing material. They argued that Meta, which ultimately benefited from and controlled aspects of their work, should also be held responsible.


Sama was not a minor contractor in Kenya. It was part of the labour pipeline that allowed a global technology company to outsource some of the most harmful work of the internet to Kenyan workers. Meta fought to remove itself from the litigation, arguing, among other things, that Kenyan courts did not have jurisdiction over the foreign company. But on 20 September 2024, the Court of Appeal rejected that argument.


Then on 11 November 2024, less than two months after that ruling, the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill was published. It proposed new rules for Kenya’s outsourcing industry, including provisions dealing with who should carry responsibility for workers employed by outsourcing companies.


Less than a month later, on 9 December, President William Ruto publicly said Sama had approached him about its legal troubles. “Now I can report to you that we have changed the law,” he said, adding that “nobody will take you to court again on any matter.”


But the bill was still before Parliament, where a fight was unfolding over who should be held responsible for outsourced workers. Business groups including KEPSA and the Kenya Association of Manufacturers

argued

 that responsibility should largely remain with the outsourcing company. Tech workers argued that companies that control or benefit from their work should also be held responsible. This was very important for workers trying to sue companies such as Meta rather than only their local contractors.


Figure 1: Africa Tech Workers Movement members during a joint press conference in August 2025, raising concerns about the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024.


The workers also went to court to try to stop the bill. In June 2026, the High Court

declined

 to intervene. On 19 August 2026, the National Assembly passed the amendments. It now awaits for presidential assent. 


For James Oyange, a former content moderator, Ruto’s statement sent a clear message about whose side the government was on. Workers had gone to court seeking protection from some of the world’s most powerful technology companies; instead, he said, the government appeared to be changing the rules in the companies’ favour.


“We are on our own. It is the responsibility of the government to protect us, but they are taking Big Tech’s side. It means the companies can do what they want.”


Oyange fears that if technology companies can turn to the government when workers sue them, while workers are left with fewer ways to hold those companies responsible, the balance of power shifts even further away from workers.


The Sama case is one part of a much wider relationship between Kenya’s government and global technology companies.

The Continent

 identified at least 12 publicly documented meetings, agreements, regulatory engagements and partnerships between the Kenyan government and Microsoft, Google, Amazon, TikTok and Starlink since 2023.


The investigation also found a pattern across these relationships. Major technology companies are being brought into public services, infrastructure and policymaking, often through agreements the public cannot see. At the same time, laws and policies are being developed that can make it easier for these companies to operate. What is much harder to find is who negotiated these arrangements, what Kenya agreed to in return, and who is checking whether they serve the public interest.


Agriculture is one example. In 2020, the Ministry of Agriculture signed an agreement with Microsoft to use technology to

improve farming and food security.

 Microsoft would provide cloud technology for digital tools using information about weather, pests, farming inputs and production.


The partnership expanded in 2022, when AGRA joined Microsoft on a digital agriculture programme that included Agribot known as Kuzabot, a service that sends farmers advice by SMS and WhatsApp. According to the

author: Brian Hioe
title: Does China Intend to Target Taiwan With New National Security Legislation?
content:
TAIWANESE GOVERNMENT officials, speaking under conditions of anonymity to the media, have warned that China may roll out national security legislation directed at Taiwan in the coming months. Such national security legislation would follow up on China’s recently passed ethnic unity law.

The law criminalizes actions aimed at disrupting a vaguely defined “national unity”. Although initial warnings were that the law was mainly aimed at Tibetans and Uyghurs, the Lai administration has framed such national security legislation as potentially a threat to Taiwan. Under such laws, after all, support for Taiwanese independence–or even just maintaining Taiwan’s current democratic freedoms and its de facto independence–could be construed as illegal and criminal under the law.

Such Taiwanese government officials have pointed to a number of laws, some of which are still in the review process, as potentially impacting Taiwan. This includes the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration, Measures for the Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security, and National Defense Mobilization Law.

In particular, the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration could be used to prevent Taiwanese who have traveled to China from leaving. This already occurred in the past, however, most prominently in the case of activist Lee Ming-che, who spent over five years in Chinese jails on charges of seeking to subvert the state. Lee is thought to have been detained over exchanges with Chinese friends on Taiwan’s experiences regarding democratization. Others imprisoned, however, have been noted to include pan-Blue academics, who seem to have fallen afoul of espionage charges in spite of pro-unification viewpoints.

Measures on cybersecurity take place at a time when the Chinese government has attempted to depict Taiwan as engaged in cyberattacks against critical infrastructure. Such allegations seem to be an attempt to depict Taiwan as engaged in the same activity it routinely accuses China of being engaged in, seeing as China consistently conducts cyberattacks on Taiwan and probes key infrastructure. Importantly, such allegations could also be used to cement a casus belli to justify war.

Indeed, to this extent, the National Defense Mobilization Law has been warned as potentially intended to provide the legal grounds for wartime mobilization. Indeed, such a law might be necessary ahead of a Chinese invasion, particularly if the Chinese government intends to move Chinese society as a whole toward war footing, and mobilize all of society to conduct an invasion.

Still, at a time of highly polarized politics between the KMT and DPP, it can be expected that the KMT will probably deny that China has intentions for future national security legislation. KMT chair Cheng Li-wun has, of course, attempted to depict China as only having goodwill toward Taiwan, while depicting the DPP as, in fact, the ones who have sought to provoke China. As such claims to the media are made ahead of elections in November, they will be depicted as simply intended to drum up public fear for the sake of electioneering.

During the first session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, governments and stakeholders convened to have open, transparent and inclusive discussions on artificial intelligence governance. We now gather experts across the spectrum of stakeholders during UNGA81 to reaffirm that human rights should be the stepping stone of this process, instead of an afterthought.


None of this is irreversible, but the security issues associated with advanced AI tools are the consequences of deliberately prioritizing profit and competitiveness over the security and safety of at-risk communities, and they will not resolve on their own. Unbridled AI adoption combined with unacceptably lax corporate security practices demands urgent intervention at all levels, starting from putting human rights back at the center of digital governance mechanisms.


This discussion has the objective to explore concrete, actionable ways in which each stakeholder can contribute to oppose the normalization of surveillance. Experts will also discuss how to chart a way forward to reaffirm digital rights as the natural first line of defense against the abuses of AI technologies.

author: Mahdi Niksefat Motlagh
title: Ending the war requires accepting Iran in the Middle East
content:
The hardest question about ending the war with Iran belongs in Washington. What place can Iran occupy after the fighting stops? A country left economically excluded, unable to rebuild and exposed to renewed attack has little reason to regard a ceasefire as a durable ending. The war cannot be politically settled while Iranian recovery remains an unacceptable outcome.

The latest diplomacy leaves that question unresolved. Tehran has received US feedback, through Qatar, on a seven-day trust-building proposal. Yet on 1 October, the US Treasury expanded sanctions against Iran’s automotive and rail sectors, alongside manufacturing and steel networks. Talks about ending the confrontation are proceeding alongside measures that further restrict Iran’s capacity to sustain its economy.

The Islamic Republic connects these claims to a revolutionary and religious account of its purpose. Ali Khamenei’s 2019 Second Phase statement, with its emphasis on building an Islamic civilisation, expressed that connection explicitly. Security, within this understanding, includes the capacity to continue a political project.

Israel also brings historical and theological claims to its modern statehood. Netanyahu has described it as the Middle East’s sole true democracy. In his September UN address, he invoked the Jewish people’s three-thousand-year history and biblical attachment to the land while anticipating the Iranian government’s fall.

Different understandings of statehood do not make war inevitable. The contradiction arises when Israeli security is defined through the dismantling of Iran’s capacity to remain an independent regional power. Under that definition, even Iranian reconstruction can appear threatening because recovery restores the resources through which Iran can act. Iran’s continued existence and Israel’s preferred regional order then become politically incompatible.

This gives the war its ontological dimension. For Iran, survival involves retaining the ability to decide its future and sustain its place in the region. For Netanyahu’s government, an Iran capable of recovering may signify the return of an existential threat. Military operations can damage Iranian capabilities. They cannot resolve this dispute over what Iran is allowed to become after the bombing.

The June 2025 war and the present confrontation make a distinction between surviving an attack and securing a durable ending especially consequential.

Its strategic implication is nevertheless clear: economic recovery itself can become a reason to preserve pressure.

A settlement built on permanent Iranian weakness would therefore contain the grounds for renewed confrontation. Iran needs the capacity to rebuild. An Israeli government that treats this capacity as intolerable would retain an incentive to obstruct it. More accurate weapons or more sophisticated surveillance cannot reconcile these positions.

Washington must confront that contradiction because the costs of the war reach beyond Israel’s objectives. Energy markets, shipping through Hormuz and the security of American partners make indefinite confrontation costly. An American exit requires persuading Israel to accept the survival of an independent Iran with an economic future in the region. It also requires Washington to accept that outcome itself.

Trump’s interview with TIME, published on 1 October, exposes the difficulty. Explaining why he had continued the campaign, he said he did not want Iran to return “in some different form”. An ending that depends on preventing Iranian reconstitution keeps the political purpose of the war open even after military objectives are declared achieved.

The tension also appears in the 2025 US National Security Strategy. It advocates accepting Middle Eastern countries’ historical forms of government while prioritising Israel’s security and the expansion of the Abraham Accords. The practical question is whether such acceptance extends to Iran, or whether Iran must remain the exception against which the region’s political and economic integration is organised.

Other regional states have a decisive role here. Their political acceptance of Iran need not involve adopting its institutions or sharing its revolutionary commitments. It means recognising that Iran’s historical and political form has a legitimate place alongside their own. Regional stability requires room for different states to pursue development without making one state’s permanent exclusion the condition of …

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: From Tigray to the Red Sea: Ethiopia’s War in a Wider Regional Struggle
content:
I am not a military expert, but I do not read the withdrawal of Tigrayan forces from towns as straightforward evidence that their military position has weakened. An army can leave towns, roads and airports without losing its ability to move, reorganize, coordinate and strike. The more important questions are whether the force remains intact, how mobile it is, whether it can coordinate across different fronts, and whether it can still choose where and when to engage.

That is how I look at what is happening around Mekelle. Reuters reported on October 2 that federal and allied forces were moving toward the Tigrayan capital, and the following day reported that they had retaken Alula Aba Nega Airport. On a conventional military map that looks like a major federal success. But the map may be giving us a false sense of what is actually happening.

Debretsion Gebremichael who is the president of Tigray had already announced a counteroffensive and said Tigrayan forces would not fight according to the government’s dictates. I therefore do not see their movement out of Mekelle as a setback. I see an orderly and deliberate withdrawal from a fixed urban position by a force whose leadership had already told us that it intended to choose a different battlefield.

That distinction is important. Under conditions of federal air and drone superiority, concentrating fighters and equipment inside a city can make them sitting ducks. Moving out can preserve forces, stretch the opponent and create possibilities elsewhere. During the struggle against the Derg, the TPLF repeatedly relied on mobility rather than treating possession of every town as the measure of military strength. Today’s circumstances are different, especially because of drones and surveillance, but that experience should not simply be forgotten.

As I argued in The Geography of Asymmetric War, military power cannot be measured only by territory. Terrain, mobility, strategic depth and the ability to force a stronger opponent to fight differently also matter. A counteroffensive does not have to begin by immediately retaking Mekelle. It can strike supply lines, isolated units, communications systems, airfields or another front entirely.

This is why I am cautious even about the language of a federal “advance.” Federal forces are certainly moving into places Tigrayan forces have left. But that does not necessarily mean that one army is advancing while the other is simply retreating. If one side is deliberately giving up fixed positions in order to preserve mobility and shift the war elsewhere, the territorial map can create an illusion of momentum that may turn out to be temporary.

Focusing only on Mekelle also misses how much the war has changed. Fighting extends through Amhara and Afar, and armed movements that were enemies only a few years ago are now cooperating against the same federal government. Afar matters because it lies between Tigray, Eritrea and the routes toward Ethiopia’s Djibouti corridor. Amhara matters because Fano and Tigrayan forces, who recently fought a devastating war against one another, are now cooperating. These are not secondary developments. They change the political and military meaning of the war.

I began writing about this changing landscape in Tsimdo and the Changing Politics of the Horn. The creation of the seven group Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival took that process much further. The political map that existed when Pretoria was signed no longer describes Ethiopia, which is why I later argued that Pretoria Cannot Explain Ethiopia Anymore.

The map can show federal troops entering Mekelle. It cannot easily show former enemies learning to fight together. Nor can it show what has happened hundreds of miles behind the supposed front line in Bishoftu and Addis Ababa.

For years the federal government could use aircraft and drones against its opponents while assuming that its own air bases, military command and political center were safely beyond their reach. That assumption has been shattered. Drones have reportedly struck Harar Meda Air Base at Bishoftu, headquarters of the Ethiopian Air Force. Ethiopia Observer reported explosions inside the base and described considerable alarm among military personnel.

This is much more than another attack on a military installation. Drone warfare was one of the decisive advantages that helped Abiy Ahmed’s government survive when Tigrayan forces approached Addis Ababa in 2021. Now the …

author: Nolan Higdon
title: Corporate Media Consolidation Is What Makes Trump’s War on the Press Possible
content:
As mergers concentrate outlets in the hands of a few billionaires, the right’s grip on mainstream media grows tighter.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

“CNN, MSNOW and Politico back at the White House, hours after judge ordered Trump to lift ban,” read a September 24, 2026 Associated Press headline, published just one week after the administration had barred the three outlets from press briefings. In response to the ban, the White House press pool — a rotating group of journalists, photographers, and broadcast technicians organized by the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) to cover the President of the United States (U.S.) — refused to participate in news conferences until the ban was lifted. Even after the federal courts put a temporary 14-day restraining order on the ban, CNN, unlike right wing media producers, was blocked from covering Trump on Air Force One. Rather than waiting for the courts to issue a permanent ruling halting the Trump administration’s punishment of CNN, the press pool abandoned its protest and returned to the White House following the restraining order. When the press pool traded collective solidarity for a rushed return to the briefing room, it laid bare a troubling structural reality: in modern journalism, the pursuit of daily access routinely overrides the defense of a free press.

President Donald Trump publicly justified the press ban on national security grounds. However, the move was more plausibly driven by political vulnerability. Facing historically low approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections — with his party underwater in 47 states and projected to lose both chambers of Congress — the administration sought to suppress widespread public discontent by censoring the press. Compounding this friction, the White House released taxpayer-funded advertisements promoting the Republican agenda that sparked bipartisan warnings of illegality, functioning essentially as state propaganda disguised as public service announcements. These spots featured dubious claims, such as pledging to dismantle the “deep state” — despite the administration’s own deep-state affiliations and ties to figures like the late Jeffrey Epstein — or promising to eliminate “warmongers” from government while simultaneously prosecuting an elective war in Iran.

The court’s decision to suspend the ban came as no surprise given that the 1977 federal appeals court ruling Sherrill v. Knight established that while the government is not strictly required to open its doors to the media, once it voluntarily establishes a public press facility or invites the press, it cannot arbitrarily ban or deny access to specific news outlets based on the content or viewpoint of their coverage. Furthermore, efforts to execute similar authoritarian bans on journalists Jim Acosta and Brian Karem during Trump’s first administration and the Associated Press in his second term failed.

Nor did it come as a surprise that other corporate-funded news outlets eventually abandoned their refusal to cover the White House, capitulating before the courts could legally invalidate the ban. The underlying reasons for this collapse are structural: contemporary media outlets are tethered above all to profit maximization. To capture market share, they routinely pander to audiences’ desires for partisan confirmation, prioritizing ideological validation over journalistic veracity. This began with Fox News Channel, which pioneered the art of hyper-partisan conservatism to attract an audience, and was subsequently copied by outlets such as MSNOW (formerly MSNBC), which soon did the same for liberals. At the same time, newspapers shifted online to a subscriber model where they, too, were caught up in ideological bias, trying to confirm the political biases of their audiences while manufacturing conflict against the “other party.”

Beyond partisan narratives, the press’s profit model remains anchored in the age-old adage that “if it bleeds, it ledes.” Consequently, corporate media outlets prioritize sensationalistic content — often described as junk food news, such as gossip, scandals, and inflammatory rhetoric — over substantive reporting. This for-profit imperative has proven uniquely detrimental in the Trump era, as his mastery of provocative staging and hyper-partisan unpredictability allows him to dictate media coverage — whether by …

title: Pervin Buldan’dan “süreç” açıklaması: “Ekim ayıyla birlikte somut bir gelişmeye tanıklık edebiliriz”
content:
DEM Parti İmralı Heyeti Üyesi Pervin Buldan, Abdullah Öcalan’ın hem silahsızlanma sürecinde hem de siyasal ve demokratik inşa sürecinde koordinatörlük görevini üstleneceğini dile getirdi. Buldan, “Önümüzdeki günlerde bu konuda somut bir gelişmeye tanıklık edebiliriz” dedi.

MA’dan Adnan Bilen’in sorularını yanıtlayan Pervin Buldan, yaptıkları son görüşmede PKK Lideri Öcalan’ın, sürecin ilerlemesi için herkesin inisiyatif alması ve siyasi feraset göstermesi gerektiğinin üzerinde durduğunu aktardı. Buldan, “Süreçte pozitif barış aşamasına geçmemizi sağlayacağını söyledi. Yani yüz yıllık meselenin silahlı kısmıyla değil, siyasal kısmıyla ilgili müzakerelerin olacağı ve adımların atılacağı aşamaya geçeceğiz” dedi.

Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan ve Meclis Başkanı Kurtulmuş’un bugüne kadar sürece pozitif katkı yaptığını belirten Buldan, “Silah bırakma meselesinin sürecin temel başlıklarından biri olduğunu biliyoruz ve bu konudaki hassasiyeti anlıyoruz. Ama bu durumun karşılıklı adımlarla çözülebileceğine inanıyoruz. Burada önemli olan, bu tür söylemlerin sürecin önünde bir ön şart olarak değil, birlikte yürüyen adımların bir parçası olarak ele alınmasıdır” diye konuştu.

Abdullah Öcalan’ın hem silahsızlanma sürecinde hem de siyasal ve demokratik inşa sürecinde koordinatörlük görevini üstleneceğini dile getiren Buldan, şöyle devam etti: “Bunun için kurulan kurulun koordinesini sağlaması, toplumun farklı kesimleriyle görüşmesi, özgür çalışma ve iletişim koşullarının sağlanması kaçınılmaz bir gerekliliktir. Kurul, sürecin ilerlemesinin deyim yerindeyse atar damarı olacak. Kurul hem silahsızlanma süreçlerini yönetecek hem de siyasallaşma sürecinde aktif rol alacak. Bu iki alanın aynı kurul çatısı altında ele alınması, birbirini tamamlayan adımların eşgüdüm içinde atılmasını sağlayacak. Silahsızlanmada atılan her adım siyasal alanı genişletecek; siyasal alanda sağlanan her güvence de silahsızlanma sürecine güven katacak. Bu yönüyle kurulun başarısı, sürecin bütününe duyulan güvenin de teminatı olacaktır. Ekim ayıyla birlikte bu görüşmelerin başlaması ve hukuki güvencelerle sürekliliğinin sağlanması gerekiyor. Önümüzdeki günlerde bu konuda somut bir gelişmeye tanıklık edebiliriz.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing opposition, reshuffled hope for Idris’s govt, tribal violence engulfs South Darfur, military opens road to West Kordofan, China on Sudan’s coast
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


Sudan’s government is taking a long hard look in the mirror, and they don’t like what they see, sources close to Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the Transitional Sovereignty Council

told

 Mada Masr this week.

 


Ushered in on a promise of hope a year ago, Idris’s government has faced significant issues. Some of those come down to war-time trials, but infighting and attempts to delimit the remit of a civilian government backed by a powerful and intrusive military council have been persistent issues. 


Now the government is considering a reshuffle of ministerial and gubernatorial appointments to address executive imbalances and shortfalls, particularly on economic and service-related issues, according to a source in Idris’s office.


While Idris and the TSC may see an administrative reshuffle as a way to address war-time woes, the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement insist that any bureaucratic rearrangement must not change the power-sharing agreement inked in the South Sudanese capital. 


For now, the reshuffle is all just talk. But the movements do not view it in isolation from the larger reshaping of the political landscape of recent months, a leader in one of the Juba armed movements told Mada Masr, particularly as the planned national dialogue will have to address their relationship with the government.


Outside military-controlled areas, the Rapid Support Forces have also been dealing with internal discord over the last two weeks, though the dispute they are presiding over has a decidedly less understanding and diplomatic tenor. 


Throughout September, deadly inter-tribal clashes have engulfed South Darfur. With heavy weapons in hand and grappling with a faltering rainy season, tribes in Gereida, about 90 km south of Nyala, and in southern parts of Nyala itself, have become embroiled in violent confrontations. 


The RSF has tried to step in to calm the situation, deploying troops to prevent it from continuing to spiral out of control. As residents look on to see how effective these immediate tamping down measures will be, civil society and RSF sources agree that the much more difficult problem will be halting the spread of heavy weapons into residential communities, which allows competition over water, pasture and farmland during droughts to become increasingly militarized. 


On Sudan’s battlefields this week, the military cleared the last major RSF defensive positions in North Kordofan, effectively opening the West Kordofan front. These losses have triggered yet another defection from the paramilitary group, as Al-Tayeb “Waheedo” Mohamed Ahmed arrived to Omdurman, saying he left after witnessing “tragedies” and “collapse” within the RSF’s ranks.


But while frontline battles remain consequential, drone warfare continues to figure in Sudan’s conflict. RSF drones struck targets in Gezira and North Kordofan over the week, reaching fuel infrastructure east of Wad Madani and multiple sites in Obeid, where at least six civilians were killed.


This week also saw a series of tense diplomatic exchanges. The first came at the UN General Assembly’s  debate on Monday, with the United Arab Emirates and Sudanese delegations engaging in tug-of-war over the narrative on Sudan’s conflict. A former official said the spat does not necessarily signal another diplomatic rupture. 


But the second tense diplomatic moment could prove more consequential. Ethiopia, recently plunged into another civil war, accused Sudan of abetting opposition fighters then took the more drastic diplomatic step of expelling Eritrean and Egyptian diplomats. 


While wars and their fallout dominate the headlines this week, Sudan is taking steps toward a post-war future. And as with previous attempts to attract foreign powers to Khartoum, this future projection involves lucrative real estate on Sudan’s Red Sea coast. 


But instead of Russia or the UAE, this time, it is China that is coming in to revive the Abu Amama port project, two years after Sudan cancelled a memorandum of understanding with an Emirati-led consortium to execute the project.  


***


After TSC review, Idris prepares for govt reshuffle, Juba armed movements to join talks


Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the members of the “Government of Hope.” Courtesy: The Government of Hope.


Prime Minister Kamel Idris has begun holding consultations in recent days in preparation for reshuffling his government just …

title: Data Center a Modena: dati in pasto alla guerra
content:
Introduzione


Brescia, 18 agosto 2026. Festa di Radio Onda d’Urto. Temperature da fornace padana, nell’estate più lunga, torrida e faticosa mai registrata in Italia. Insieme a noi, sotto la tensostruttura dove si svolge il dibattito, decine e decine di persone. Provenienti da tutta la Lombardia e, come noi modenesi, anche da fuori regione. A prendere parola sono esperti, giornalisti, analisti, cittadini preoccupati e incazzati, ex consiglieri comunali, appartenenti a realtà territoriali e comitati locali, e militanti. Il tema, non a caso, non è mai stato più “caldo”:

Data Center: il volto materiale dell’Intelligenza Artificiale

. 


Il dibattito è un prezioso momento di informazione sulla mobilitazione popolare e territoriale che, dalla provincia lombarda e non solo, sta emergendo con sempre più voce in contrapposizione alla proliferazione e alla nocività di imponenti Data Center nell’hinterland milanese e bresciano al servizio delle capacità di elaborazione delle AI. Una lotta che, dalle periferie degli Stati Uniti dove è in avanzamento sempre più di massa a quelle italiane dove comincia a muovere i primi embrionali passi, sta già facendo fare i conti con le contraddizioni e le ambivalenze dentro questa fase di ristrutturazione capitalistica, con i costi e la direzione di un certo tipo di sviluppo, con le scelte politiche (e geopolitiche) di chi comanda la vita del Paese e sui territori dove cresciamo, abitiamo, lavoriamo. Territori come anche quello di Modena. 


Ristrutturazione e guerra


Nonostante lo spazio emiliano non risulti essere – per il momento… – nell’area di maggior interesse di questo specifico e accelerato sviluppo, a tratti e insieme fortemente speculativo, che sta scompaginando equilibri ecologici, politici e del “quieto vivere cittadino” lombardo, vogliamo provare a ipotizzare la traiettoria della linea che collega la proliferazione dei Data Center allo strutturarsi in «fabbrica della guerra» della nostra provincia. 


Come mostrato nell’inchiesta di Kamo Modena

Il laboratorio della guerra. Tracce per un’inchiesta sull’università dentro la «fabbrica della guerra» di Modena

, infatti, l’implementazione dell’intelligenza artificiale – nella cui ricerca, non a caso anche a fini bellici, e promozione è protagonista Rita Cucchiara, la nuova rettrice dell’Università di Modena e Reggio – è materializzata nei numerosi progetti e laboratori Unimore in tale ambito presenti in città,  ed è considerata il principale driver di trasformazione produttiva (ma non solo: pensiamo alla sua implementazione nei processi dell’«industria della formazione», che fa dell’intera «fabbrica sociale» e di produzione della soggettività il campo della sua azione) necessario a una ristrutturazione del tessuto industriale composto, a livello locale, prevalentemente da attori e imprese di medio-piccole dimensioni ben inserite nelle catene del valore nazionali e globali. Ristrutturazione che risulta strategica nell’ottica di rientrare competitivamente e cavalcare

«la curva dell’accumulazione capitalistica nel tempo della crisi e della guerra»

. 


Si tratta quindi di implementazione dell’intelligenza artificiale nei processi produttivi, produzione di tipo

dual use

 civile-militare di tecnologia, integrazione e reindirizzamento delle filiere, politiche belliche e commesse militari orientate al riarmo. Dalla

«Motor Valley» alla «Drone Valley»

. È un sistema industriale complessivo, allargato e integrato, che prende una direzione precisa, più che la somma aritmetica delle singole imprese. È qui, in questo processo territorializzato, che si produce per la guerra, e quindi la guerra stessa. Cosa c’entrano i Data Center?


Il volto materiale e geopolitico dell’AI 


Come suggerito dal nome scelto per il dibattito e riportato nella

pemultima uscita della newsletter Orizzonti

, che riprende i principali aspetti discussi a Brescia durante l’iniziativa, i Data Center rappresentano, di fatto, la dimensione materiale e per ora maggiormente tangibile della scala di diffusione sempre più accelerata dell’AI, specialmente in termini di impatti diretti sulla popolazione che vive e lavora dove sorgono queste abnormi strutture. Questi mostruosi centri di calcolo altamente energivori rappresentano infatti una componente fondamentale dell’infrastruttura fisica sulla quale in particolare i modelli AI sviluppati dalle Big Tech fanno affidamento per poter essere addestrati, grazie all’accumulazione ed elaborazione continua di sempre maggiori …

author: webadmin
title: Lessons in Hare Hunting: Inside Britain’s School Beagle Packs
content:
The private schools schooling children in a masterclass of wildlife criminality.


Recently we revealed the

full footage of the Stowe School Beagles

 during what school headteacher, Dr Anthony Wallersteiner, describes as a

“huge variety of activities”

 available to pupils, including

“field games…beagling”

.


Kennedy giving direction to the pupils


The school’s Games Coach, Phillip Kennedy, was in the fields surrounding Crockwell Farm, alongside school pupils, ‘coaching’ them as the Stowe School Beagles hunted a hare.


The school lesson ended with a dead hare and a criminal conviction for its Games Coach.


The now-deleted reference to Kennedy’s role at the Stowe School.


Kennedy pleaded guilty to hunting a wild mammal with dogs after drone footage captured his pack chasing the hare, first through the farmyard and then across open fields before catching and killing her against a fence.

Police said

 that Kennedy knew allowing his dogs to chase and kill the hare was cruel and illegal.


Just as importantly, the footage shone a spotlight on something that has gone on behind the closed doors of some of Britain’s most prestigious private schools: children being introduced to illegal hunting, more than twenty years after hunting wild mammals with dogs was banned.


There are serious safeguarding questions which Stowe School, in particular, appear determined to ignore. What risk assessments are made before children are taken out with packs of hunting dogs? What are staff instructed to do when those hounds begin pursuing a live animal? What safeguarding procedures kick in when pupils witness that animal being caught and killed?


Nothing in the footage suggests this was some unexpected aberration. They all know the routine, the kids congratulate each other, congratulate the dogs. Nobody looks shocked. The huntsman joins in with the handshaking. They’ve clearly done this before haven’t they!


Games Coach Philip Kennedy congratulating pupils as the hounds rip the remains of the hare apart close by.


Stowe is not alone.


There are other school beagle packs still taking children out into the countryside, maintaining the hounds and traditions of hare hunting.


Eton College has one of the oldest and most famous school beagle packs in the country.


Its history stretches back to the nineteenth century

. Long before the Hunting Act, generations of Eton boys learned their “hound lore” by pursuing hares with the school pack. Boys became Masters and Whips, and learned to handle hounds.


The Hunting Act came into force in 2005, but school lessons in hare-hunting continue.


In 2013, eight years after the ban, the Hunt Saboteurs Association

revealed plans

 for a Young Hare-Hunters’ Day at Eton. This was no historical re-enactment of hunting, children were actually being offered coaching in the skills and traditions of hare hunting.


Pupils were to receive training in hare hunting from experienced huntsmen, including Steven Duckmanton, the huntsman of the Dummer Beagles.


Steven Duckmanton, hare-hunting huntsman of the Dummer Beagles. Image: West Midlands Hunt Saboteurs.


In 2024,

West Midlands Hunt Saboteurs

 put a drone above those same Dummer Beagles. The footage they captured showed a hare breaking from the field and the pack pursuing her line across field after field, whilst hunt staff watched.


In October 2015,

footage was filmed

 at an Eton College Beagles meet in North Yorkshire, which showed a live hare fleeing across a field with the pack in pursuit. The footage was handed to North Yorkshire Police in January 2016 and Eton announced an urgent investigation.


Eleven years after hunting with dogs had supposedly been consigned to history, one of Britain’s most prestigious schools was having to investigate its own beagle pack over footage of a hare being hunted.


This year, Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg revealed his eldest son had brought 41 Eton beagles home with him during the school holidays.


His son, Peter Theodore Aphege Rees-Mogg, left Eton this summer. He wasn’t a mere follower of the hunt – he had been a Master of the Eton College Hunt during his final year.


Peter Theodore Aphege Rees-Mogg at home out with the Mendip Farmers Hunt. Image: Mendip Hunt Sabs.


Peter’s mother Helena, herself a regular fox hunter and meet host for the

recently-charged

 Mendip Farmers Hunt, went even further in an article published in September 2026.


Writing about why she believes Eton should remain an all-boys school …

content:
Dixon Mink Farm at 15028 Pony Express Road in the town of Bluffdale, Utah will be forced to close.
