author: winter oak
title: Never Accidentally Offer Luxury Recycled Cream Cakes to Portuguese Vegan Punks!
content:
This is the fifth and final chapter from the book 

King of the Squatters

 by jaybo which we are delighted to be able to share on Winter Oak. The whole text can be found as a pdf

here

.


I had enjoyed going for food at the social centre twice weekly. But it became tiresome for me to recognise blatant hierarchies and leaders when their on-line blurb claimed that they were anarchists against leaders, organised along horizontal lines, not vertical, top-down power structures. But my relationship with the social centre was completely destroyed one afternoon, after I had just recycled some expensive, fancy cream cakes.


In front of our house, a fiesta had been happening all weekend, so lots of drunken revellers engulfed our usually quiet home. Our squat had been under siege for the three days, being attacked by young adults who threw stones and came into our building looking for trouble. I had not been sleeping well and was very tired one day as I ate some luxury recycled cream cakes in the city centre. Then the social centre’s leader passed me and stopped to speak. We had only ever seen each other previously at the centre, never in public. I offered yer man a fancy cake, without thinking that they were patently not vegan.


He refused and asked me exactly where our squat was. I innocently told him directions to our home. Then he left to go on a demonstration against workers’ exploitation. That night as I walked home, I was stopped dead in my tracks by fresh graffiti on the bridge just before our squat. In big white letters it simply stated, “vegan limit!!!” I had no doubt that the vegan punk anarchist leader had just sprayed the graffiti as some kind of attempted bullshit intimidation directed at me. Because I had offered to share my hard-earned cakes with him.


I never went back to the social centre after that. I was so angry that I knew if I had returned then I would have certainly made trouble and probably have given the leader an excuse to ban me anyway. I hate egos and authoritarians. However, as always, I tried to turn a negative into a positive. That incident inspired one of my most popular signs for The Whimsical Atrocity Theatre (TWAT): “I only eat vegans”.


The next day, TWAT proudly unveiled its new message to the world. It worked immediately. The show was good. I was a little bit worried that one or more of the social centre vegan punks would pass by, see the sign and beat me up. I was probably safe in my theatre, as I usually had a police escort at one side, looking out for the tourists’ safety. But they knew where I lived.


Some brave souls came and spoke to me during or after my cardboard shenanigans. But things reached dizzying heights for TWAT when an American woman came up to me and asked me how much my signs were. I was absolutely flabbergasted. Someone wanted to buy my recycled carton signs. I replied to her spontaneously that, if she wanted to buy a sign, then she had to tell me how much it was. She put four euros into my hat for “I only eat vegans”. Black permanent marker pen on quality recycled cardboard.


Women were flirting with me almost every day when I performed, but I was caught completely off guard when an extremely attractive, well-dressed young French woman came up to me with her friends, picked up the condoms and said, “OK, let’s go!” She was absolutely serious and in a pathetic response, I replied, “You’re wearing a wedding ring.” She countered with, “It’s only an engagement ring. This is my last chance. Are you coming?” Her friends’ looks assured me that she was absolutely serious. I did not go. One of her friends looked at me as though I must have been insane. One of several potentially delicious sexual opportunities that I missed in life.


As the summer really heated up, it felt as though all of Portugal’s crazy folk were coming out of the woodwork and heading for fun in Lisbon. As I worked one day, a sun-drenched, handsome, young man swaggered up the steps towards me. He wore rags as clothes, had matted, unkempt hair flopping all over his face and had a long stick over his shoulder, with a cloth bundle tied up at the other end. He asked if he could write something on one of my signs. I told him he could, so he picked up “this sign was my bed” and wrote on it, “but I washed it in my jacuzzi first”, which killed me and the audience. Then he shouted for all to hear, “We are homeless because we choose to be.”


Before his departure, he asked me if he could take a condom because …

author: PETA-Team
title: Geheimsache Tierversuche: Neue ZDF-Doku zeigt Tierleid hinter verschlossenen Labortüren
content:
Symbolbild


Die neue „37°“-Dokumentation „Geheimsache Tierversuche – Unter Ausschluss der Öffentlichkeit“ geht der Frage nach, was eigentlich mit Tieren in Versuchslaboren geschieht – und warum die Öffentlichkeit so wenig davon sehen darf.


Am 

29. September 2026 um 22:15 Uhr im ZDF

 sehen die Zuschauer:innen hinter die Kulissen einer Branche, in der Mäuse, Ratten, Hunde, Affen, Kaninchen, Schweine und viele weitere Tiere für Experimente missbraucht werden.


Millionen Tiere leiden für „wissenschaftliche Zwecke“


Nach den offiziellen Zahlen wurden in Deutschland

im Jahr 2024 über drei Millionen Tiere

 für „wissenschaftliche Zwecke“ missbraucht. Einen großen Teil nimmt die Grundlagenforschung ein, in der Tieren zum Beispiel der Schädel aufgebohrt wird, um Elektroden in ihr Gehirn zu setzen. In regulatorischen, gesetzlich vorgeschriebenen Tests werden die Tiere teils vergiftet und getötet.


Solche Experimente finden nicht irgendwo weit entfernt statt, sondern an verschiedenen Forschungseinrichtungen in Deutschland.

Experimente an Affen

, die in der Dokumentation ebenfalls thematisiert werden, sind in der Hälfte der Bundesländer vertreten.


Was passiert in den Versuchslaboren?


Für die Dokumentation hat der Journalist Manfred Karremann mehr als ein Jahr lang versucht, Einblicke in deutsche Tierversuchslabore zu bekommen. Trotz angebotener Anonymität erklärte sich nur eine Einrichtung bereit, ein wenig Einblick zu geben.


Die Dokumentation macht damit ein Problem sichtbar, das Tierschützer:innen seit Jahren kritisieren: Tierversuche finden weitgehend im Verborgenen statt. Sie werden verharmlost und die wenigsten Menschen erfahren, was den Tieren tatsächlich angetan wird. Dabei geht es um Lebewesen, die Angst und Schmerzen empfinden wie wir – und die schlichtweg nicht dazu da sind, dass wir an ihnen experimentieren.


Die Dokumentation zeigt unter anderem Aufnahmen aus einem britischen Labor. Zu sehen sind Hunde,

Affen

, Kaninchen und Ratten, die für sogenannte

Giftigkeitstests

 missbraucht werden. Die Versuche gelten als standardisierte Verfahren und werden nach internationalen Richtlinien durchgeführt – auch in der EU. Tiere müssen dabei beispielsweise Chemikalien einatmen oder bekommen Testsubstanzen über einen Schlauch direkt in den Magen verabreicht.


Jetzt lesen


Forschung und Medizin


Tierversuche in Deutschland: Was wirklich in den Versuchslaboren passiert


In deutschen Tierversuchslaboren werden Affen, Hunde, Katzen, Nagetiere, Fische & Insekten gequält. Erfahren Sie hier mehr über die Versuche!


Jetzt lesen


Tierversuche sind keine gute Wissenschaft


Tierversuche werden oft als „wissenschaftlich notwendig“ gerechtfertigt – doch die Dokumentation zeigt, dass die Wissenschaft längst mit Methoden arbeitet, die ohne Tiermissbrauch auskommen. Expert:innen aus Industrie und Wissenschaft kommen zu Wort und erklären, warum modernste Methoden wie menschliche Zellkulturen oder Organs-on-a-Chip Tierversuchen nicht nur ethisch, sondern auch wissenschaftlich überlegen sind.


Diese Ansätze arbeiten direkt mit menschlichen Zellen und menschlichem Gewebe. Dadurch können sie bei bestimmten Fragestellungen auch Erkenntnisse liefern, die sich besser auf Menschen übertragen lassen.


Jetzt einschalten und hinschauen!


Die „37°“-Dokumentation gibt einen seltenen Einblick in die abgeschottete Welt, in der Tiere in Laboren ihr Leben lang gefangen sind – und zeigt gleichzeitig, warum es längst überfällig ist, dass sich Wissenschaft und Forschung von Tierversuchen abwenden.


„37°: Geheimsache Tierversuche – Unter Ausschluss der Öffentlichkeit“

 läuft am

Dienstag, 29. September 2026, um 22:15 Uhr im ZDF.

 Ab 5:00 Uhr ist die Dokumentation auch über das ZDF-Streaming-Angebot abrufbar.


Jede Unterschrift zählt


PETA fordert von nationalen und internationalen Entscheidungsträger:innen einen strategischen Ausstieg aus Tierversuchen und eine Modernisierung der Forschung. Unterstützen Sie den Research Modernisation Deal und helfen Sie uns, grausame Tierversuche endlich zu beenden.


Jetzt unterschreiben


The post

Geheimsache Tierversuche: Neue ZDF-Doku zeigt Tierleid hinter verschlossenen Labortüren

 appeared first on

PETA Deutschland e.V.

.

author: L214
title: Nourrir ou trahir. Comment l’élevage intensif saigne la France.
content:
On doit changer de modèle, découvrez comment :

Peu importe qui vous êtes et ce en quoi vous croyez : l’élevage intensif trahit vos valeurs.

Nous mangeons 85 kilos de viande par personne et par an, le double de la moyenne mondiale. Ni accident ni dérive, cette consommation de masse est le produit d’un système dont l’élevage intensif est la pierre angulaire.

Souveraineté alimentaire, santé publique, déforestation, biodiversité, ressource en eau, revenu des agriculteurs, sort des animaux : sur chacun de ces fronts, l’élevage intensif nous trahit. Il nous rend dépendants d’engrais et de soja importés, endette les éleveurs, favorise pandémies et antibiorésistance, nuit à l’environnement et entraîne l’abattage de plus de 3 millions d’animaux chaque jour pour la seule consommation française.

Nous n’avons pas choisi ce modèle. D’autres l’ont choisi pour nous. Ce livre, rédigé par Brigitte Gothière et Sébastien Arsac, cofondateurs de L214, défend une proposition pour reprendre la main ensemble : donnons-nous l’objectif de réduire de moitié le nombre d’animaux tués d’ici 2030. Parce que c’est possible. Parce que c’est vital.

d’animaux abattus chaque jour pour la seule consommation française.

Vous entrez dans un supermarché. Vous prenez un caddie. Vous suivez un itinéraire balisé. Vous voyez ce qui doit être vu, à la hauteur qu'il faut, au prix qu'il faut. Vous croisez la viande partout, les légumineuses presque nulle part. À la sortie, vous avez le sentiment d'avoir choisi.

« On nous a fait croire qu’il fallait choisir son camp : pour les agriculteurs ou pour les animaux, pour le climat ou pour la souveraineté alimentaire. Mais l’élevage intensif ne défend aucun de ces camps, il les renie tous en même temps. C’est ce que ce livre documente, chiffres à l’appui. »

« C’est un livre sur une impasse dont nous devons sortir collectivement. Réduire de moitié le nombre d’animaux tués d’ici 2030 est une nécessité, soutenue par une majorité de Français. Ceux qui croient que l’élevage intensif peut durer se bercent d’illusions. »

Nourrir ou trahir, comment l’élevage intensif saigne la France paru le 30 septembre 2026 aux éditions Payot, disponible au prix de 19 € sur notre boutique en ligne et en librairie.

author: Animal Rising Press
title: Guilty Verdict For King’s Sheep Rescuers In Theft Trial
content:
After a four-day trial at Norwich Crown Court, Rose Patterson, Sarah Foy, and Rosa Sharkey have all been found guilty of theft after the rescue of three lambs from King Charles III’s Sandringham Estate in May 2023. Sentencing to follow today.

Despite the verdict, Animal Rising claims that the rescue and subsequent trial have helped to put a spotlight on the reality behind animal farming in the UK, with over 10 million sheep being slaughtered yearly [1].

The controversial rescue made front-page news across the UK and headlines around the world [2]. It captured the attention of the British public, questioning how we relate to animals in the food system and if it’s a rescue or a theft to take them from farms.

Animal Rising director Rose Patterson, alongside Rosa Sharkey and Sarah Foy, rescued the lambs - Sammy, Sunny and Sooty - before informing police the following day. The women held signs outside Windsor Castle reading “I rescued the King’s sheep” before reporting what they had done to police. They each face up to 7 years' imprisonment.

Earlier this year, Patterson was found not guilty by a jury over another Animal Rising open rescue, after helping to rescue beagle puppies from MBR Acres, a facility breeding animals for testing [3].

Animal Rising director Rose Patterson, one of the three defendants found guilty today, said:

Sammy, Sunny and Sooty remain safe and are now fully grown.

The trial followed a series of open-rescue trials relating to Animal Rising’s rescue of beagles from MBR Acres. In January this year, Animal Rising made history by securing the UK’s first-ever not-guilty verdict in an open-rescue case [4]. The lambs were rescued from Appleton Farm, which forms part of the Sandringham estate.

Defendants Patterson and Foy are available for comment or broadcast interview upon request.

For further information, comment, or to arrange an interview, please email press@animalrising.org or call +44 1225 29 6691

High-Quality Pictures and Videos: https://show.pics.io/animal-rising-breaking-news

All images and videos in this file, on our social media, and website can be used with credit to Animal Rising under ‘fair use’ for the purposes of reporting.

[1] https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/cattle-sheep-and-pig-slaughter

[2] https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-12431619/Animal-Rising-protesters-charged-stealing-Kings-sheep-royal-Sandringham-Estate-driving-away-animals.html

https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-12126009/Will-stop-eco-clowns-Just-Stop-Oil-throw-orange-powder-Animal-Rising-kidnap-lambs.html

[3] https://www.cambsnews.co.uk/peterborough-court-acquittal-animal-rescue-beagles/

[4] https://www.animalrising.org/post/not-guilty-verdict-for-beagle-puppy-rescuers-in-landmark-legal-case

Rose Patterson, 37, is the Director of Animal Rising. An advocate for animals since 2012, she holds an MSc in Animal Welfare Science, Ethics, and Law and previously worked with World Animal Protection before joining Animal Rising in 2020.

Sarah Foy, 26, has been involved in a range of campaigns advocating for a just and sustainable food system that works for animals, farmers, and the planet. She brings a practical, hands-on approach to her advocacy, with real-world experience caring for rescued farm animals at sanctuaries and protesting alongside farmers.

Rosa Sharkey, 26, is a food charity worker. She is passionately committed to reducing the impact of our food system on the climate crisis, community action, and animal rights.

Animal Rising is a nonviolent campaign group working to fundamentally transform our relationship with animals and nature, and build a more sustainable future for animals, people and the planet. Animal Rising is calling on the Government to end factory farming by 2040 and support a transition to a sustainable plant-based food system.

The group has used a variety of civil disobedience and nonviolent direct action tactics, notably blockading McDonald's distribution centres in May 2021, blockading dairy industry sites in September 2022, disrupting the 2023 Grand National, rescuing lambs belonging to King Charles III in May 2023, and carrying out the UK’s largest undercover farm investigation in 2024.

author: Sophie Lemcke
title: So ist es, als Huhn in der Fleischindustrie leben zu müssen
content:
Die Hühnermast ist ein grausames System, das auf maximale Schnelligkeit, Wachstum und Profit ausgelegt ist und mit einem gewaltvollen Tod für die Tiere endet.


Wie fühlt es sich an, als „Masthuhn“ geboren zu werden

, ohne die Möglichkeit, der leidvollen Industrie zu entkommen

?


Der einzige Grund, weshalb die Industrie dich „produziert“ hat: Du sollst so schnell wie möglich so schwer wie möglich werden – und wirst dann getötet.


Du kommst in einem Hühnerschlupfbetrieb mit tausenden anderen Küken zur Welt. Um dich herum piepsen sie verzweifelt. Und auch du suchst nach Nähe und Wärme. Aber da ist keine Mutter, in deren Gefieder du dich kuscheln kannst – und du wirst sie auch niemals kennenlernen.

Noch am ersten Tag deines Lebens wirst du über Förderbänder geschleudert und in eine Kiste gepackt. Dann beginnt die oftmals stundenlange Fahrt zum Mastbetrieb – eingepfercht mit Dutzenden anderen Küken, ohne Wasser, ohne Nahrung.


Foto: Andrew Skowron


Du kommst in einer riesigen Halle an. Hier wirst du die nächsten rund 5 Wochen verbringen – die einzigen Wochen deines Lebens.


Um dich herum Tausende andere Küken. Du teilst dir einen Quadratmeter mit bis zu 23 anderen Tieren. Jetzt seid ihr noch klein, doch das wird sich schnell ändern.


Du wächst. Unnatürlich schnell. Das Futter steht dir Tag und Nacht zur Verfügung – hochkalorisch, proteinreich, entwickelt für maximales Wachstum in kürzester Zeit.


Du hast keinen Platz, um dich natürlich zu bewegen, es gibt nichts zum Erkunden. Keinerlei Möglichkeiten, deine natürlichen Verhaltensweisen auszuleben. Es ist trist und laut. Da ist nur diese Enge.


Die Luft ist stickig. Der Ammoniakgeruch von den Ausscheidungen Tausender Tiere brennt in deinen Augen, in deinen Lungen. Du bekommst Atemwegserkrankungen. Jeder Atemzug tut weh.


Dein Körper wurde durch jahrzehntelange Züchtung so manipuliert, dass du in wenigen Wochen das Gewicht erreichst, für das ein Huhn unter natürlichen Bedingungen Monate bräuchte.


Foto: Andrew Skowron


Deine Brustmuskeln wachsen so schnell und werden so schwer, dass deine Knochen dein Gewicht nicht mehr tragen können. Deine Beine verformen sich. Dein Herz ist zu klein für deinen massiven Körper, es hat Probleme, deine Organe mit ausreichend Blut zu versorgen. Du hast Schmerzen beim Gehen und deine Gelenke sind entzündet.


Um dich herum sind Hühner, die gar nicht mehr aufstehen können. Sie liegen in ihrem eigenen Kot und leiden unter extremen Schmerzen. Sie verdursten und verhungern.


Andere Hühner werden aufgrund der Enge von ihren Artgenossen versehentlich totgetrampelt und erdrückt – ihre Körper verwesen zwischen dir und den tausenden anderen Tieren. Auch du hast keine Chance, den anderen Hühnern auszuweichen.


Dann ist es soweit. Menschen kommen und packen dich. An deinen Beinen, kopfüber, werden du und deine Artgenossen gegriffen und in enge Transportkisten geworfen. Deine ohnehin schon schmerzenden Beine brechen unter der groben Behandlung. Du hast Schmerzen und Todesangst.


Zusammengepfercht, ohne Wasser, ohne Futter, geht es zum Schlachthof. Die Fahrt kann Stunden dauern. Manche Hühner sterben bereits im Transporter – vor Stress, vor Erschöpfung, erdrückt von anderen Tieren.


Foto: Andrew Skowron


Im Schlachthof riechst du Blut. Du hörst die Schreie anderer Hühner. Dann bist du selbst an der Reihe. Unter grausamen Bedingungen wirst du betäubt und getötet. Du bist gerade einmal 35 bis 42 Tage alt geworden.


Es ist unvorstellbar, was Hühner in der Fleischindustrie erleiden müssen.


Die Wahrheit hinter „Hähnchenfleisch“


Wie grausam das kurze Leben von sogenannten Masthühnern ist, haben wir schon mehrfach bei Undercover-Recherchen aufgedeckt, beispielsweise in einem (jetzt ehemaligen) Zuliefererbetrieb der großen Marke Wiesenhof. Hier erfährst du mehr über unsere Aufdeckungen und kannst unsere Petition für strengere Tierschutzvorgaben, -kontrollen und -strafen unterzeichnen:


Jetzt für Hühner unterschreiben 


In Deutschland wird mehr Fleisch von Hühnern konsumiert als produziert – und die Nachfrage ist in den vergangenen Jahren stetig gestiegen. Unterstütze dieses grausame System nicht: Entscheide dich konsequent für pflanzliche Lebensmittel.


In den meisten Supermärkten findest du mittlerweile eine Vielfalt tierfreundlicher Alternativen, die hervorragende Proteinquellen sind – probiere sie aus. Oder koche unsere zahlreichen pflanzlichen Rezepte von Love Veg nach, wie unsere

knusprigen Tofu-Nuggets

.

author: webadmin
title: Eggesford in the Dock: Huntsman Convicted of Illegal Hunting
content:
Eggesford Hunt huntsman Jason Marles has been convicted of illegally hunting a fox with hounds following an incident captured on drone footage during the hunt’s Boxing Day meet in December 2025.


Jason Marles, huntsman of the Eggesford Hunt.


Marles, 44, pleaded guilty to hunting a wild mammal with dogs at Pudson Farm, near Okehampton, when he appeared before Exeter Magistrates’ Court on 23 September 2026.


His conviction followed footage recorded by Devon County Hunt Saboteurs which showed a fox being bolted from an area of rubble before being pursued by hounds. Hunt saboteurs positioned on a farm track nearby were in position to stop the hounds from chasing the fox, and they confirmed that the fox managed to evade capture.


The footage shows Marles standing beside the area where the fox had taken refuge, close to a cattle barn. Two men with spades are moving rubble and digging at the site, while a child, who had dismounted from their pony, also watches what is happening.


Huntsman Jason Marles looks on as landowner Lloyd Heard and terrier-man Tom Bounsall dig and remove the rubble protecting the hunted fox. Image credit: Devon County Hunt Saboteurs.


Devon County Hunt Sabs identify the two men digging as Eggesford terrier man Tom Bounsall and landowner Lloyd Heard.


WATCH THE VIDEO


After Marles realised a drone was overhead, and they had walked back to the farmyard, Marles and Heard swapped coats in a comical, and ultimately futile attempt to avoid identification.


Huntsman Jason Marles wearing Lloyd Heard’s jacket after the dig out. Tom Bounsall follows behind on a quad. Image: Devon County Hunt Saboteurs.


Bounsall is a terrier-man for both the Eggesford Hunt and the Spooners & West Dartmoor Hunt. Pictured here at a Spooners meet in March 2026. Image: Plymouth & West Devon Hunt Sabs.


After several minutes, the fox bolts from its refuge and runs for the surrounding cover. The hounds follow, beginning the chase. No attempt to call the hounds back was made.


Heard was also charged alongside Marles with hunting offences relating to both the Boxing Day incident at Pudson Farm and a second incident near Crediton in February 2026.


As the landowner of Pudson Farm, Heard also faced a further charge under Section 3 of the Hunting Act of knowingly permitting his land to be used for hunting a wild mammal with dogs.


Lloyd Heard, landowner of Pudson Farm, where the fox was dug out and subsequently pursued by hounds. Image: Devon County Hunt Saboteurs.


The proceedings against Heard were

subsequently withdrawn by the prosecution

. No reason for that decision has been made public.


Heard also has a close family connection to the leadership of hunting’s governing body. He is the son-in-law of British Hound Sports Association

Executive Director Julian Barnfield

.


Barnfield is himself a former huntsman with previous Hunting Act convictions. Whilst huntsman of the Heythrop Hunt, he pleaded guilty to

four separate counts of unlawfully hunting foxes

 between 2011 and 2012.


Julian Barnfield (right), who turned up to Crewe Magistrates court in 2022 to support another convicted fox hunter – former Quorn Huntsman Ollie Finnegan (left). Image: Cheshire Against Blood Sports (CABS).


Barnfield also has a longstanding connection to former Prime Minister David Cameron. In 2008, when Barnfield was facing an earlier prosecution under the Hunting Act, Cameron – then leader of the Opposition and Barnfield’s constituency MP –

wrote to the Attorney General on his behalf

 following a private meeting between the two. Those proceedings against Barnfield were subsequently discontinued on a technical issue.


The connection is worth noting. The Heythrop was David Cameron’s local hunt, and

he rode with it on numerous occasions

 before the Hunting Act came into force. It is also reported that David Cameron is ‘friendly’ with Barnfield, Heard’s father-in-law.


David Cameron

 pictured with the Heythrop Hunt in 2004. Image: Daily Mail.


Cameron remains a vocal supporter of fox hunting. As recently as September 2026,

he described the incoming ban on so-called ‘trail hunting

’ as “completely wrong”, urging the minority within the rural community who support hunting to “stand together and fight together”.


None of this establishes that political connections played any part in the decision to drop the charges against Heard. But it does illustrate something that has long characterised fox hunting – those who enjoy hunting …

author: groundxero
title: Purulia’s Bero-Chandi Pahar Faces Renewed Threat from Granite Mining
content:
Community-led ecological restoration and a centuries-old cultural landscape face destruction as quarrying resumes; villagers allege criminalisation of resistance


 


Purulia, West Bengal:

 The Bero-Chandi hillocks in Purulia’s Raghunathpur subdivision are facing renewed threats from granite and stone mining, with local communities and environmental activists warning that continued quarrying could destroy a landscape shaped by decades of ecological regeneration, traditional worship and local cultural history.


 


An appeal issued by those supporting the local resistance has called on civil society organisations, environmental groups, human rights organisations, student movements and cultural activists across West Bengal to intervene against what it describes as the “aggressive granite stone mining” now threatening Bero-Chandi Pahar. The appeal demands an immediate and unconditional halt to all granite and stone mining activities and the withdrawal of criminal cases against villagers and environmental activists.


 


Ecological Restoration and Wildlife Resurgence


 


According to the appeal, the Bero-Chandi hillocks are far more than geological formations. They represent a vibrant, living landscape in which ecology, community life, traditional practices and literary history are closely intertwined. The area had suffered extensive loss of tree cover for decades. Local residents subsequently undertook sustained community-led afforestation, gradually restoring the green cover and reviving the local ecosystem.


 


The restoration reportedly brought back a range of wildlife, including striped hyenas, wild pigs, Indian pythons, jackals and two species of rabbits, alongside numerous resident and migratory birds. The return of avifauna, the appeal states, also contributed to improved soil enrichment, water retention and the local micro-hydrological cycle.


 


This fragile ecosystem and the peaceful lives of the local communities protecting it face imminent destruction due to resumption of aggressive granite stone mining.


 


Living Cultural Heritage and Historical Roots


 


The Bero-Chandi hills are deeply intertwined with the spiritual and cultural identity of the region. The sacred worship of Devi Chandi at this site dates back at least 300 years, anchoring the traditional spiritual practices of the local populace.


 


The landscape holds profound literary value for Bengal. It served as the central backdrop for Bibhutisbhusan Bandyopadhyay’s classic Bengali masterpiece,

“Rankini Devir Kharag”

 written over 80 years ago.


 


The hills harbour ancient natural cave systems that form an integral part of the local terrain and ecosystem.


 


It is this historical and cultural heritage that villagers say is now at risk from renewed quarrying.


 


Villagers’ Resistance

to Mining and Criminalisation of Dissent


 


Low-intensity granite quarrying in the region began around 2014. Facing the threat of ecological devastation, local villagers mounted a peaceful yet resolute resistance, eventually succeeding in stopping operations by 2018.


 


Commercial mining operations, however, resumed in 2024. The resumption was preceded by the targeting of local leadership and environment activists. At least 14 villagers were implicated in fabricated criminal charges, thrust into police custody, and incarcerated for 14 days before securing bail. The use of state force and intimidation to silence environmental defenders and suppress local resistance to mining is a gross violation of democratic norms and community rights.


 


For the communities resisting the mining, the issue is not simply one of land use or quarrying. They argue that the destruction of the hillocks would also mean the loss of a regenerated forest landscape, wildlife habitat and water catchment areas on which surrounding agriculture and community life depend. They warn that continued industrial-scale granite and stone extraction could permanently damage sacred sites, cultural traditions and geological formations associated with the hills.


 


Urgent Appeal to Civil Society


 


The appeal argues that local communities have shown exemplary courage in safeguarding their environment, but they cannot be expected to confront politicians backed powerful commercial mining interests on their own, particularly amid a reign of intimidation and repression.


 


It calls on democratic organisations, environmental and human rights groups, students, cultural …

author: Maia Siegel
title: Corporations Are Dodging Accountability for PFAS Contamination Around the Globe
content:
A landmark settlement confronts decades of pollution — but the corporate system keeps moving the toxic waste elsewhere.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

I grew up walking the boardwalk in downtown Wilmington, North Carolina, peering into the froth of the Cape Fear River. The name came from 16th-century mariners who feared its mouth, which was known to churn ships into wrecks. But for the last few decades, there has been something new to fear in the river.

The Cape Fear River was tainted with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the Wilmington Star-News reported in 2017, a group of synthetic compounds now commonly known as “forever chemicals.”

As their name suggests, forever chemicals are renowned for their persistence. One of the strongest bonds in chemistry, carbon and fluorine, gives PFAS their nonstick properties. A seemingly endless list of products — dental floss, tampons, cellphones, wall paint, yoga pants, carpets, contact lenses, hair-straightening treatments, toilet paper — rely on those bonds to smooth, harden, slicken, and withstand heat and wear. But that chemical strength also means that PFAS don’t break down in the environment. They accumulate over time, contaminating our soil, produce, fish, and drinking water — and eventually finding their way into us.

These forever chemicals were flowing into the river from a production facility in Bladen County, North Carolina, operated by Chemours, a chemical company that manufactures Teflon, the coating used in nonstick cookware. When the news broke, I was 15 years old and had been drinking the city’s tap water all my life. Nearly all of Wilmington had: The Cape Fear, the state’s largest river, supplies 80 percent of the city’s drinking water. The water was clear, and it tasted fine — but that didn’t mean it was clean. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has linked PFAS chemicals to a host of severe health issues, including increased risk of prostate, kidney, and testicular cancers, as well as decreased fertility, reduced ability to fight infections, and developmental delays in children.

After years of public outcry, state officials announced a breakthrough earlier this month. The state had reached a $590 million deal with Chemours and associated companies to provide residents with clean water and repair the damage the pollution has caused. Politicians hailed the payout — the largest environmental-damages settlement in North Carolina history — as a major step forward in holding the company accountable for decades of damage.

But the agreement stops at the state line — while the contamination does not.

I had assumed, when I began researching Chemours’ pollution, that it was a local problem. But I quickly learned that it’s not just North Carolina struggling to navigate a new forever-chemical normal; it’s not even just the United States. The fluorochemical industry has a pattern of shuffling around PFAS production and waste, from North Carolina to Texas, from Italy to India. Every stop leaves a trail of contamination in its wake.

Chemours operates offices in North and South America, Europe, and Asia, as well as 21 production facilities across the world, not counting research and development sites. Alongside my home state, PFAS contamination has been reported around Chemours’ production plant in West Virginia, as well as around its facilities in Changshu, China, Villers-Saint-Paul, France, Dordrecht, Netherlands, and Mechelen, Belgium. One of the main PFAS chemicals made at Fayetteville Works has even been found in the snow at Antarctica’s Dome.

Tightening regulations in one state or country, I learned, pushes PFAS to another. And because PFAS are so durable, “destroying” them is more like moving them somewhere else for a while; common destruction methods, such as incineration, are often unable to fully destroy the compound. The Department of Defense has described thermal technologies like incineration as having “higher levels of uncertainties regarding their capacity to control the migration of PFAS into the environment.”

In other words, removing forever chemicals from one country, state, or river, such as the Cape Fear, just leads to a larger question: Where will they go next?

On an oppressively muggy day last July, I visited an organic farm in Castle Hayne, North Carolina, run by Ty Jacobus. He grows the essential ingredient in …

title: Göksu: Lasting peace requires stronger democratisation
content:
Musician Yasemin Göksu told ANF that lasting peace could only be achieved through democratisation and said, “Replacing violence with dialogue and weapons with politics offers an invaluable opportunity for society.”


Göksu said music was one of the most powerful carriers of memory and that an environment of lasting peace would also contribute to the freedom of the arts. She also said: “Once lasting peace is established, artists will be able to create more freely and people will have greater access to one another’s cultures.”


How can artists contribute to building peace and making it part of society during this period? What role can music play in ensuring that peace resonates not only at the negotiating table but also in everyday life, in people’s minds and consciences?


I do not see peace as an issue that should be discussed only at the negotiating table by political actors. The real test of peace, and of the parties involved, takes place in everyday life. How we see one another, how much we listen to and truly hear each other’s stories, and how well we manage to live alongside one another with our differences are all vitally important.


Art, and music in particular, undoubtedly has a very special power in this respect. Music has the ability to bridge in an instant distances that cannot be overcome through words alone. I have been singing songs in different languages for years. Every language contains a different story, a different pain and a different joy.


I see something very clearly on stage: even when people do not understand one another’s languages, they can still understand the emotion of a melody, and this can change the way they see one another. The real challenge is to resist obsessive and toxic political arguments and internalise the beauty of hearing a sentence or a word expressed in every language, rather than insisting on hearing only one.


For me, this is precisely where art can contribute to peace: not by making us all the same, but by allowing us to hear one another through our differences and come together through shared emotions.


We should now be able to speak freely about living in a more democratic society in which all citizens of Turkey can feel equal, free and safe, and where differences are not regarded as a threat. For me, that too is part of what peace means.


It is also said that the path to peace requires confronting past suffering and the truth. How does music serve as a space of memory in this process of reckoning?


Music is one of the most powerful carriers of memory anywhere in the world. You can read about certain events in books or see them documented in records, but music can make you feel the full emotion of what happened deep within you. It can also heighten the impact of an image even without being its central element.


The music of our region also carries an immense memory: migration, separation, loss, love, poverty, war, longing and massacres. All of these continue to live through music as life goes on.


Memory, of course, is not simply about remembering pain. I believe confronting the past begins with acknowledging the existence of different forms of suffering without setting them against one another.


Our role here is not to pass judgement like historians or politicians. What you can do politically is help people hear, understand and feel one another’s past and present. When you sing a folk song, you may touch the pain or happiness of someone you have never met. I believe genuine reckoning begins with being able to look impartially at the mistakes and wrongdoings of individuals or states, without taking ownership of them, and say, “Your pain is as real as mine.”


Conflict and violence place the heaviest burden on women. Militarism and male domination seem to reinforce one another. What can a women’s perspective contribute to peace and to the language of peace?


Women’s experience of war and conflict is often not limited to what happens on the battlefield. It has profound consequences at home, within families, in children’s lives, and through displacement, poverty and loss.


But I do not want to reduce women’s contribution to peace to a statement such as “women are more peaceful”. There are, after all, many women around the world who willingly serve patriarchal structures and see themselves as actors within that system.


I believe women’s different experiences and the lessons they draw from everyday life need to play a greater role in shaping the factors that …

author: Charlize Tomaselli
title: Not Energy, But Power: why Geothermal Energy Benefits Everyone in Iceland but not Kenya
content:
This article draws on in-person interviews at Mt Suswa, Olkaria, and Menengai with


Coalition for Human Rights in Development

 (CHRD) members and partners directly affected by geothermal projects. Interviews were led by the Coalition’s Research and Learning Facilitator and interviewees identified through the


Community Resource Exchange

 (CRE),

a system to facilitate collaborations and co-develop strategies with and among communities defending their rights in the context of international investments and development projects. The analysis also incorporates a review of Kenyan and Icelandic energy policy documents and insights from the Coalition’s roles in the


AfDB Civil Society Working Group

 and its Energy Sub-Group.


 

In Iceland, geothermal energy – one of the cleanest solutions to the climate crisis – is widely hailed as a success story. It supplies

65 % of the country’s electricity

 and heats

nearly 90%

 of its households. Everyone benefits from it.


Thousands of kilometres away, in Kenya, steam rising from the Rift Valley drives one of Africa’s

largest geothermal programmes

, supplying

nearly half of the country’s electricity

. According to recent data, Kenya is the world’s

sixth-largest geothermal producer

. Yet, its projects are entangled in disputes over land, livelihoods and rights, with local communities left grappling with acid rain, noise pollution and toxic soil.


Steam pipe in Hell’s Gate natural park, Kenya. 2017. Photo credit: Wikimedia Commons.


So how can geothermal energy be celebrated as a success story in one country, and a source of conflict, contestation and environmental harm in another? The difference lies not in the energy resource itself, but in how this resource is governed, financed, and embedded within different social and political contexts. It’s not about energy, it’s about power.


Different technologies, different risks


Different technologies used in geothermal systems, particularly with regard to the management of by-products such as brine and emissions, can lead to different levels of environmental risk.


In Iceland, geothermal operations are characterised by high rates of reinjection to reduce water use, minimal use of open brine storage, and increasing efforts to capture and reinject emissions such as hydrogen sulphide. Environmental challenges are largely approached as technical problems, with the resources and institutional capacity to address them and minimize harm.


In Kenya, while water reinjection does take place, it is not always consistent or effective. In some cases, particularly during drilling or testing phases, geothermal fluids are stored in open, unattended ponds. Infrastructure limitations, cost constraints, and poor monitoring lead to air, water and noise pollution, which has a harmful impact on the health and livelihoods of affected communities.


Communities living near the Menengai Geothermal Power Project in Nakuru County, for example, complain of loud noises disrupting sleep and school activities, hydrogen sulphide emissions, dust, and water pollution. Respiratory problems, particularly among children and older people, are common. Community members are also concerned that geothermal emissions and open brine ponds could be linked to acid rains in the area, which are corroding their house roofs, water tanks and farm equipment.


A different geography, a different history


In Iceland, geothermal resources are largely located in sparsely populated volcanic zones. Land tenure is relatively stable, and there is little legacy of large-scale dispossession shaping current development.


On the contrary, the Rift Valley is a

highly populated lived space

, where pastoralist communities have deep historical and cultural ties to their land. Here, geothermal projects sit atop layered histories of

colonial and postcolonial land alienation

 and violent evictions. Maasai communities still lack deeds to their land and are treated as guests of the government without their own rights. In this context, the expansion of geothermal projects has led to further resettlement, restricted access to grazing areas, loss of livelihoods, and ongoing disputes over compensation and participation.


In 2014, for example, a group of Indigenous Maasai pastoralist communities submitted a complaint to the accountability mechanisms of the

World Bank

 and

European Investment Bank

 for their investment in the Olkaria IV geothermal project, which caused the …

title: Li Somayê di hilweşîna kana madenê de 5 karker mirin
content:
Li Soma, navçeya Manîsayê kana komirê a bin erdê duh (1ê Cotmehê) di saet 14.00an de hilweşiya. Di helweşîna kanayê de hejmara karkerên mirine derket 5an. Kana komirê ya İmbat Madencilikê ye.


Di xebatên lêgerîn û rizgarkirinê yên di şevê de hatin kirin de gihîştin cenazeyên du karkeran û xebat hatibûn berdewam kirin. Walîtiya Manisayê vê sibê daxûyanî da. Di daxuyaniyê de hat diyar kirin ku ew gihîştine cenazeyên sê karkerên din û xebatên lêgerîn û rizgarkirinê bi dawî bûne.


Di hilweşînê de Halit Ersay, Kerim Oren, Ramazan İnce, Omer Karakaya û İsa Olcay mirin.


AFADê daxuyanî daye û gotiye ku heft karkerên di bin hilweşîna kanayê de mabûn, hatine derxistin û dermankirina du karkerên ku sax hatine rizgarkirin li nexweşxaneyê temam bûye.


Di xebatên lêgerîn û rizgarkirinê de AFAD, Ekîbên Agirkujîyê, Cenderme, Emniyet, UMKE, Ekîbên Tenduristiyê yên 112an, Heyva Sor, Rêveberiya Xizmetên Malbat û Civakî, Ekîbên Şaredariyê jî di nav de bi giştî 756 personel û 76 wesayîtan cih girtin. Ji Rêveberiya AFADê ya Bajarê Îzmîrê cîhazê dîtina bin erdê (M5) û cîhazê dîtina binê kavilan û ekîbên wan tevlî xebatan hatin kirin. 


AFADê destnîşan kiriye û gotiye:


“Di encama xebatên lêgerîn û rizgarkirinê de 7 hemwelatiyên me yên madenkar ji bin hilweşînê hatin derxistin. Ji ber hilweşînê 5 hemwelatiyên me yên madenkar jiyana xwe ji dest dan, ji 2 hemwelatiyên me jî sax hatine rizgarkirin. Dermankirina yekî ji wan li nexweşxaneyê berdewam dike û dermankirina yê din jî temam bûye.”


Sendikaya Maden-Îşê a Serbixwe jî daxuyanî da û weha got:


"Cenazeyên 3 birayên me yên ku di bin hilweşîna li Soma İmbat Madencilikê de mabûn hatin dîtin û hejmara miriyan derket 5an. Rêveberê Şaxa me ya 1emîn a Egeyê Ramazan İnce, endamên me Halit Ersay, Kerim Oren, Omer Karakaya û İsa Olcay madenkarên ku jiyana xwe ji dest dane ne. Em ê daxuyaniya berfireh paşê di Navenda xwe ya Giştî de bidin. Bila serê me hemûyan sax be."


Soma İmbat Madencilik önünde Genel Merkez yönetimimizle bekleyişteyiz, sonuna kadar takip edeceğiz.

Hazırlık aşamasındaki Doğu 5 ayağında gerçekleşen göçükte 7 madenci kalmış olup 1 kardeşimiz hayatını kaybetmiş, 2 kardeşimiz yaralı olarak kurtarılmıştır. Arama kurtarma…

pic.twitter.com/0atQsmOnCT


— Bağımsız Maden İş (@bagimsizmadenis)

October 1, 2026


Di heman kargehê di sala 2020an de jî karker miribûn


Hilweşîna di 1ê Cotmehê de, li kargehên İmbat Madencilikê bûyera yekem a ku bi mirinê encam dayî nîn e.


Di 10ê Nîsana 2020an de di xebatên lênêrîn û çakkirinê yên li beşa galeriyê ya kana şîrketê ya li Somayê de hilweşîn pêk hatibû û di encamê de Ersin Ozdogan, Salih Ayber û Erdinç Karaveli miribûn û karkerek jî bi birîndarî hatibû rizgarkirin.


Di 27ê Sibata 2015an de di kana lînyîtê ya İmbat Madencilik A.Şyê de qeza pêk hatibû û di encamê de Yusuf Çakiroğlu (35) jiyana xwe ji dest dabû.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Labnotes | Ang kontradiksyon ng renewable energy transition sa Pilipinas
content:
The 54MW Pililla Wind Power Project in Pililla, Rizal is operated by Vena Energy. Photo by Chantal Eco

Sa kalagitnaan ng krisis sa klima, ibinibida ng gobyerno at ng mga malalakihang korporasyon ang transition sa renewable energy bilang solusyon — na ang mga solar, wind farm, at iba pa ay susi sa mura’t malinis na enerhiya. Pero habang kinakalbo ang mga kabundukan para itayo ang wind turbines, solar panels, at mga dambuhalang dams, ang bill ng kuryente—palagi pang tumataas!

Ang mga dapat itanong: sino ang may-ari ng mga planta, sinu-sino ang may kontrol ng transmisyon at distribusyon, at para saan ba talaga ang Electric Power Industry Reform Act o EPIRA?

Patuloy ang pagdami ng mga wind at solar farm sa Pilipinas. Noong 2022, 1,530 megawatt (MW) na kuryente ang mula sa solar, at nadoble ito noong 2025 sa 3,003 MW. Umaabot na ngayon sa 3,892 MW (3.9 GW) ang kapasidad mula sa solar, habang ang wind farm o kuryenteng mula sa hangin ay nananatili sa 427 MW lamang.

Sinasabing malinis at mas mura ang kuryenteng nagmumula sa modernong teknolohiyang Renewable Energy (RE) tulad ng solar at wind farm. Ang RE ay teknolohiyang gumagamit ng mga likas na yamang halos di-nauubos tulad ng araw, hangin, at tubig. Mahigit 22 porsyento ng kuryente sa bansa ang galing sa RE — nagmumula ito sa geothermal plants (9.1%), hydroelectric dams (8.7%), solar farm (2.2%), wind farm (1.1%), at iba pang planta ng enerhiyang hindi umaasa sa petrolyong rekurso.

Sinasabi na kapag nagtayo ka ng RE tulad ng solar farm, ito ay mas mura kaysa sa paggamit ng coal power plant na karaniwang itinatayo ngayon ng mga pribadong korporasyon sa enerhiya. Nasa P2.99 kada kilowatt-oras (kWh) lamang ang gastos sa kuryente kapag solar ang gamit, habang PHP3.50/kWh naman kapag hangin ang gamit. Malaking mura ito kumpara sa paggamit ng karbon o coal na may presyong PHP3.80–5.50/kWh, o sa imported na diesel na umaabot sa PHP15–28/kWh. (Tingnan ang Talahanayan 2.) Hindi na rin bumibili ng panggatong tulad ng langis, diesel, o coal ang mga pribadong kumpanya upang paganahin ang kanilang mga planta, dahil tuloy-tuloy at libre ang suplay ng rekurso tulad ng hangin at araw.

Kung kaya ito ang paborito ngayon ng gobyerno at ng mga monopolyong korporasyon sa enerhiya tulad ng MERALCO at First Gen ni Manny Pangilinan, ng Aboitiz Power ng mga Aboitiz, San Miguel Global Power ni Ramon Ang, Prime Infrastructure ni Enrique Razon, at ACEN ng mga Ayala. Sinasabi ng mga korporasyon na magpapababa ito ng singil sa kuryente. Sa ilalim ng Philippine Energy Plan 2023–2050 ng gobyernong Marcos Jr., layunin nitong pataasin ang suplay ng kuryenteng nagmumula sa RE hanggang 35 porsyento sa 2030 at 50 porsyento sa 2050. Sa kasalukuyan, tumaya ang DOE sa 16,337 MW na solar farm at 5,377 MW ng wind farm na proyekto sa buong bansa — lahat ng ito ay pag-aari ng mga pribado at dayuhang korporasyon.

Kung mura ang teknolohiyang RE, bakit patuloy pa ring tumataas ang singil sa kuryente? Bakit hindi nakikinabang dito ang mga mahihirap at maliliit na konsumer? Sa kasalukuyan, nagbabayad ang mga konsumer ng P13 hanggang PHP16 kada kWh sa mga distributor ng kuryente. Ang Pilipinas ngayon ang may pinakamahal na singil sa kuryente sa Asya, habang isa naman ito sa mga bansang may pinakamababang minimum wage sa rehiyon. Mahal na ang kuryente, mababa pa ang kita ng mga ordinaryong pamilyang Pilipino.

Kailan lamang pinayagan ng Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) ang MERALCO na magdagdag ng singil sa kuryente. Kalakip dito ang pagtaas ng FIT-All (Feed-in Tariff Allowance) mula P0.2011 patungong P0.3359 kada kWh. Ayon sa batas, garantisado ng gobyerno ang pagbayad sa mga korporasyon para sa kanilang mga proyektong RE sa loob ng 20 taon — dagdag na mabigat na pasanin sa mamamayan sa loob ng dalawang dekada.

Hindi pa rito natatapos ang pangongotong ng mga kumpanya sa elektrisidad. May nakaambang dagdag na singil sa tinatawag na GEA-All o Green Energy Auction Allowance, na nagpopondo sa mga inaprubahang proyektong RE ng gobyernong Marcos — ilan sa mga ito ay nabanggit na sa itaas. Ibig sabihin, ang mamamayan mismo ang pinagkukuhanan ng puhunan para sa pagtatayo ng mga bagong proyektong RE. Mamamayan ang magpopondo sa mga proyektong ito, at sisingilin pa tayo ng mahal na presyo ng kuryente. Ginigisa tayo sa sarili nating mantika!

Ayon sa mga taunang ulat ng mga kumpanya, kumita ang MERALCO ng P38 bilyon, P45.86 bilyon, at P51.13 bilyon noong 2023, 2024, at 2025, ayon sa pagkakasunod-sunod. Samantala, kumita …

author: admin
title: KIITG Report September 2026
content:
Brenna Yellowthunder (Lead Coordinator, KIITG) spoke at the Oregon Data Center Moratorium Rally on Sept. 8 in Oregon’s capitol, Salem. Alongside Governor Kotek, they emphasized the effect hyper scale data centers have on rivers and salmon, a cornerstone of local tribes culture. They also joined the lobby day, urging state legislators to support a 3-year moratorium on data centers. The event was organized by the Columbia Riverkeepers, Food and Water Watch, and more.

Following the largest pipeline spill in Wisconsin last month, by Canadian pipeline giant Embridge, the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe declared a disaster for their reservation after the spill, and Chairperson Liz Arbuckle said, “This is what we said would happen.”

The break triggered a massive spill of 1.3 million gallons of natural gas liquids. Federal data shows the leak is the largest reported oil and gas spill ever in Wisconsin.

Michigan’s 12 federally recognized tribes led the Mackinac Bridge Walk, with several tribal chairs, chiefs, and presidents joining together to activate the ancestral Three Fires Confederacy’s first collective call to action.

On Labor Day, Sept. 7, 2026, roughly 34,000 people participated in the Mackinac Bridge Walk, with Michigan tribes leading a unified stand against Line 5.

Arbuckle said the tribe had warned that the reroute would still put their reservation at risk. “This is our UnCeded Territory,” she said. “This is where our people have always hunted, fished, gathered and lived and all of that’s at risk.” Tribal leaders say the incident underscores a truth the Anishinaabe have voiced for years: Enbridge’s safety practices rely on luck, not containment.

The Mackinac Bridge Walk was a ceremony, not just a demonstration, to honor the responsibility to the water and remind the world that Anishinaabe people are still here, still protecting their homelands.

Joe Bates, an environmental activist and member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe, captured drone footage of the leak after hearing reports from community members.

We ask you to consider supporting the local community on the ground, who has asked us to share this fundraiser for an infrared drone. Observers need this equipment to document pipeline leaks and highlight the risks to Indigenous waterways. Joe Bates is one of the people who broke the story about Enbridge’s leaking pipeline with his drone footage. He has frequently used drone footage to document conditions along Enbridge’s Line 5 corridor, including construction, erosion concerns, and suspected drilling-fluid releases. But an infrared drone would let observers see what the naked eye cannot: gas plumes, thermal anomalies, and leaks that would otherwise go undetected.

The community is asking for support so that the documentation can continue. Please donate if you can. Share if you cannot.

author: Paul Messersmith-Glavin
title: A Lifelong Organizer Shares Lessons on Sustaining Activism for the Long Haul
content:
Organizer Chris Dixon discusses how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Writer and organizer Chris Dixon has his fingers on the pulse of North American grassroots movement. Dixon has extensively and repeatedly traveled throughout North America, talking with people working for social change — engaging with activists concerning their successes and heartbreaks, their frustrations and dreams. His first book, Another Politics: Talking Across Today’s Transformative Movements, published in 2014, focused on antiauthoritarian organizers and politics across a range of movements of the 2000s and early 2010s, including migrant justice, prison abolitionism, and Occupy Wall Street. His new book, For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World, focuses on how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Movement elders I am close to — now in their 70s — who maintain radical political commitments developed in their youth, benefitted from both the intense community that formed around movements for Black Power and liberation, the youthful counterculture and the New Left, and anti-war movements, as well as from their own inner convictions that served as an animating passion. For these elders, political engagement is a kind of vocation. Though they continue to maintain relationships with those comrades who are also still alive and committed to political struggle, those vibrant communities they once thrived in are gone. Only their specific commitment to the possibility of freedom and liberation keeps them going.

Coming of age politically in the 1990s, we also had strong bonds of friendship born through relentless organizing meetings, demonstrations, and coalition work. It seemed we could collectively change the world. Thirty years later, only a handful of us remain involved. Why? Why do people stop organizing, beyond and in addition to the realities of acquiring increasing responsibilities as we age? Why do people give up on the possibility of creating fundamental social and structural change together over the long term? How can we cultivate and sustain caring radical communities that support us all, while drawing new people in, or welcoming them back? These are some of the questions Chris Dixon sets out to answer in For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World. The interview that follows has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Paul Messersmith-Glavin: Who should read your book?

Chris Dixon: I wrote For the Long Haul as a practical guide with two main audiences in mind. On the one hand, I wanted to warmly welcome people who have recently become involved in radical political efforts, especially those who have joined movement upsurges since 2020. I’m particularly thinking of the Movement for Black Lives and Palestine solidarity organizing, but also renewed labor militancy and collective defense of queer and trans people. A lot of people I talk to who are newer to movements — many but not all of them younger people — are hungry for conversations about how to sustain lifelong political commitments.

On the other hand, I wanted to speak lovingly to my peers — long-time activists and organizers who have been involved in movements for decades. Many of us talk informally with our friends about the challenges we face in staying actively involved on the left. We’re working a lot to pay our bills, reckoning with disabilities and chronic health conditions, and holding significant care responsibilities for kids, elders, and others in our lives. So many of us are deeply exhausted and hungry for realistic advice about how to stay steady in the fight.

I also wanted to sympathetically address people who participated in movements of the left at one time or another and then moved away from active involvement. I know many people who have followed this trajectory. Rather than being moralistic or dismissive, I wanted to remind them that they’re always welcome back. And I wanted to suggest that perhaps, together, we can build some better structures and practices for helping people stay engaged.

You have spent a tremendous amount of time travelling around the U.S. and Canada, listening to on-the-ground organizers. What have you learned?

I have learned a lot! My most intense and sustained travel was connected to the process of …

content:
Eylem Nazlıer [email protected]

Türkiye’de koruyucu, birinci basamak sağlık hizmetlerinin yurttaşla buluştuğu en önemli noktalardan biri olan Aile Sağlığı Merkezlerinin (ASM) geleceği, merkezlerin fiziki koşullarından kira giderlerine, deprem güvenliğinden personel eksikliğine kadar risk altında. Kamuya ait binalarda bile kiralarına yüzde 300’e varan zamlar istenen ASM’lerde aile hekimleri zor durumda.

Birlik ve Dayanışma Sendikası Genel Başkanı Dr. Ahmet Mehlepçi, ASM’lerin mümkün olduğunca kamuya ait, depreme dayanıklı ve sağlık hizmetinin gerektirdiği fiziki standartlara uygun binalarda hizmet vermesi gerektiğine vurgu yaparak “ASM’ler yalnızca hekim, ebe ve hemşirelerin görev yaptığı binalar değildi. ASM’ler; koruyucu sağlık hizmetlerinin, gebe, bebek ve çocuk izlemlerinin, bağışıklama hizmetlerinin, kronik hastalık takiplerinin ve vatandaşın sağlık sistemiyle ilk temasının gerçekleştiği temel sağlık kuruluşlarıdır” hatırlatmasını yaptı. Bu nedenle ASM’lerin geleceğine ilişkin kararların yalnızca bina, taşınmaz veya bütçe konusu olarak değerlendirilemeyeceğini dile getiren Mehlepçi, “Konu doğrudan sağlık hizmetine erişim, hizmetin sürekliliği ve kamu yararıdır” diye konuştu.

Sağlık Bakanı Kemal Memişoğlu’nun Kasım 2025’te 1000 yeni ASM yapacaklarını açıklamasından bu yana sadece 278 ASM’nin hizmete girdiğini, 370 ASM’nin inşaatının sürdüğünü ve 352 ASM’nin proje aşamasında olduğu bilgisini veren Mehlepçi, Türkiye genelinde ise yaklaşık 8 bin 300 ASM bulunduğunu söyledi.

Yeni ASM yatırımlarının elbette önemli olduğunu belirten Mehlepçi, mevcut merkezlerin ise kentsel dönüşüm, deprem riski, yüksek kiralar veya taşınmaz satışları nedeniyle hizmet dışı kalmasının önlenmesi gerektiğini vurguladı.

Bir taraftan yeni ASM’ler yapılırken diğer taraftan mevcut merkezlerin kentsel dönüşüm, deprem riski, yüksek kiralar veya taşınmaz satışları nedeniyle hizmet dışı kalma tehlikesiyle karşı karşıya olduğuna dikkati çeken Mehlpeçi “Mart 2026’da TBMM’ye sunulan soru önergesine verilen cevapta İstanbul Kadıköy’deki 33 ASM’den 7’sinin kentsel dönüşüm nedeniyle yıkıldığı ve hizmet veremez hale geldiğini söyledi. Mahlepçi kaç yeni ASM açıldığı kadar, kaç ASM’nin kapandığı, yıkıldığı, tahliye edildiği, taşındığı veya başka bir ASM’nin içine sıkıştırıldığının da kamuoyuyla paylaşılması gerektiğini aktardı.

ASM binalarının deprem güvenliğinin de önemli bir sorun olduğunu belirten Mehlepçi, 2025 yılında yapılan bir çalışmada ASM binalarının yaklaşık üçte birinin 1999 öncesinde inşa edildiğinin ortaya çıktığını söyledi. 6 Şubat 2023 yaşanan depremlerde ortaya çıkan tablonun bu konuda vahim olduğunu hatırlatan Mehlepçi “2026 yılı başında sahadan elde edilen verilere göre Hatay’da 96 ASM konteynerlerde hizmet veriyor. 103 ASM kendi binasında hizmet vermeye devam ediyor ancak bunların bir bölümü deprem güvenliği açısından risk taşıyor. Yaklaşık 56 ASM ise tahliye veya yıkım sürecinde” dedi.

Öte yandan ASM’ler için sorunun yalnızca deprem güvenliğiyle sınırlı olmadığını, ASM’lerdeki sağlık hizmetinin niteliği ve çalışanların koşullarını etkileyen başka fiziki sorunların bulunduğunu da dile getiren Mehlepçi durumu şöyle anlattı: “Penceresi, yeterli mekanik havalandırması bulunmayan kan alma odaları, lavabosu olmayan, iki veya üç sağlık çalışanının aynı odayı kullanmak zorunda kaldığı ASM’ler de var. Hatta bazı çalışma alanları hasta mahremiyetini sağlamaya da elverişli değil.”

Yıkım veya tahliye kararı verilen merkezlerde görev yapan sağlık çalışanlarının başka bir ASM’nin mutfağına, dinlenme odasına veya ortak kullanım alanına yerleştirilerek yeni bir aile hekimliği birimi oluşturulmasının kalıcı bir çözüm olmadığının altını çizen Mehlepçi, “Bir sağlık hizmetinin verilebilmesi için yalnızca bir oda bulunması yeterli değildir. O alanın sağlık hizmetinin niteliğine, çalışan güvenliğine ve hasta mahremiyetine uygun olması gerekir” dedi.

Kamusal sağlık hizmeti sunulan ASM’lerde yükün önemli bir bölümünün aile hekimlerinin üzerine yıkıldığına ve özellikle büyükşehirlerde uygun bina bulmanın giderek zorlaştığına işaret eden Mehlepçi “Kiralar da ASM’lerin sürdürülebilirliğini tehdit eden seviyelere ulaştı. Aylık 100 bin TL ve üzerinde kira ödeyen ASM örnekleri var. Elazığ’da bazı ASM’ler yüzde 350’ye varan kira artış talepleriyle karşılaştı. ASM’ler birer ticarethane değildir. Burada yürütülen faaliyet kamu sağlık hizmetidir” uyarısını yaparak buna rağmen yüksek kira bedellerinin yanı sıra elektrik, su, doğalgaz, temizlik, bakım-onarım …

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Limpopo district hospital ‘filthy’, ‘broken’ and leaderless
content:
Filthy conditions, a shortage of warm water, a broken emergency communications system, and unresolved complaints from nurses are some of the adversities being faced by both patients and healthcare workers at Nkhensani hospital in Giyani, Limpopo.


The root cause


According to healthcare workers stationed at the hospital, the woes at the public facility are fuelled by a lack of leadership. For the past eight years, the hospital has not had a permanent CEO. Five individuals have, in ten years, acted as CEOs on a temporary basis but were never permanently appointed.


The Limpopo department of health has blamed a lack of suitable candidates as the main reason for not appointing a permanent CEO. The CEO position has been vacant since 2016 following the removal of Themba Mhlanga.


“We are leaderless at this hospital and everyone does what they want; hence everything is a mess at Nkhensani. I can confidently tell that at night, patients at this hospital bath using cold water as warm water gets finished in the early hours of the morning; and the kitchen does not operate during the night and those who want tea or coffee are always left wanting,” said a staff nurse stationed at Nkhensani hospital.


Lives of patients at risk


The nurse further said that the hospital is filthy and rarely cleaned: “This hospital is never cleaned, we often go for days without it being cleaned and no one cares and cleaners are also never reprimanded as there is no one to reprimand them and they do as they like. This puts the lives of patients and healthcare workers at risk.”


The emergency communications system has not been working for months at the hospital and nurses are forced to use their personal cell phones during emergencies. “Alerting doctors of emergencies at this hospital has become extra difficult as we have to use our own personal cell phones because the hospital does not have a working emergency dial; it has not been working for months. What if I do not have airtime and a patient is in need of a doctor urgently? It might lead to an avoidable death of a patient,” she said.


The nurse also told

Elitsha

 that she has personally raised most of these issues with previous acting CEOs but nothing has ever been done to address her concerns. “Even if you complain to those superior to you, nothing is ever done to address your concerns. No one is prepared to take responsibility and all this has got to do with the lack of leadership at Nkhensani hospital,” she said.


Derrick Mashaba, a local community member in Giyani residing about 2 kilometres away from Nkhensani, told

Elitsha

 that he has witnessed the tumble of the hospital over the past decade. “We have witnessed the fall of our precious hospital over the past ten years. We have seen overcrowding, dilapidating buildings, shortage of water and lack of leadership, and all this has contributed to the fall of the mighty hospital,” said Mashaba.


It hurts him to see the fall of the hospital which is so close to his home. “This is a district hospital and it is supposed to be the best in our region but it is not being prioritised. A hospital as big as this one cannot operate without a permanent CEO; it is wrong and it is something which is supposed to be addressed immediately,” he said.


Limpopo health spokesperson, Neil Shikwambana said that the department is working towards appointing a permanent CEO. “The recruitment process is underway and an acting CEO has been appointed to ensure continuity during this process,” he said.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Mental Health Reminders
content:
These are dark times. It is, in fact, the world that is crazy – despair and anxiety are natural responses to watching society destroy itself for the wealthy and powerful. But by reaching out to each other, we can find the courage to stay engaged with the world, to survive, and to fight back. Mental health and mental health crises vary a lot between people, and are often intertwined with class, race, gender, and activism. These suggestions are generic, but may be useful for yourself or others. If you find yourself or someone you love having delusional thinking or consider self-harm or other violence, these suggestions probably aren’t enough. Remember that it is okay to reach out for professional help!

• Our brains are connected to our bodies, so physical health can help with mental distress. Eating healthy food on a regular schedule and getting enough sleep are necessary for mental stability and sustained activism. Exercise, dance, and physical movement help, too. So can fresh air and having a stable, calming place to stay. Try to recognize if you’re missing one of these, and if that’s causing distress.

• An important component of mental health is the ability to know ourselves, understand our needs, and be able to talk about them to the other people in our lives. This can be really challenging and can often take guidance from others who have learned how to do it with one another.

• It can help to have language for mental crisis that feels comfortable and makes more sense than the dominant medical language. Transmission of language often happens in groups. Talk to friends about the different ways you can feel “off” and develop your own shorthand to describe them.

• Joining a mutual support group of peers listening to and helping peers as equals can be validating, while not necessarily endorsing your feelings. You can form one yourself or join an ongoing group.

• If possible, find a therapist or counselor who supports your self-determination. Ask about confidentiality if someone else — such as your parents, boss, or governmental program — is paying.

• Drugs and alcohol usually make mental health problems worse.

• Psychiatric drugs such as those for depression or bipolar disorder can help some people reduce distress and maintain stability, while other people with similar symptoms may experience distress or harm from the same drugs. Figuring out what works for you can be a process because people differ.

• Nature and wilderness can be our greatest healers. Spend some time outside the city to get centered. Get away from pollution, which is in itself mind-altering. Look up “Ecopsychology” to learn more.

• Allow social, political, and environmental crises unfolding around you to radicalize you, rather than driving you to despair. Actually articulate the world you would want to be living in; work towards it. Remember change happens collectively – look for ways to plug in. Small acts like talking to neighbors or submitting art to Slingshot can help you feel political agency between larger or more radical actions.

• Many communities have 24 hour a day crisis hotlines or crisis centers. Call 800-SUICIDE if you’re thinking about killing yourself or 800 646-HOPE to reach a rape crisis line for survivors of sexual violence. Warning: if you call and say you want to kill yourself police may arrive at your door.

• Things that can help your mental health day-to-day might not be as effective when you’re in crisis. Review the above reminders, and try to eat, exercise, journal, etc., but it’s okay if that isn’t helping.

• Distracting yourself from depressed or anxious thoughts can help: listening to music, making art, washing dishes, doing a project alone or with others. Embrace sensation: use your hands or massage your fingers. Hold onto an ice cube, or take a hot or cold shower. Give yourself time to gather resources.

• Some current emotional crises may be caused by traumas from the past, which may need to be emotionally and consciously processed in order not to keep recurring; that processing might take time.

• When in crisis, it may help to realize that the feeling will eventually pass and your life will begin to feel manageable and meaningful again later. Depression may feel like lack of feelings and a lack of connection to feeling. Anxiety may feel like rapidly cycling concern for what might happen. Both inhibit your ability to perceive and understand the world correctly. Your perceptions of hopelessness are NOT …
