author: Unknown
title: Diecimila in marcia da Sant’Ambrogio ad Avigliana
content:
Ci sono giornate in cui una valle intera decide di mostrarsi per quello che è.

Ieri è successo tra Sant’Ambrogio e Avigliana. Un numero enorme di persone ha percorso insieme la Valsusa, in una marcia popolare che ha attraversato i due paesi portando in strada una cosa che forse è ancora più importante del numero dei partecipanti: la capacità di una Valle di riconoscersi, ancora una volta, nella difesa del proprio territorio.


Da Notav Info


Diecimila persone sono tante, ma a raccontare questa giornata sono soprattutto i volti e la composizione del corteo.

C’erano gli amministratori locali e d’oltralpe e le famiglie, i comitati e le realtà che compongono il Movimento No Tav, persone che questa battaglia la portano avanti da decenni e giovani che hanno scelto di raccoglierne il testimone. C’erano i comitati No Tav francesi, i movimenti legati alla Palestina e chi da anni si batte per la difesa dei territori. C’era una valle intera che ieri ha deciso di camminare nella stessa direzione con la determinazione e l’entusiamo che da sempre accompagnano le giornate di mobilitazione popolare valsusina.


La ragione della marcia era precisa: fermare l’Avigliana-Orbassano. Un nuovo progetto che si inserisce nel quadro più ampio della Torino-Lione e che arriva all’interno di un territorio che da più di trent’anni è obbligato a sentire l’ormai stantio racconto che le grandi opere sono necessarie, inevitabili, strategiche ed indispensabili. Tutto questo mentre sul territorio rimangono aperti temi molto più concreti che attraversano tutti gli aspetti della vita quotidiana: a partire dal caro vita, la sanità sempre più inaccessibile arrivando poi alla mobilità, con il costo sempre più alto del carburante e gli scarsi investimenti nel trasporto pubblico locale. Il tema che porta con sé l’apertura di questi nuovo progetto non è semplicemente costruire nuove infrastrutture, ma decidere quali trasporti servono davvero a chi vive questo territorio e dove devono essere investite le risorse pubbliche. Ieri, insieme alla critica alla tratta Avigliana-Orbassano, è tornata quindi anche la richiesta di investire nel trasporto pubblico e nella metropolitana, invece di continuare a concentrare risorse su opere pensate secondo una logica diversa da quella dei bisogni quotidiani di chi abita la Valle e l’area metropolitana.


I tanti interventi hanno infatti poi anche allargato il ragionamento anche alle altre emergenze che attraversano il territorio e l’intero Paese: la sanità pubblica, le scuole, i servizi, il trasporto per studenti e pendolari, la crisi climatica e la necessità di prendersi cura dei territori invece di consumarli.

È anche su questo terreno che l’Avigliana-Orbassano diventa parte di una discussione più ampia sulle priorità e sul modello di sviluppo.

Sono passati governi, ministri, presidenti di Regione. Sono cambiate le parole utilizzate per imporre la Torino-Lione e il modello che in cui si inserisce e sono cambiate le motivazioni con cui se ne è sostenuta la necessità.

Quello che invece non è mutata è la voglia di chi abita questo territorio, di organizzarsi per difenderlo.

La manifestazione di ieri è il risultato di una storia lunga, nella quale si è costruita una capacità collettiva fatta di resistenza, organizzazione e mobilitazione, alimentata negli anni da migliaia di persone, esperienze e percorsi differenti.

È questa esperienza che ha permesso al Movimento No Tav di andare oltre la semplice opposizione a una singola opera e di costruire, insieme alla critica, un’idea diversa di territorio, di comunità e di futuro.

La giornata ha mostrato, ancora una volta, come la discussione non possa essere rinchiusa nei confini di una singola tratta ferroviaria.

Questa mobilitazione ha sottolineato la capacità di mettere insieme soggetti differenti: amministratori locali e Movimento No Tav, famiglie e giovani, comitati Valsusini e francesi, persone che partecipano da decenni alle mobilitazioni e una nuova generazione che prende parola e spazio.


Insieme a loro movimenti ambientalisti, realtà legate alla Palestina, esperienze di difesa del territorio come Bosco Ospizio.

Una molteplicità di percorsi che non ha bisogno di essere omologata per condividere prospettive e percorsi condivisi.

La presenza dei giovani è stata una delle immagini più forti della marcia. In una mobilitazione che affonda le proprie radici in più di trent’anni di storia, la loro presenza dice che questa non è una storia chiusa, né una battaglia …

author: Unknown
title: Data center: incontro pubblico a Pavia
content:
Sabato 26 settembre a Milano è nata ufficialmente la rete regionale dei comitati stop data center, che scenderà in piazza con una manifestazione a Milano il prossimo 10 ottobre.

Sul tema si terrà un incontro pubblico di approfondimento a Pavia, martedì 6 ottobre alle ore 21, presso la sala conferenze del Broletto.​ ​


Relatori saranno

Enrico Duranti, ambientalista e fondatore del Comitato Ciarlasco

 per la tutela del territorio, già intervistato da Infoaut:

Data center: bolla o nuova rivoluzione industriale?

Intervista al Comitato Ciarlasco per la Tutela del Territorio e

il fisico Sergio Manera, del comitato di Certosa

, che si è interessato in modo particolare del fenomeno delle isole di calore (approfondisci

qui: L’effetto isola di calore dei data center

) Infrastrutture materiali dell’intelligenza artificiale, questi centri stanno recentemente balzando alla cronaca locale e nazionale. Sono numerosi i progetti, a vari stadi di avanzamento, prevalentemente concentrati sul territorio lombardo. ​ Anche

la provincia di Pavia è interessata dal fenomeno: dalla proposta di ampliamento del campus Stack di Siziano, al cantiere Microsoft di Bornasco, passando per Certosa, dove è sorto uno dei primi comitati di cittadini contrari ai data center, e Garlasco, dove si è recentemente costituito un altro comitato.

 ​ Le cronache cittadine degli ultimissimi giorni, poi hanno riportato dell’esistenza di un progetto presentato a marzo agli uffici del settore urbanistica del Comune di Pavia, di cui l’Amministrazione per mesi non ha fatto pervenire nessuna notizia ai cittadini. Sino al 28 agosto risultava dal portale di Terna una richiesta di allaccio alla rete elettrica per un data center nel territorio comunale per 50 MW di potenza. Oggi ne risulta una per il triplo. Verosimilmente è stata avanzata dai proprietari dell’area dismessa ex Chatillon, alla periferia della città. Mentre sindaco, assessore all’ambiente e alcuni consiglieri comunali, dopo mesi di silenzio, assicurano che non autorizzeranno nessun progetto di data center in città, la capogruppo del PD, partito di maggioranza relativa in consiglio comunale, dichiara che «Pavia ha aree dismesse in cui la realizzazione di un data center potrebbe essere un volano di innovazione straordinario». Non resta che dire che, come in altri territori, toccherà ai cittadini pavesi informarsi, attivarsi e dare battaglia per preservare salute e territorio.​ ​

Nel corso dell’incontro verranno analizzati gli impatti ambientali, sanitari, energetici e sociali dei centri dati, ma si parlerà anche della situazione nazionale e di quella lombarda, dell’assenza di un piano strategico e della svendita dei territori alle Big tech americane. ​

author: Kieler Open Source und Linux Tage
title: Nie wieder Copy & Paste: Reporting mit Quarto [24. Kielux 2026]
content:
Ein Vortrag von Gerhard Nachtmann (Gerhard Nachtmann)


Manuelle Berichte und Präsentationen kosten Zeit, sind fehleranfällig und oft schwer nachvollziehbar. Mit Quarto gibt es eine Open-Source-Lösung, die Code, Daten, Analysen und Text vereint.


Der Vortrag zeigt, wie sich mit Quarto reproduzierbare Berichte und Präsentationen erstellen lassen, die ausführbaren Code (z. B. in R oder Python) enthalten und ihre Inhalte automatisch aus aktuellen Daten generieren. Zudem wird gezeigt, wie sich die Erstellung und Aktualisierung dieser Dokumente unter Linux automatisieren lässt.


Der Vortrag richtet sich an Entwickler, Data Scientists und Linux-Anwender, die Reporting und Präsentationserstellung als Code verstehen und wiederholbare Prozesse ohne Copy & Paste etablieren möchten.


Der Vortrag wurde auf den Kieler Open Source und Linux Tagen im Jahr 2026 gehalten.


Für Inhalt und Richtigkeit sind ausschließlich die jeweiligen Referenten verantwortlich.

title: Der Weg zur digitalen Unabhängigkeit mit BlossomOS [24. Kielux 2026]
content:
Ein Vortrag von Leonie Eleanor Ain (Blossom), Yannik Joel Ain (Blossom)


Diese Präsentation zeigt den Weg zur digitalen Unabhängigkeit mit BlossomOS, den aktuellen Entwicklungsstand und die nächsten Schritte. Sie fasst zusammen, was wir bisher geschafft und herausgefunden haben. Im Fokus stehen Datenschutz, Open Source, eine moderne UI/UX und ein konsequent einfaches Nutzungserlebnis mit einem Klick. BlossomOS ist für private Nutzer, Unternehmen und Behörden gedacht und zielt darauf ab, mehr Kontrolle über Daten und digitale Infrastruktur zu ermöglichen.

author: Kieler Open Source und Linux Tage
title: EGroupware - Was mit KI... [24. Kielux 2026]
content:
Ein Vortrag von Stefan Unverricht (

EGroupware.org

)


Auch EGroupware macht etwas mit KI... Aber eben digital souverän (so weit wie man das möchte).


EGroupware integriert KI-Funktionen in seine Anwendungen und stellt Anwender damit entsprechende Werkzeuge zur Verfügung. Dies ermöglicht eine höhere Produktivität und gewisse Automatisierung.


Umfangreiche Konfigurationsmöglichkeiten geben Administratoren die Kontrolle und ermöglichen es, Anwendern mithilfe geschickter Prompts Werkzeuge zur Verfügung zu stellen, ohne dass diese Prompt-Experten sein müssen.


Durch die Integration von Open WebUI, die Anbindung per API an EGroupware für die Automation und die Möglichkeit, eigene LMM anzubinden, kann man den Anwendern ein System anbieten, das man unter Kontrolle hat. Digitale Souveränität eben.


Dieses gesamte Thema wird vermutlich noch längere Zeit WIP sein. Jedoch stehen bereits jetzt viele wesentliche Funktionen bereit.


Es liegt noch ein gewisses Stück Lernkurve vor uns: für uns als Entwickler von EGroupware, für Admins und insbesondere für die Anwender.


Der Vortrag gibt einen Überblick über den aktuellen Stand.


Im Anschluss gibt es eine QA-Runde und gerne auch einen Austausch zu sinnvollen Funktionen für Anwender.


Der Vortrag wurde auf den Kieler Open Source und Linux Tagen im Jahr 2026 gehalten.

author: anred
title: Juicio por el transfemicidio de Azul Semeñenko: una vida atravesada por el odio a la identidad
content:
El juicio por el transfemicidio de Azul Mía Natasha Semeñenko comenzó en Neuquén mientras afuera del tribunal permanecía una pregunta que excede la responsabilidad penal de un acusado: ¿qué significa vivir siendo una mujer trans en una sociedad que todavía expone a esas vidas a la discriminación, la violencia y la precariedad? Por Manuela Wilhelm (ANRed).


 


Durante la primera jornada del juicio por jurados, la Fiscalía, la querella y la defensa presentaron sus teorías sobre lo ocurrido durante la madrugada del 25 de septiembre de 2025. Para las partes acusadoras,

Roberto Daniel Sánchez asesinó a Azul Semeñenko

 en un ataque de extrema violencia y la Fiscalía buscará acreditar un

homicidio triplemente agravado por ensañamiento, violencia de género y odio hacia su identidad de género

.


La defensa sostiene otra hipótesis: que la muerte ocurrió durante un episodio de violencia en el que Sánchez reaccionó bajo un estado de emoción violenta. Cabe destacar que el abogado contratado por el acusado, Ezequiel Leanza intentó pasar como prueba un “informe médico” que fue rechazado por el juez de garantias por considerarlo “inexistente” debido a que la mujer que lo firmaba tenía tres condenas por estafas en torno a un título trucho.


Gentileza


Además, el debate continuó con la prueba y el jurado popular escuchó a la primera testigo, Romina Millapán, hermana de Azul, quien reconstruyó una vida marcada por la violencia hacia su identidad que había comenzado mucho antes de aquella madrugada.


Azul Semeñenko fue discriminada y abusada en la infancia


Romina contó que Azul nació en Uruguay y que a los seis años llegó a Neuquén junto a su madre y sus hermanos. Según relató, desde pequeña manifestó que quería ser una niña. Sin embargo, comenzó la escuela con un nombre y una identidad que no eran los que reconocía como propios.


En la Escuela 61, recordó su hermana, era apartada y molestada porque prefería relacionarse con las niñas. Los insultos y las burlas continuaron durante la primaria y la secundaria. “Los compañeros consideraban que no era normal, que era un raro”, relató Romina ante el jurado.


La violencia tampoco quedó encerrada en las paredes de la escuela. Cuando Azul tenía alrededor de nueve o diez años, según el relato de su hermana, sufrió un abuso sexual dentro del hogar. Su madre lo denunció y el hombre que Romina señaló como responsable estuvo tres años preso. Sin embargo, posteriormente regresó a la familia y, según contó la testigo, continuó ejerciendo violencia y rechazando la identidad de Azul.“Mi mamá recuerda que si bien no lo volvió a tocar siempre le reprochó que no era su hijo y que en su familia no tenía un hijo maricón”, relató Romina.


Ese rechazo familiar se superponía con la violencia social. Durante su declaración, la hermana contó que Azul sufrió agresiones físicas y verbales en distintos momentos de su vida. En una ocasión, cuando había conseguido un trabajo nocturno en un puesto de panchos, un grupo de jóvenes la esperó a la salida, la golpeó, le rompió el teléfono y le fracturó un brazo.


“Yo me voy a matar porque soy un fracasado”


Uno de los momentos más duros del testimonio de Romina apareció cuando reconstruyó las consecuencias que tuvieron sobre Azul los años de discriminación, rechazo y dificultades para acceder a un trabajo.


Contó que cuando tenía 14 años encontró a Daniel —como todavía era llamada entonces— con una gillette en la mano y heridas en uno de sus brazos. Semanas después, atravesando nuevamente un período sin trabajo, le dijo que quería quitarse la vida.


“Yo me voy a matar porque soy un fracasado de mierda, nadie me quiere y nadie me va a dar una oportunidad. Yo me voy a tirar al río”, recordó Romina que le dijo.


La hermana lo siguió hasta el río y logró convencerlo de regresar a la casa. Una vez allí, Azul le pidió ayuda. “Ro, por favor ayudame porque yo así no puedo seguir. Necesito que me ayudes”, recordó.


Su madre buscó asistencia y, según el relato de Romina, comenzó un tratamiento psicológico que duró aproximadamente tres años. Después tuvo que interrumpirlo porque, al tratarse de atención en el sistema público, la falta de especialistas hizo imposible continuar.


Esos episodios fueron incorporados al juicio como parte de la historia de vida de Azul. La defensa cuestionó que se incluyeran hechos de su infancia y adolescencia que no estaban vinculados directamente con el homicidio. El juez Luciano Hermosilla, sin embargo, permitió que continuara el …

author: Novara Media
title: Trauma Farming: the New Politics of Public Suffering
content:
Are we in the era of trauma Top Trumps? ‘Lived Experience’ has become a byword for standpoint authority and progressive politics. It has allowed people from marginalised groups to speak and be heard, and forced us to confront how power plays out in interpersonal dynamics. But it has also become a way for people to brand themselves online, and excuse antisocial or even downright nasty behaviours. Has ‘lived experience’ helped the left, or turned us into self-obsessed therapy-speakers, incapable of communicating with the majority of people?


At the latest Downstream IRL, Ash Sarkar sat down with Catherine Liu – cultural theorist, professor and author of Virtue Hoarders – to discuss her new book, Traumatized: The New Politics of Public Suffering. Liu argues that as class politics has declined, the language of psychology has stepped in to explain problems rooted in capitalism. But what happens when trauma becomes content and politics gives way to what Liu calls the ‘gentrification of pain’? Is ‘lived experience’ a prerequisite for legitimate political analysis? Why do movements so often end up policing each other rather than confronting power? And if politics becomes about who’s hurting most, who benefits?

author: Paul Buhle
title: The Communitarian Mind of Michael Albert
content:
Somewhere, in the complex and often confused history of anarchist and communitarian movements of the US, Michael Albert resides, now almost 80, a veteran of endless campaigns but still eager to make his familiar points. Communitarianism of some kind can work, can create a substitute for the miserable economic arrangements of the present, and engage ordinary people in the process of changing themselves as they endeavor to change the world.

This sentiment has a more than honorable history even in the US, historically known for its weak and fragile Left institutions. Its origins should properly be placed well before the rise of the Marxist-related movements, mostly German immigrants, during the 1860s-70s. Indeed, the communitarian experiments of the 1820s-40s engaged some of the great figures of the age, from Shakers to Bohemians, and even produced a remarkable literature, including Nathaniel Hawthorne’s rather satirical Blithedale Romance.

The ideas of dress reform (mainly for women), healthy foods, and even freer sexual relations flowed into Abolitionist and Women’s Rights movements. The Civil War swallowed a large chunk of utopianism, but enough survived to prompt a rebirth in successive generations. Edward Bellamy’s best-selling novel, Looking Backward , published in 1887, seemed, by example, to make small-scale cooperative living imaginable, even if colonies nearly always failed in their first (under-capitalization and too few agricultural skills counted heavily). Hope is ever-born or perhaps never really goes away. Skinny-dipping and open curricula for children’s education, known in the 1910s, also found their way into the hippie mini-societies of the 1960s-70s.

It would be hard to say how deeply anarchist and communitarian ideas penetrated the “Counter Culture”—a phrase so dated and imprecise that we now set it off— but the sentiment was sincere and deep. “Share the Land” by the Canadian group Guess Who still resonates on YouTube with a confidence of “Brothers and Sisters Who Care” sharing valuables in common. It just didn’t work out in life.

To his credit, Michael Albert never gave up. Student activist, antiwar protester, launched South End Press in Boston of the 1970s, and the avowedly anarchist/libertarian Z Magazine in 1989. Thereafter, Albert and various collaborators, notably Robin Hahnel, worked out theories of alternatives to the market economy along lines that Prince Peter Kropotkin surely would have approved. At what might be called a literary highpoint, he published Parecon: Life After Capitalism (2003), a book translated into a couple dozen languages. Albert took his message to the world. The specifics of the furious debates over whether his proposal would work in practical economic terms, are now long past and largely forgotten—but the debate inevitably goes on. Beneath the specifics could be found a deeper plan, a vision based more on ethics than practical details.

And here we are twenty-some years later. And, no doubt, with the enriching personal experience of establishing, through an extended Z Media Institute, a world of training for the next generations of media and grassroots activists, now emphatically including podcasters, including Michael and the Z folks.

The conceit of this fat volume is that the Revolution has been successful, as related by an aged activist and SDS veteran to an oral historian. Like the most rigorous of oral histories, it encompasses a life story or rather a number of life stories. These mostly lack—according to me, an experienced oral historian and director of a couple of oral history programs—the deep family and community background that is most useful. But it emphatically includes details of the process of participation and learning, from a couple dozen imagined participants of widely different backgrounds, through lives of many struggles.

A little backstory from my end is useful. Oral history, the practical use of oral history, fell upon me in the 1970s as I realized that the vital living memories of the 1920s-40s Left—what they believed and what they did, far from the centers of Leftwing national leadership—were slipping away fast. The field had emerged around this time, more activist than academic, with some thousands of activists. Amongst these, the Oral History of the American Left archive (NYU), my veritable brain-child. And later more oral history on Rhode Island working people; still later teaching oral history for a decade at Brown.

I mention these …

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: A general demobilisation
content:
“The Worker” by Vladimir Serov, 1964


In 1932, Ernst Jünger published

Der Arbeiter

 [

The Worker

], a work in which this new figure of humanity pointed to the new world order. The centrality of work corresponds to the dominance of technology. Expanding on concepts he had expressed in his book of two years prior,

Total Mobilization

, Jünger writes: “Technology is the way in which the worker form mobilises the world.” This diagnosis, which revisited Marx’s analyses from an entirely different perspective, exerted considerable influence on both the right and the left of the political spectrum.


It is therefore all the more surprising that this decisive figure of the era has disappeared for some decades now. Technology continues to govern the world and has certainly increased its power everywhere, but it is no longer “the way in which the worker form mobilises the world.” On the contrary, in the form of artificial intelligence, it seems to imply rather the decline of the centrality of work that Jünger had in mind. Instead of the servitude linked to exploitation and mobilisation, technology, by progressively blurring the identities of social classes and estates, seems today to be heading towards an unprecedented form of subjugation through a kind of general demobilisation.


Quodlibet

, 01/10/2026

title: DFG publishes September report on rights violations against journalists
content:
The Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) released its “September Report on Rights Violations Against Journalists.” The report stated that, in September, access restrictions were at the forefront in terms of press and freedom of expression.


The report emphasized that access to social media accounts had been blocked and stated: “According to the September data, access to 3,492 digital media content was blocked on the internet and digital media sphere. In addition, access to 15 news reports was blocked, while 4 websites were shut down. In September, the accounts or websites of media outlets such as JINNEWS, Mezopotamya Agency, Evrensel, Kısa Dalga and T24 faced access restrictions and platform interventions. In addition, the personal X accounts of numerous journalists were made invisible in Turkey on grounds such as ‘the protection of national security and public order.’”


The DFG report also included the following points.


“In September, 15 journalists were detained, and 8 journalists were arrested. The homes of 4 journalists were raided, 3 journalists were threatened, journalists were prevented from covering the news in 5 incidents, and 2 journalists were subjected to ill-treatment. During the same period, investigations were launched against 2 journalists under freedom of thought and expression, while cases were filed against 10 journalists. There are 80 journalists involved in 25 ongoing cases. As of 4 October 2026, the number of jailed journalists is 29.


A significant portion of the interventions against journalists in September took place directly over the news reports they produced or their posts on digital media. Journalist Oya Lale Arslan was detained and arrested on the grounds of her digital media posts and YouTube broadcasts. Journalist Selahattin Günday was arrested over footage he reported on as part of the Kaşif Kozinoğlu investigation, and a second arrest warrant was subsequently issued against him. Journalist Tuğba Tekerek was arrested over a report she produced for Kaos GL, while Hüseyin Aykan, Editor-in-Chief of Bolu Gündem, was also arrested over a report he published.


In September, the interventions journalists encountered while covering the news also reached notable levels. In 5 incidents in September, journalists were prevented from covering the news, while 3 journalists were threatened and 2 journalists were subjected to ill-treatment.


One of the forms of attack faced by journalists was judicial pressure. Investigations were launched against 2 journalists in September, while investigations involving 10 journalists were turned into court cases. While the trials of 80 journalists in 25 cases are ongoing, ETHA reporter Züleyha Müldür was sentenced to 6 years and 3 months in prison.”


According to the report, 2 journalists were attacked, 1 journalist was targeted, the homes of 4 journalists were raided, 15 journalists were detained, 8 journalists were arrested, 2 journalists were subjected to ill-treatment, 3 journalists were threatened, 5 journalists were prevented from covering the news, and 1 journalist experienced rights violation in prison.


The report stated that investigations were launched against 2 journalists and cases were filed against 10 journalists; 2 journalists were sentenced to a total of 6 years, 5 months and 24 days; there were 25 ongoing journalist cases, 80 journalists were on trial, and the number of jailed journalists was 30 as of October 3.


The report stated that 10 journalists had lost their jobs and that RTÜK had imposed penalties on 14 broadcasts. It also emphasized that 4 websites had been shut down, access to 15 news reports had been blocked, and access to 3,492 social media posts had been restricted.

title: Geothermal plants and rising costs hit fig producers
content:
Fig producers in Yaykın neighbourhood in the Karacasu district of Aydın are struggling with high input costs and falling crop prices. Gülhanım Tarhan, one of the producers who spoke to ANKA News Agency, said they sorted their figs according to quality, yet the average selling price still failed to reach even 100 Turkish Lira (TL, around 1.81 euros) per kilogram. Tarhan said they were making a loss this season on figs they had sold for between 225 and 250 lira per kilogram last year, adding that their income no longer covered production costs.


Average selling price falls to 67–70 TL


Another fig producer, Yeliz Tüzyılmaz, provided details of this year’s market prices. First-grade figs are sold for around 120 TL per kilogram, second-grade figs for 60–70 TL, and third-grade figs, known among producers as “baby” figs, for around 50 TL.


Tüzyılmaz said that once all grades were taken into account, the average income per kilogram had fallen to between 67 and 70 TL. Last year, she said, first-grade figs sold for 210 TL per kilogram and second-grade figs for between 120 and 130 TL.


Twenty kilos of figs do not cover a day’s wage


Tüzyılmaz said producers were being squeezed by rising fertiliser, diesel and labor costs, while Tariş had still not announced a base price despite the season nearing its end. She said this had deepened uncertainty in the market.


Tüzyılmaz described fig production as an extremely demanding process, involving labor-intensive stages such as shaking the trees, harvesting the fruit, drying it in greenhouses, grading it and selecting the figs individually. She added that producers had to sell at least 20 kilograms of figs simply to cover the daily wage of one agricultural worker.


Producers face market pressures and geothermal plants


Aydın has been a centre of commercial fig production for thousands of years. Even the fig’s scientific name, Ficus carica, derives from Caria (Karya), the ancient name of the region.


Another problem affecting fig production in Aydın is geothermal power plants. Producers and local campaigners have linked geothermal operations to declining yields, while environmental and public health concerns associated with the plants have also intensified across the province.


An environmental impact assessment approving three new geothermal wells on land used for vegetable cultivation has been issued in the Germencik district of Aydın. Leaks and pipeline ruptures at geothermal facilities have brought agricultural production close to a standstill, while it has been reported that the cancer rate in the district has reached four times the national average.


Source: Yeni Yaşam

title: Director Ismail Güneş: Peace should be at the heart of cinema and art - Part One
content:
As the Peace and Democratic Society Process enters its second year, debates surrounding the process in Turkey continue across different social and cultural spheres. Artists share their views and criticisms of the process with the public through their statements and works.


Director Ismail Güneş, who brought the torture experienced in Turkey following the 12 September 1980 military coup to the screen with his movie 

Where the Rose Ends,

 approaches the Kurdish issue from a different perspective in his latest movie,

One of the Unplastered Houses

. Director Güneş spoke to ANF not only about his own cinema, but also about the current state of political cinema in Turkey and the role of art in the peace process.


Discussing the socialization of violence in his movies, Güneş said that violence emerges at the point where an individual loses the ability to establish a civilized and philosophical bond with “the other,” and continued: “Because violence is a primitive form of ‘imposing truth’ that begins where an individual loses the ability to establish a civilized and philosophical bond with the other, emerging at the moment when words run out. As I have tried to show in films such as ‘Where the Rose Ends’ and ‘Where the Fire Fell,’ violence hiding behind sacred armor such as tradition, custom, or ideology is in fact a tragic manifestation of our collective social memory’s inability to confront past traumas and the vertical forms of oppression imposed by the system, and of its loss of the feeling of compassion.


Within this culture of power that flows from the top down and is sustained by impunity, people attempt to prove the agency they have lost and their shaken sense of existence only by establishing authority over an ‘other’ weaker than themselves—that is, by aestheticizing and legitimizing violence.


Therefore, the reflection of violence across every sphere is connected to society being in a state of moral and philosophical decay. The only way to break this structural vicious cycle is a cultural and artistic revolution that will confront human beings with their own brutality, reminding them not of the monster in the mirror but of that noble conscience and ontological compassion they have forgotten deep within their souls.”


Violence becomes institutionalized because of lack of education 


Güneş also addressed his decision to portray the socialization of violence in his films through poor people, explaining this choice in terms of the impact of poverty on an individual’s dignity, existential resilience, and moral values. He continued: “The reason I portray the socialization of violent tendencies, particularly through poor and conservative sections of the population is that I see poverty not merely as an economic deprivation but as the most radical ontological sphere of existence in which a person’s dignity, existential resilience, and moral values are tested. Because the poor person living under the vertical pressure of capitalist mechanisms and macro systems conducts their struggle to survive and realize themselves face-to-face with the most naked and raw reality of life, far removed from the intellectual masks of the bourgeoisie.


At this social level, violence becomes institutionalized beyond the madness brought about by economic desperation; it becomes institutionalized when an individual trapped within the narrow boundaries of lack of education, helpless anger toward the system, and traditional codes resorts to bodily domination—the last primitive language remaining to them—in order to protect their battered honor and sphere of power.


Therefore, when I tell the story of poor people, I position them not as an aestheticized form of misery or as a focus of crime, but as a mirror in which the structural injustice produced by the system turns into a spiral of violence. My aim is not to blame poverty; on the contrary, it is to seek the philosophical possibility of remaining human—to explore how that ancient conscience and compassion within a person can endure despite all the brutality and feudal oppression—and to remind society, through this unsettling reality, of the profound responsibility it has forgotten.”


Cinemas showing my movie were threatened

Where the Rose Ends

title: KCK commemorates Mam Jalal Talabani
content:
The Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) commemorated Jalal Talabani, founder of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the first Kurdish president of Iraq, on the ninth anniversary of his death. In its statement, the KCK particularly highlighted Talabani’s role in the Kurdish freedom struggle, his efforts toward national unity, and his commitment to a political solution to the Kurdish question.


The KCK statement on Saturday reads as follows:


“Today marks the ninth anniversary of the death of President Mam (Uncle) Jalal Talabani, founder of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan and the first Kurdish president of the Federal Republic of Iraq. As an intellectual, revolutionary, Peshmerga, commander and accomplished Kurdish politician, President Mam Jalal Talabani shaped more than 50 years of the history of the freedom struggle of Kurdistan and the Kurdish people. Throughout numerous phases of the national and political struggle, he achieved significant gains for the Kurdish people.


Mam Jalal’s work and struggle for the freedom of Kurdistan and the Kurdish people were not limited to Southern Kurdistan. Whenever necessary, he supported and participated in the armed struggle in other parts of Kurdistan. Whenever required, he assumed a leading role in politics and diplomacy in pursuit of a solution and peace.


President Mam Jalal Talabani played an important role in the struggle and efforts for the national unity of the Kurdish people. In this regard, the close friendship and ties between Mamoste Ibrahim Ahmed, Leader Abdullah Öcalan, and President Mam Jalal developed into a significant force in efforts to achieve Kurdish national unity. The establishment of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) was one of the outcomes of this friendship and solidarity.


President Mam Jalal also played a significant role in efforts to resolve the Kurdish question in other parts of Kurdistan. In particular, his mediation between Leader Öcalan and then-Turkish President Turgut Özal initiated a process of dialogue with the Turkish state.


Even after Leader Öcalan was abducted and handed over to the Turkish state as a result of an international conspiracy, President Mam Jalal continued these efforts. Before falling ill in 2012, he was preparing, together and in consultation with prominent figures from Southern Kurdistan and internationally renowned personalities, a congress intended to launch an initiative for the freedom of Leader Öcalan under the name “Mandela Project.”


Today, 34 years later, we once again find ourselves in a period of dialogue between the Turkish state and Leader Öcalan and are engaged in the process for peace and a democratic society. At this particular moment, President Mam Jalal’s skills and experience are needed more than ever for the success of this process.


Therefore, to struggle for the democratic unity of the people of Kurdistan, for the freedom of Leader Öcalan, and for a democratic solution to the Kurdish question in Northern Kurdistan also means preserving the legacy of struggle left by President Mam Jalal and working to realize the hopes and goals for which he himself fought.


On the ninth anniversary of his death, we respectfully honor the memory of President Mam Jalal. We renew our promise and pledge to preserve the national legacy of Kurdistan’s freedom struggle and its aspirations for peace and freedom.”

author: Miguel Enrique Stédile
title: How Trump Tries to Decide the Elections in Brazil
content:
On the last Friday before the first round of Brazil’s presidential elections, the U.S. embassy and consulates in the country remained closed, following a generic order from the State Department regarding ‘security concerns.’ Elections in Brazil proceed peacefully; there are no civil conflicts or military threats, no records of political violence above normal levels, nor any threats to American citizens or diplomatic structures. But the decision, followed solely and inexplicably by the Australian embassy, is part of a set of actions by Washington to attempt to interfere in the Brazilian elections.

The actions began more than a year ago, when the United States linked increased tariffs on items imported from Brazil to the ongoing process to try former President Jair Bolsonaro for an attempted coup d’état. The relationship between political pressure to prevent the conviction of an ally and economic measures was publicized by the White House itself, as well as used to persecute the Supreme Court Justice responsible for the trial, blocking financial movements in the U.S. and preventing his entry into the country, and with ministers of the Lula da Silva government. A document delivered to Brazilian diplomats presented 21 demands to the Brazilian government including, among them, guaranteeing freedom for what the U.S. calls ‘political dissidents’; advantages for the U.S. in accessing Brazilian critical minerals; and not regulating big techs.

The list of demands is instructive for understanding why the Brazilian elections are so important to Trump. Brazil is rich in minerals, especially those fundamental to the technology industry, used in chip manufacturing and data centre installation; it also has numerous sources of renewable energy, especially hydroelectric and solar; it is beginning to prospect a new oil region in the Amazon area, near the blocks explored by ExxonMobil in Suriname and Guyana. Furthermore, Brazil’s largest trading partner is China, and both are part of the BRICS bloc. Brazil is also not a signatory to the Shield of the Americas, the contemporary version of Operation Condor, and chose the Chinese initiative for AI cooperation instead of the U.S. proposal. Additionally, on the map of South America, Brazil is one of the few countries not governed by a Trump ally. And it is not a small country, but a regional leader with presence in international articulations.

Therefore, one understands not only the economic and public actions, but also the clandestine ones unleashed from Washington. On 30 September, the British newspaper The Guardian revealed that Donald Trump’s government allocated US$1 million to a project called ‘Combating Weaponized Litigation and Censorship in Brazil,’ aimed at funding civil society organizations that challenge the actions of the Supreme Federal Court. The funds are part of a package of 43 grants totalling US$176.9 million, destined for conservative projects in various countries. The same State Department that remains silent about its own foreign influence scheme now sponsors the ‘defence of freedom of expression’ in Brazil. Before that, in July, Trump tried to send two State Department officials to meetings with authorities and civil society entities to question the electronic voting machines used in Brazilian elections. This is one of the main narratives of the Brazilian far-right that, despite having elected a President and most parliamentarians, insists that elections are fraudulent and illegal. This was, in fact, one of the motivations for the attacks on the Presidential Palace and Supreme Federal Court buildings on January 8, 2023, by Bolsonaro supporters, which would be the civil spark for a frustrated coup d’état.

Another common mechanism of U.S. interference is the use of non-governmental organizations. The Rockbridge Network — a network of conservative funders founded in 2019 by U.S. Vice-President J.D. Vance and businessman Chris Buskirk — tried to establish itself in Brazil with a plan that included creating a Technology Council of 23 businessmen to directly advise Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign. Of the 23 executives listed, 19 are foreigners. Brazilian law is clear: candidates and parties cannot receive, directly or indirectly, money, goods, or services from foreign entities or governments.

Funders of the Rockbridge network are the Rebekah Mercer, conservative megadonor and heiress of the Mercer hedge fund fortune, Peter Thiel, a fascist billionaire tech investor and …

title: Barry Pateman - Tensions in Anarchism
content:
Author

: Barry Pateman

Title

: Tensions in Anarchism

Notes

: ‘Anarchist Tension #1-#4’ From

Mob action against the state: collected speeches from the Bay Area Anarchist Book Fair

 (AK Press, 2002), ISBN 1902593510. Recorded by DJ Slo-Mo and Rad, compiled, edited and produced by DJ Slo-Mo of Entartete Kunst with assistance from RK of AK Press. Now out of print.

https://web.archive.org/web/20221129074326/https://www.akpress.org/mobactionagainstthestate.html


 This is a transcript of a talk by Barry Pateman at the Bay Area Anarchist Bookfair in San Francisco. It shows something of his approach to anarchism, and the history of anarchism, and mentions some of the important people and experiences in his life. Barry spoke with passion and a greater concern for people than abstract ideas. As you’ll see, his humour (and swearing) were always self-deprecating: ‘Thank you for your time. I’m really sorry that you’ve got nothing else to do.’


 I just want to talk about some tensions I think that us as anarchists or people sympathetic to anarchism need to try and consider. ’Cause… I suddenly realised last night when I was laying in bed and just looking at the ceiling that I’m tending to become a bookfair groupie. There’s a bookfair in London. I go to a bookfair in London. It’s an anarchist bookfair, I sell anarchist books. I come to San Francisco. And I’m really talking, I guess, about how we as each other, as a group, as an organisation, as people who share a similar – what Galleani called the ideal, the dream – How we gonna make that real? And so, there are some tensions I think we have to face.


 The first tension is ourselves and our history. There

is

 a history of anarchism. But within that history of anarchism, there are things and people who have been forgotten. Now, with the Kate Sharpley Library, we have two reasons to exist. One is, yes, flowers for the fallen. We printed a pamphlet called

Anarchists against Franco

* where there were twenty anarchists who’d been killed between 1942 and 1960 in guerrilla warfare against Franco. And Frank Torres who wrote it in Spanish says – and I couldn’t agree more – it doesn’t matter whether you think libertarian communism, anarchism will happen, it doesn’t matter whether you think it’s silly, it doesn’t even matter if you think you’re cleverer than those anarchists who went out there. What matters is how

dare

 we forget them? How

dare

 you and I sitting in this room not know about them? How dare we forget their bravery and their courage when they went over the mountains against stupidly impossible odds for that dream? So, any anarchist, any person sympathetic to us has to be aware of our history, not the history of ideas, that’s something I’ll talk about in a second, but simply the people who have suffered physically and emotionally for our belief.

You’ll

 know some of them, nah? But we’ll also not know a lot of them and one of the things we must do is to revise history, to give them that dignity of that memory.


 And the second thing of course is that if we’re canny we learn from history. We have to

learn

. Look, I’ve been an anarchist for thirty years, so you’re not going to learn much from me because we haven’t got that far. But I do know what’ve we done wrong. I do think I’ve got an idea that what we’ve done has gone wrong. But we have to learn from our history. We can’t just pretend that we exist now and that really that those people were a bit strange or not like us because they spoke a different language. If we’re not guided by our history, we have no foundation, nothing, except living on our wits. So that I think is the first tension, how we discover and make our history come alive for all of us.


 The second tension is, is between us as anarchists or sympathetic who are clever buggers ’cause we are… and ordinary people… who aren’t. I don’t mean racist, nasty people, I mean ordinary people who get up every morning, go to work, watch telly, watch baseball, go to bed… yeah? I mean those people. And you know what, there’s a lot more of them than us.


 OK, so one of the things that’s disturbed me lately is there’s been a trend in anarchism to think that ordinary people are sort of fucking stupid. Yeah? They’re not clever or, really, they’re the problem. No, they’re not the problem. Look, every time there’s been some type of thing kicking off, starting, some insurrection, its come from dispossessed, poor people, ordinary people. And if we’re not there, if …

title: DFG commemorates Nagihan Akarsel on the fourth anniversary of her killing
content:
In a written statement, the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) commemorated Nagihan Akarsel, a journalist and member of the Jineology Research Center who was killed on 4 October 2022, and called for those responsible to be identified and brought to justice.


“This year, as her colleagues and those who have followed in her footsteps, we once again call for the real perpetrators to be exposed and prosecuted,” the statement said.


“On the fourth anniversary of the killing of Nagihan Akarsel, one of the pioneers of the Free Press, we remember her with respect, love, and an enduring sense of longing,” the DFG said, adding: “Nagihan Akarsel once said 'I am an adventurer; I do not settle in one place.'


The struggle for freedom that she began within herself has today become a path for millions of women. Women, journalists who have followed in her footsteps, and the students she taught are keeping Nagihan Akarsel’s dreams alive through the struggle for women’s freedom. Nagihan Akarsel’s pen continues to write at every level of the Free Media. We once again reaffirm our commitment to preserving the legacy she left us and keeping her dreams alive.”


Nagihan Akarsel


Nagihan Akarsel (Zîlan) was born in 1976 in the village of Gölyazı in Cihanbeyli district of Konya province in central Turkey. The Kurdish name of the village is Xelîkan. 


Between 2001 and 2007, she was imprisoned for her political activity at universities. After her release from prison, she worked as an editor and reporter at the Dicle News Agency between 2008 and 2014. During this period, she also followed the lectures of Hacettepe University Women’s Studies Department in order to deepen her understanding of women’s liberation. She took part in the establishment of the first women’s press agency, JINHA. For years, she worked as a reporter in the Kurdish press, chasing news. She was a hard worker, a teacher, a friend and comrade in the development of Kurdish women’s journalism.


She answered the call of Jineology (Women's Science), to which Abdullah Öcalan attaches great importance, at the highest level in both its academic and institutional dimensions. When the process of institutionalization of Jineology began, she took part in the work of the Jineology Academy. She worked hard during the establishment of the Jineology journal. She not only served as a member of the editorial board of the journal, but also constantly fed it with her articles.  She never stopped knocking on new doors to transform the Jineology magazine into a women’s freedom platform.


She conducted research and educational activities in many areas of Bakur, Bashur and Rojava (North, South and West Kurdistan). She educated thousands of people and wrote for many newspapers and magazines. Everywhere she went, she was a beacon of light, especially for young people. Children and mothers moved close to her. After 2018, she continued her sociological studies in Afrin and Shengal, to be published in a book. As someone in love with the culture of Hewreman and the resistance culture of Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan) women, she continued her research in this field, but she always felt a loss at not being able to go to Rojhilat.


From 2019 until the date of her assassination, she worked tirelessly for the development of Jineology studies in Bashur, South Kurdistan. Although she had only just learned the Sorani dialect, she gave dozens of courses and seminars on JineoJineologyoji in Bashur, and organized Jineology camps with young people.

title: Prof. Doğu Ergil: A search for a new order has begun in Turkey
content:
Recent developments in the relationship between the economy and politics in Turkey have sparked debate over whether the country is entering a new political era. Alongside the fund investigation and the reopening or renewed discussion of certain cases that previously generated public controversy, debates over legal arrangements concerning the resolution of the Kurdish question are also being viewed as possible signs of change in the structure of the state and politics.


Political scientist Prof. Dr. Doğu Ergil spoke to ANF about what these developments mean in terms of the relationship between the state, politics and capital.


‘The beginning of a transformation’


Stating that the developments in Turkey mark the beginning of a transformation, Ergil pointed out that the current system of governance is no longer capable of sustaining the country:


“It may be overly optimistic, but it is certainly the beginning of a transformation. Why am I certain? First, because the methods being employed in Turkey, the system of administration, the understanding of law and the concept of citizenship can no longer sustain the country. Crises are erupting in every area, and these crises show us that the existing mode of governance and the methods being used are no longer adequate and are no longer functioning.


What kind of order are we going to establish from now on? In other words, adherence to the law, adherence to the Constitution and, above all, the rule of law… We are experiencing a concentration in which democracy becomes ever more centralized, manifested and ultimately personalized. How will this come to an end, and how will this personalization and arbitrariness be replaced by institutionalization? In other words, how will institutions prevail?


As this latest crisis has also demonstrated, a search has begun for a new order that will replace a system in which wealth creation and enrichment are achieved through political favoritism and connections with one in which prosperity is achieved through production, merit, accomplishment, hard work and honest conduct. But how will this happen?


Then, of course, there is the issue of equality. There is the question of equality and how legitimacy is produced… Is it being imposed through force, pressure and intimidation? Or is it generated through acceptance and voluntary consent? We are living through a period in which all of these questions are being debated.


Much will be required before these issues can be clarified. Above all, the major question before us is how a new order will be established through society’s reactions, preferences and political choices.”


‘The different manifestations of a structural problem must be examined’


Doğu Ergil stated that it would not be sufficient to assess the re-emergence of past events in Turkey solely through the relationship between capital and politics, arguing that the different manifestations of a structural problem must be examined. Recalling incidents from the past that have never been fully clarified, he continued:


“Rather than evaluating this in terms of the relationship between capital and politics, we need to look at the different manifestations of a structural problem. There used to be unsolved killings, as you know. Even today, some mothers are still asking what happened to their children. There are many things that have never been explained. Take what happened in Roboski, for example. What happened? Who did it? Why did it happen? Who was responsible? Who made the decisions? We do not know.


Most recently, an investigation has been launched into what happened in the Muhsin Yazıcıoğlu case and into how and why Kaşif Kozinoğlu was killed and who was responsible. This is an indication that the state may be beginning to fulfill a duty incumbent upon it. I am not saying that this duty is being fulfilled—you can see that for yourselves.


In other words, investigating past mistakes and crimes is just as important for a state as building its future. A state must have the capacity to confront the mistakes it made in the past and also to successfully carry out the positive actions it intends to take in the future. This is what we call state capacity.


In Turkey, the state appeared to be far from demonstrating this capacity. It may now be making an effort to develop that capacity.”


‘The current system is unsustainable’

author: Mada Masr
title: Security prosecution detains Abu Emaira for 15 days, whereabouts of 5 other Matsda2sh journalists unknown
content:
Journalist Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira has been issued a 15-day detention order by the Supreme State Security Prosecution, Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights lawyer Islam Salama told Mada Masr.


Abu Emaira was presented before prosecutors for the first time at 10 pm on Saturday night, five days after security authorities launched an arrest campaign targeting him and five of his colleagues from the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh.


The whereabouts of the other five Matsda2sh journalists are still unknown as of time of publishing.


Salama told Mada Masr he attended with Abu Emaira the investigation session which began at 10 pm on Saturday evening and continued for over 10 hours. Prosecutors questioned Abu Emaira during the session on three criminal charges: joining a terrorist group, publishing and broadcasting false news, and using a social media platform to these ends.


The investigation was established as Supreme State Security Case 8083/2026.


Prosecutors questioned Abu Emaria about several items published on Matsda2sh’s platform. They asked how topics are selected for coverage and questioned him regarding the purpose and aim of publication, EIPR head Hossam Bahgat told Mada Masr.


Before his arrival at the prosecution premises, Abu Emaira had been held at National Security Agency premises for the five preceding days, his lawyer learned during the investigation session. His extended detention without being brought before prosecutors was done with reference to Article 40 of the counterterrorism law and on the basis of a custody decision issued by the Supreme State Security Prosecution.


Bahgat told Mada Masr that the Interior Ministry acted in violation of the counterterrorism law in prohibiting Abu Emaira from communicating with his family or lawyers and in failing to inform them of his whereabouts.


During the investigation, EIPR requested the prosecution permit Abu Emaria to visit a hospital, as he suffers with a number of chronic illnesses, Bahgat said. He added that the prosecution had allowed Abu Emaira access to his medications.


EIPR demanded the public prosecutor drop all charges brought against Abu Emaira and the rest of the arrested Matsda2sh team, citing lack of evidence.


EIPR also demanded the immediate release of all the journalists and the dismissal of all cases in which they are accused, confirming that they have not committed any crime and that they carried out their journalistic work professionally. Bahgat described their continued detention as an assault on press freedom.


Security authorities initiated an arrest campaign on Monday, arresting all of Abu Emaira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal within 24 hours.


The whereabouts of all of the journalists remained unknown until Abu Emaira appeared before the prosecution Saturday evening. The Interior Ministry published a statement on Thursday announcing their arrest and claiming that the platform was a “[Muslim] Brotherhood cell.” The statement’s publication came alongside a widespread media campaign reproducing the same claims, while a report published by the privately owned Al-Masry Al-Youm newspaper claimed that a prosecution order for their remand detention had been issued, a claim the Supreme State Security Prosecution later denied in conversation with lawyers representing the journalists.

The post

Security prosecution detains Abu Emaira for 15 days, whereabouts of 5 other Matsda2sh journalists unknown

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

.

author: Katja Diehl
title: Zwölf Motorräder, ein Aufzug und der beste Kaffee am Bahnhof. Meine Delegation nach Graubünden.
content:
Ich stehe an einer Kreuzung in Chur. Zwölf Motorräder rollen vorbei, ich rieche sie. Und plötzlich stehen wir in einem der schönsten Panoramen des Kantons und hören den Verkehr. Die Felswand gegenüber reflektiert den Schall wie ein Spiegel.


Am letzten Abend meiner Delegationsreise nach Graubünden ziehe ich das Fazit: Die Verkehrswende ist keine Exceltabelle. Sie ist eine Entscheidung, die vor Ort getroffen wird. Jemand, der dranbleibt.


Das Format der Delegationsreisen wirkt nachhaltig. Ich möchte dieses Format verstetigen und Menschen an Regionen heranführen, in denen Mobilität nicht gleichbedeutend mit „AUTO!” ist, sondern „ich bin mobil, egal, was ich gerade wähle”. Dieses Mal ging es nach Chur, dem Regionalzentrum von Mittelbünden. Unser Thema: Wie kann der Verkehr im Kanton bis in die Dörfer hinein aufeinander abgestimmt werden? E-Mobilität, Bikesharing, Radinfrastruktur, ÖPNV.


In Deutschland erhalten Gemeinden 7,5 Prozent der Einkommensteuer. In Graubünden bleiben etwa 60 Prozent der direkten Steuern in der Gemeinde. Der Rest geht zum Kanton und zum Bund. Das bedeutet: Wer hier mobil sein will, muss mit der Gemeinde reden. Mit den Verantwortlichen vor Ort, die sich auskennen. Denn die Gemeinde trägt Schulen, Sozialdienste, Straßen, Feuerwehr – alles. Und sie entscheidet, was machbar ist.


Werner Glünkin sagte sinngemäß: „Hier sind die Gemeinden autonome Republiken.” Ohne ein gutes Verhältnis zur Gemeinde geht nichts. Das ist eine der wichtigsten Erkenntnisse, die ich auf dieser Reise gewonnen habe.


Und ja, das macht Dinge langsamer. Man muss mitsprechen. Man muss sich einigen. Aber so werden sie auch echt. Denn die Menschen, die entscheiden, sind dieselben, die jeden Tag durch den Ort fahren.


Tourismus als Türöffner


Der spannendste Hebel, den ich dort gesehen habe, war nicht technologischer Natur. Sondern organisatorisch.


Chur liegt an der Rhätischen Bahn, die zum UNESCO-Welterbe gehört. Tausende Menschen kommen jedes Jahr nur für diese Bahn. Doch der Bahnhof ist schlecht erschlossen. Die Viamala-Schlucht liegt einen Kilometer entfernt und ist vom Bahnhof aus kaum erreichbar. Es gibt keinen Aufzug, stattdessen wird man von einer Elektroschrottannahmestelle begrüßt.


Die Lösung? Ein Elektro-Tuk-Tuk. Es ist klein, flexibel und niedrigschwellig. Es bringt einen vom Bahnhof in die Schlucht, zum Kaffeetrinken ins Dorf und zurück zum Zug. Eine Stunde Wertschöpfung, die heute verloren geht.


Der Tourismusdirektor Rheto ist hier der Multiplikator. Er braucht bestimmte Dinge für seine Gäste. Wenn Politik, Region, Naturpark Beverin und Tourismus zusammenarbeiten – über eine Plattform namens „E-Mobility Circle“ –, dann sprechen alle endlich über dasselbe, wenn sie von „Mobilität“ reden. Das ist lokale Wertschöpfung, die auch ohne Auto funktioniert.


Direkte Demokratie in Aktion.


Am selben Tag, an dem wir uns unterhalten haben, wurde abgestimmt. Zwei nationale, eine kantonale und zwei kommunale Vorlagen.


Eine davon war die Alpeninitiative. Ein verfassungsrechtliches Ausbauverbot für die Gotthard-Achse. Schwerverkehr auf die Schiene. Keine neue Röhre für gut eine Milliarde Franken.


Das ist direkte Demokratie in der Praxis. Sie ist eine Realität, die Entscheidungen blockiert, beschleunigt oder umlenkt. Und die man respektieren muss, wenn man in der Schweiz arbeiten will.


Was fehlt in Deutschland? Die Umsetzung. Ein Plan. Eine Vision.


Die Umsetzung ist nicht das Konzept. Die Kür ist die Umsetzung.


Und dafür braucht es Geld, politische Willensbildung und Menschen, die vor Ort bleiben und dranbleiben.

author: Unknown
title: Эррико Малатеста - Вопрос честности. МЫ И СОЦИАЛИСТЫ
content:
Автор

: Эррико Малатеста

Название

: Вопрос честности. МЫ И СОЦИАЛИСТЫ

Дата

: 22 апреля 1920

Дополнительная информация

: Статья была написана в разгар "красного двухлетия" в Италии, когда, казалось, Социальная Революция не за горами. Через полгода эти мечты развеятся и наступит "черное двухлетие", с господством фашистских банд Муссолини.

Источник

: Umanita Nova, год 1-й, №47


Вопрос честности

 МЫ И СОЦИАЛИСТЫ


 Все наши читатели, все, кто с нами знаком, знают, с какой страстью мы желаем и проповедуем согласие между революционными рабочими, то есть

единый фронт

 пролетариата против буржуазии и против правительства.


 И всё же на каждом шагу, как только представляется случай сделать что-нибудь, мы оказываемся в конфликте с деятелями социалистической партии.


 Стоит объясниться ещё раз.


 Мы революционеры, потому что верим, что только революция, революция насильственная, может разрешить социальный вопрос. Мы верим, что в нынешний период революцию можно совершить легче, чем когда-либо, и что откладывать её – значит утомлять рабочих, которые находятся в состоянии душевного напряжения, не могущего длиться вечно, значит давать время правительству лучше организовать репрессивные силы, а буржуазии – вновь оправиться. Мы верим, кроме того, что революция есть акт воли – воли индивидов и воли масс; что для успеха ей нужны определённые объективные условия, но что она не приходит необходимо, фатально в силу одних лишь экономических и политических факторов.


 Есть ли у социалистических вождей охота делать революцию?


 Среди них есть такие, кто откровенно называет себя реформистами. Они говорят, что революцию нельзя сделать, потому что пролетариат не созрел, потому что нельзя было бы обеспечить снабжение, потому что не хватает сырья, потому что вооружённая сила правительства такова, что было бы безумием идти против неё, и так далее.


 Это мнение, которое мы считаем ошибочным, но которое в конечном счёте можно отстаивать с хорошими аргументами. И мы не только не питаем никакой неприязни к тем, кто его исповедует, но даже охотно признаём, что их критика крайне полезна, чтобы побудить революционеров усилить свою подготовку и позаботиться – больше, чем они, быть может, это делают, – о проблемах, которые встанут остро и грозно на следующий день после материальной победы пролетариата.


 Есть и другие, которые часто суть те же самые, кто называет себя

фаталистами

 и верит, что революция созревает сама собой; что буржуазное общество увядает и разлагается естественным образом и будет заменено коммунистическим обществом в силу необходимости вещей; что человеческая воля не значит ничего и не может ни изменить, ни ускорить, ни задержать ход вещей. С этой логикой они затем ведут пропаганду или занимаются какой-либо деятельностью – об этом сейчас нет нужды рассуждать; но если они не выдают себя за революционеров, нам остаётся лишь вести с ними академические споры, когда у нас есть время и охота. Если же на практике они забывают, что они фаталисты, и работают для революции, мы с удовольствием прощаем все их философские и доктринёрские причуды.


 Но есть социалистические вожди, которые называют себя революционерами и даже повстанцами на митингах, вожди, которые подогревают пламенное желание революции, волнующее сегодня пролетариат... а затем, как только представляется случай, льют воду на огонь, который сами же зажгли. Они говорят о военной подготовке, о группах действия и так далее; а потом, как только люди начинают всерьёз относиться к их речам, они вспоминают, что не хватает хлеба, не хватает угля, не хватает… каучука.


 Именно с этими последними мы в конфликте.


 Мы всегда готовы заключить союз с теми, кто действительно революционер – революционер в том смысле, что считает возможной и хочет осуществить революцию немедленно, при первом благоприятном случае.


 У других мы просим честно высказать своё мнение и не выдавать себя за революционеров, чтобы затем отступить и предать, когда появится подходящий случай.


Эррико Малатеста.

title: À nos enfants et lycéens
content:
Des représentants de parents d'élèves inquiets nous ont transmis cette adresse aux élèves, à leurs professeurs mais aussi aux ministres qui orchestrent la répression du mouvement lycéen. Une analyse de la situation autant qu'un témoignage.


À nos enfants et lycéens


Merci pour tout. L'audace, le courage et la détermination.


Merci de nous rappeler qu'il n'y a rien à attendre. Nous avons nous-même tellement attendu que nous savons ce qu'il en coûte

à la fin.


Attendre la fin de la journée, la fin de la semaine, le début du mois, le rappel de la CAF. Attendre que ça se tasse, attendre des jours meilleurs, attendre les élections, attendre le bus, le métro. Attendre d'enfin se coucher. De toujours se coucher.


À vous aussi on vous a dit d'attendre. La fin de la journée, le début des vacances, les résultats de Parcoursup. Attendre une formation, pourquoi pas un taf, d'être indépendants et de découvrir que c'est le contraire d'être libres. Attendre que la vie commence là-même où elle finit.


Vous avez vraiment bien fait de cesser d'attendre.


Bravo pour l'humour, les déguisements, les feux d'artifices, la solidarité et tout ce qu'on a vu dans les rues.


Le monde qu'on vous laisse est une ruine, l'avenir qu'on vous prépare un cauchemar, et vous parvenez encore à vous amuser. Vous êtes la meilleure version de nous-mêmes, l'addition de tout ce que l'on a raté, de tout ce à quoi nous avons renoncé.


Vous le savez mais c'est important de vous le répéter. Nous sommes aussi très inquiets. Mais nous le serions davantage encore si vous acceptiez le monde tel qu'il est.


Aux professeurs, surveillants et chefs d'établissements


Mardi, vous étiez en grève pour réclamer de meilleures conditions de travail. Vous avez marché, défilé et scandé et puis vous êtes rentrés. Le gouvernement n'a même pas fait l'effort de vous mépriser.


En deux jours de blocages vos élèves ont déclenché une cellule de crise à l'Élysée, la panique sur les plateaux télé et la fermeture d'une grande partie des lycées français. Il y a une leçon à en tirer.


Toutes leurs revendications, vous les connaissez et vous les partagez : les classes surchargées, les collègues pas remplacés, les locaux insalubres et les couvertures de survies sur les fenêtres pour ne pas cuire dès le mois de mai. Et Parcoursup évidemment, vous en connaissez par cœur les méfaits et les injustices. Cette sale petite machine de sélection et de mise sous pression qui pèse chaque jour sur vos élèves autant que sur vous. Pédagogie de l'humiliation. Et pourtant vos élèves sont venus vous le rappeler : rien de ce qui a été fait ne peut être défait.


Merci à celles et ceux parmi vous qui ont rejoint les blocages, soutenu leurs élèves. L'équation est simple : vous n'avez objectivement rien à perdre et tout à gagner, à commencer par le fait de ne plus vous laisser,

vous aussi

, humilier.


Si vous refusiez

sincèrement

 votre condition commune, ce serait une autre histoire : c'est moins facile pour un gouvernement d'étrangler un prof de Math ou de tirer au LBD dans la tête de la prof de Français. Peut-être qu'alors tout le monde suivrait.


À Laurent Nuñez, Edouard Geffray et aux préfets


C'est sous vos ordres que depuis plusieurs jours, la police harcèle des enfants. C'est sous vos ordres qu'ils ont été fracassés, traînés sur le sol, étranglés, dégommés à bout portant au LBD. Vous n'avez pas seulement voulu les blesser, vous avez tout fait pour les humilier.


1949 lycéens interpellés, combien de policiers inquiétés ? Quelles leçons en tirer ?


Et pourtant, vous vous enferrez dans le mensonge et l'irresponsabilité.


Il faut vraiment ne pas avoir mis un pied devant un lycée pour croire que la France insoumise aurait la moindre responsabilité dans cette éruption de la jeunesse. Il faut être particulièrement mal informé pour s'imaginer que des « proxys d'ultragauche » téléguideraient souterrainement les poubelles entassées devant les établissements. Seulement et salement, vous mentez.


Alors que les élèves réclament des profs, des moyens et un peu de considération, vous appelez la police à se « désinhiber de l'usage proportionné de la force », quand des syndicats de police réclament de pouvoir leur tirer dessus au LBD vous mettez en garde les préfets contre toute « instruction contraire localement ». On n'invente ou n'extrapole rien, on vous lit dans

Le Monde

 du 2 octobre 2026. Vous appelez et encouragez la violence contre nos enfants. Calfeutrés au milieu de vos bureaux dorés …

author: Unknown
title: This is the exact kind of insufferable I want to highlight here.
content:
A lot of people become insufferable when you point out that “You need to learn a dozen new 6-syllable words derived from Greek to participate in our conversation” and “our entire community is white college-graduates and all our efforts to diversify have failed” constantly overlap for really obvious reasons.

#you would think those 6 syllable words were being taken away

Well, yes, kinda. I’m not cancelling words but I am challenging people to think of possible easier words.

If the best thing we can come up with for “stop doing man/woman and cis/trans binaries!” is ‘exorsexism’, we’re shit at accessible communication. Sorry, not sorry.

If the Germans can call combined oral contraceptives 'anti-baby-pills’, then we can decide to come up with simpler, more intuitive and easier-to-remember words for the concepts that we want a lot of people of all backgrounds to understand.

So many replies and responses are essentially versions of “oh so you want us to reduce language and only use stupid words” and the actual point OP is making is — know your audience.

Creating jargon is absolutely fine. Having new words to describe complex sociological issues is absolutely fine. But MOST people aren’t at a place to intuitively understand jargon. And so if you’re trying to create a mass politic for the left, do you want to sound ‘smart’ or do you want to build a coalition? Because if you want to coalition, you have to know who you’re talking to and what words will be effective and how your message can come across.

Otherwise you’re just being Sheldon Cooper from the Big Bang Theory, and you will turn people off not because you’re wrong, but because you are perceived as a know-it-all condescending prick (regardless of your intent).

It’s not just 'know your audience’. Having one set of words for the in-crowd and one set of words for everyone else would just amplify the effect where a lot of people just do not feel welcome in our spaces because they sound like white academia spaces. So I’m also saying: if we’re creating jargon, why are we constantly creating jargon by borrowing from the academic tradition of 'translate it to greek or latin and slap it all together into one word’? instead of thinking 'what word is easy to remember and easy to understand for the largest number of people’?

Antibabypille is six syllables, but most people would know what it means without anyone explaining the meaning, and after hearing it once or twice they would remember it and be able to use it in a sentence. That’s what good jargon could try to be like.

because language is an art as much as it is a tool. and frankly, because antibabypills has no flair and sounds stupid (not to mention anti is a Greek word, too). kill the max efficiency cop in your mind

This is the exact kind of insufferable I want to highlight here.

Like, get your head out of your ass and consider why you think words from the academic tradition are more aesthetically pleasing and what that says about biases on which cultural traditions are valuable and which lack 'flair’ or are 'stupid’.

I bet you think AAVE or rural accents in the workplace are 'unprofessional’.
